concepts.concept: Commander's intent: purpose, end state, limits, trip wires; four steps
concepts.name: Commander's intent

card.title: Commander's intent
idea: Commander's intent is a way of handing over a task so the other person can still act sensibly when the plan stops fitting the situation. The person delegating states the strategy, the reasons for it, how the decision was reached, and what is completely off the table. The person doing the work decides the rest.

The term comes from the military. Parrish writes that it was first applied to the Germans who were trying to defeat Napoleon. The Great Mental Models, Volume 2 adds the background: the German armies of that time had "linear tactics, iron discipline, blind obedience and intolerance of independent action". Troops were discouraged from asking for the reason behind an order, so they had nothing to draw on when Napoleon changed his tactics in the middle of a battle. The Germans then developed Auftragstaktik, which is what we now call commander's intent.
why: Parrish describes what happens without it. If employees cannot act until the boss approves, there is a single point of failure. When something happens to the boss, the business and the mission fail. With commander's intent each person can start and improvise while carrying out the plan, the leader stops being the bottleneck, and the team can hold each other to the goal without the leader in the room.

Doshi and McGregor quote a former US Army officer who calls the concept "the lifeblood of how we operate" and says that without it "you can't expect people on the ground to make decisions for themselves". They give an example of why the stated intent matters. If the intent of a mission is to demolish a target at all costs, soldiers will improvise in a very different way than if the intent is to keep good relations with the local people.

stories.text:
In 1805, off the coast of Spain, Napoleon had assembled a fleet of forty ships to invade England. Britain's Admiral Lord Nelson had thirty-three. His opponent had over 21 percent more ships and almost 24 percent more cannons. Navies normally formed two parallel lines and opened fire, for two reasons: the side-facing cannons meant a straight line avoided hitting friendly ships, and the admiral on the flagship gave orders by signal flags, so the whole fleet needed a line of sight to him. Such battles rarely ended decisively, and Nelson wanted, in his own words, to "make the business decisive".

He split the plan into two parts. The tactical part was simple and unconventional. His ships would approach the enemy head-on in two perpendicular lines and cut the enemy line into three pieces as quickly as possible, taking fire they could not return. Nelson would lead the charge himself and direct his own ship at the enemy flagship. The adaptive part came after that. He told each captain they had discretion over which targets to choose and how to attack them.

Nelson set this out in what the authors call the Trafalgar Memorandum. It admits that a fleet cannot be brought into a perfect line in variable winds and thick weather, that "something must be left to chance", and that if signals cannot be seen or understood, "no Captain can do very wrong if he places his Ship alongside that of an Enemy". During the battle he issued only three signals, all at the start, including "England expects that every man will do his duty". He was shot shortly after crippling the enemy flagship. The French lost twenty-two ships and the British lost none. French casualties are estimated at more than three times the British.

The authors add that Nelson did not arrive at this on the morning of the battle. Throughout his career he spent hours dining with each of his captains, sharing his ideas and listening to theirs. A contemporary wrote that the captains could "ascertain with precision what were the ideas and intentions of their commander without the aid of further instructions".

method.intro: Parrish lists four components. The first two belong to the senior commander and the last two to the subordinate.
steps: Formulate: decide the strategy.
Communicate: tell the team the strategy, the rationale, how you arrived at the decision, and the operational limits, meaning what is completely off the table.
Interpret: the people doing the work read the changing situation against the stated intent.
Implement: they act within the limits you set.

Before you start executing, ask three questions. Who needs to know my goals and the outcomes I am working toward? Do they know what the most important objective is? Do they know the positive and negative signs to look for, and what trip wires are attached to them?

limits: Parrish names two ways it fails. The first is the ego default: insisting that everything is done your way. Good leaders set what needs to get done and the parameters, and accept that others will do it differently. His test for the second is whether you can be away from the office for a week without things falling apart. He says that a leader who cannot be away is an incompetent communicator, and he rejects the idea that the team's dependence shows the leader is indispensable.

The Great Mental Models, Volume 2 lists four things a commander has to do: explain the rationale, set the operational limits, get feedback often, and recognise individual differences between subordinates. It also warns that flexibility cannot cost the commander the ability to synchronise events to carry out the strategy. Major Jim Storr, quoted in Primed to Perform, says mission command "can only work where both parties trust each other to act appropriately".

quotes.text: Tell them not just what to do, but why to do it, how you arrived at your decision, so they understand the context, as well as the boundaries for effective action—what is completely off the table.
quotes.source: Shane Parrish, Clear Thinking

quotes.text: Superiors should state a minimum of control measures, so as not to constrain subordinates' freedom of action.
quotes.source: Major Jim Storr, quoted in Primed to Perform

concepts.concept: Fix-Flex: name what's fixed and what's flexible before delegating
concepts.name: Fix and flex

card.title: Fix and flex
idea: Before you hand over a piece of work, ask yourself where your own views on it are fixed and where they are flexible. Then tell the other person about both. Webb's aim is to leave as much room as possible for the other person to shape the work, because even a little autonomy is more motivating than none. Where you do have a strong preference, say so.

Webb runs the Fix-Flex check through three steps. The what: define the deliverable, meaning its format, content, quality and timing. The how: ask the person how they plan to tackle it, then set the guardrails you care about and say where you do not mind. The when: agree on when you will next review progress.
why: If you ask for someone's views when you already know the answer you want, the conversation turns awkward. They answer, you frown, and they wonder why they said anything. That is why the approach has two sides: look for all the flex you can, and be honest about what is already fixed in your mind.

Webb also says leaders often forget to be clear about where the room is. Naming the areas where you truly do not mind what the person does earns you more room to be clear about the things you do care about, without eroding their autonomy. Her examples of unspoken assumptions: you may think a 'report' means a three-page memo while your colleague builds a twenty-page deck, or you may want forward-looking customer trends while they assume recent years.

stories.text:
Elena Sukacheva is CEO of UCAN, a company that makes functional food for endurance athletes. A team member she calls Stan suggested a sample-size package so customers could try the product for free. In earlier roles she might have led the project herself. Instead she said, "Great idea. Let's meet in three days to discuss it—could you bring me some thoughts on how it could work?" That was her first piece of flex.

When they met, she had firm views about what a well-scoped sample plan needs, because she had done this kind of launch dozens of times. Stan's plan had to say which products would get samples, who the audience would be, and how the samples would be distributed. Those questions were fixed. The answers were left entirely to him.

On the how, she set financial guardrails. Stan had to consider the assumed demand, the assumed conversion to sales of the full-sized product, his best estimate of the cost per sample, and the maximum the samples could cost for the program to make financial sense. That was her fixed list. Everything else was flex, and she told him he could try any assumptions and scenarios he liked.

She checked in as often as daily in the intense early stage. Once the project was running she went back to what she calls a 30,000-foot view, checking weekly or less, and dropped to a 'five-foot view' only when something was going badly, then pulled back up. Some of what Stan brought her did not work. The program was first aimed at too many products, and some marketing channels, such as podcast ads, had little effect. She says she never starts from blame and says 'we' rather than 'you'. The sample program became the main way UCAN acquires customers.

steps: The what. Agree the output (format, content, quality) and the timing. Where possible ask the colleague to suggest their own ideas first. Ask: "Based on experience, how long will this take?"
The how. Ask "How are you going to tackle the work?" Fix any guardrails you have. Say out loud where you are flexible so they can see their room to choose.
The when. Put the next review on the calendar, soon enough to correct course before the deadline, and agree what they will bring to it. Step back until then.
Adjust as you go. Start with a standard rhythm, such as a week, then change it according to what you learn about how the person handles the work.

If you are sure where you are fixed and flexible, say: "This is where I have a clear view...and here's where I'm open to any suggestions you have..." If you are not sure, say: "I have some thoughts, but tell me first how you'd think about this, and then we'll discuss options."

limits: Webb says the right balance differs by colleague and by task, so it has to be adjusted each time. Some people are proven in their role and others are less reliable, and it is fine to reflect that in how often you check in. She suggests telling high performers that you check less because you are confident in them.

She also warns about the tune-out effect. If people feel simply left alone to fail, they often become demotivated. Missteps teach a lot when the manager helps the person reflect on what went wrong. Her suggested questions: "Tell me about the choices you made." "What do you think caused this to fall short of what we'd hoped?" "So, what should be done differently going forward?"

quotes.text: Look for all the Flex you can, but be honest about what's already Fixed in your mind.
quotes.source: Caroline Webb, Leadership Intelligence

concepts.concept: Spend most time on why, be clear on what, least on how
concepts.name: What, why and how

card.title: What, why and how
idea: Maister says that when you manage the work of others you can focus on what is to be done, how it is to be done, or why it is to be done. For professionals he recommends being very clear on the what, spending only the bare minimum of time on the how, and spending a lot of time on the why. He adds that this is particularly important for junior professionals.
why: He draws on his own experience. A piece of professional work can strike you as stimulating and worth your energy, or it can look meaningless, repetitive and dull. The difference depends on whether you can see where the challenge in the work lies and whether you feel the work is a worthy use of your talents. He concludes that the supervisor's job is to help the professional find the meaning in the work.

On routine tasks, Maister says the manager has to help the person place the task in context, see its importance and accept it as worthy of professional effort. He calls it profoundly demotivating when the work is presented as "Yes, I agree it's dull and boring, but it's got to be done and you've been chosen to do it". A good manager conveys that there is "no task too trivial to be done well". He writes that young professionals are rarely demotivated by too much work. Most often the cause is too much meaningless work, and since almost no work in a professional firm is meaningless, he calls that syndrome a failure of management.
limits: Maister's own description of project types shows the how cannot always be kept to a minimum. In 'Brains' projects, at the frontier of knowledge, each project is one-off and the tasks cannot be clearly specified in advance, so middle-level professionals have to be involved continuously. In 'Grey Hair' projects the problem is familiar, so some tasks, especially the early ones, can be specified and delegated. In 'Procedure' projects the steps are so well established that they can be delegated under supervision to junior staff, and responses to some steps can be 'programmed'. He adds that these are points along a spectrum.

quotes.text: In the management of professionals the supervisor should be very clear on the what ("provide clear goals"), spend only the bare minimum of time on the how ("involve them in decision-making," "provide autonomy") and spend a lot of time on the why ("provide meaning").
quotes.source: David H. Maister, Managing the Professional Service Firm

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: In a brief for an agent, write the goal precisely and give the reason a full paragraph: who will use the result and what decision it feeds. Prescribe steps only when the work is routine and the steps are known. For open-ended work, expect to stay involved while it runs.

concepts.concept: 2×2 of consequence and your conviction decides how much to delegate
concepts.name: Conviction and consequence

card.title: Conviction and consequence
idea: Super Thinking presents a matrix that venture capitalist Keith Rabois developed to decide which tasks to hand to others. One axis is your conviction about a decision. You sort it as extremely high or extremely low: there are times you know something is a mistake, and times you would not do it that way but have no idea whether it is right or wrong. The other axis is consequence. Some wrong decisions are catastrophic for the company. Others have little impact, at least at first.

The grid has four cells. High conviction with high consequence: do not delegate. Low conviction with low consequence: delegate completely. The two other cells, high conviction with low consequence and low conviction with high consequence, are both labelled 'delegate sometimes'.
why: The authors say the matrix frees up a leader's time and sorts situations into learning opportunities for the team. Rabois's point about the top cell: where the consequences are dramatic and you are extremely sure you are right, you cannot let a junior colleague make a mistake.

The authors place the high-conviction, low-consequence cell next to deliberate practice. In that cell you know what should be done, so coaching works well, and failure costs the organisation little. Tasks at or just beyond the edge of someone's ability are delegated, and the person then gets radically candid feedback on how to improve. The authors describe this as a compelling way to help people grow quickly, including in new roles.

stories.text: The authors apply the matrix at home. They try to have their kids attempt things that cause little harm if they fail, such as buying something at a store by themselves or making their own lunch.

steps: Rate your conviction about the right decision: very high or very low.
Rate the consequence if the decision is wrong: catastrophic or low impact.
Place the task in the grid and delegate as the cell indicates.
For high conviction and low consequence, hand over tasks at the edge of the person's ability and follow up with specific, candid feedback.

limits: The book does not say how to decide inside the two 'delegate sometimes' cells. It also does not discuss cases where your conviction is wrong while feeling high.

quotes.text: Where there is low consequence and you have very low confidence in your own opinion, you should absolutely delegate.
quotes.source: Keith Rabois, quoted in Super Thinking

concepts.concept: Performance standard, finish line, boundaries; negotiate the necessities
concepts.name: The statement of work

card.title: The statement of work
idea: Wiseman's first Smart Play for finishing strong is to draft a Statement of Work (SOW). It has three parts: the performance standard (what a great job looks like), the finish line (what a complete job looks like), and the boundaries (what is not part of the job). You do not need to wait for your boss or client to supply it. Start with what you have already heard, fill gaps with your own judgment, and review it with stakeholders to confirm that expectations match.
She suggests opening that review with: "Here is what I think success looks like. Where am I off?" Once you have agreement, you have a clear SOW and can take ownership of completing it.

The second Smart Play goes with it: negotiate the necessities. Be clear about what you need to succeed, such as information, time, access, guidance and resources, and negotiate for it at the outset, before you need it. A formal negotiation is not required. Wiseman offers an if/then statement: "If I am to be able to do [this thing you need from me] then I will need you to do [this thing I'll need to be successful]."
why: Wiseman's research is about what makes people finish. In her survey of 170 managers, three of the top ten frustrations involved failure to finish. She writes that the real value of a reliable person comes from the 'always' factor. The managers also said high-value contributors get the job done without being reminded 98 percent of the time. For typical contributors the figure is 48 percent, and for under-contributors 12 percent.

On resources, the Wiseman Group asked 120 professionals what they most need to succeed. Six factors rated similarly high: access to information, action from leaders, feedback or coaching, access to key meetings and people, time, and help establishing credibility. Budget and head count came seventh and eighth. She advises negotiating at the outset, while your influence is high and before you have committed to the work. People who skip this must handle problems alone or hand responsibility upward when they run out of personal power.

For managers, she lists clarity as one of the conditions for a high-impact team. When it is hard to have quick conversations about expectations, obstacles get magnified and employees defer to higher-ups. A clear SOW helps people keep ownership.

stories.text:
Wiseman was the junior member of a team running a leadership program at Oracle, the Leaders Forum. The first program had been a success, apart from feedback that the strategy was unclear. Three senior executives sat at the table, and she worried they would be pulled in other directions. The president, Ray Lane, was responsible for $25 billion in revenue a year.

As the meeting ended and they were about to stand up, she decided to speak. She said: "I will work my tail off, but the day you no longer have time for this is the day I stop working on it." Then she restated it for clarity: "So if you stop, I stop." She knew the program would fail without the executives' personal involvement and was not willing to fail. Lane paused to take it in and answered, "You have a deal." He walked to his executive assistant's office and told her that for the next year Liz had whatever time she needed on his calendar.

Lane never backed off. He attended every session and every meeting she called. Wiseman writes that it was a time when she did her best work, and that the support came because she negotiated the necessities.

steps: Write down the performance standard: what a great job looks like.
Write down the finish line: what a complete job looks like.
Write down the boundaries: what is not part of the job.
Start from what you have already heard, then use your judgment to fill what is missing.
Review it with the stakeholders and ask what they would add. Say: "Here is what I think success looks like. Where am I off?"
List what you need to deliver (information, time, access, guidance, resources) and agree on it at the outset with an if/then statement.

quotes.text: Be sure to negotiate this support at the outset of the work, before you'll need it.
quotes.source: Liz Wiseman, Impact Players

concepts.concept: Trouble, Owner, Success, Constraints, Actors → core question
concepts.name: TOSCA problem statement

card.title: TOSCA problem statement

sources.authors: Bernard Garrette, Corey Phelps, Olivier Sibony

idea: TOSCA is the first step of the book's 4S method, "state the problem". Before writing the question you want answered, ask five questions. Trouble: what makes this problem real and present? Owner: whose problem is it? Success criteria: what will success look like, and when? Constraints: what limits the solution space? Actors: who has a say in how it gets solved, and what do they want? Once those are answered, you write a core question.

The authors define 'trouble' as a gap between an observation and an aspiration. If you aim to grow revenue and it falls, that is trouble. A perceived opportunity also counts. They take the acronym from Puccini's opera.
why: The authors argue that a sharply stated problem is a valuable discipline, and that business problems are rarely as neatly defined as Tosca's. They warn about defining a problem by its proposed solution. When a problem is stated so that it suggests the answer, the team is in danger of blindly confirming that answer. To define a problem properly, they say, you must resist the urge to solve it too quickly.

They also warn that experienced people are the most likely to wrongly recognise a new situation as a familiar one, and to make a misguided diagnosis. Their advice for the trouble step is: when in doubt, stick to trouble, meaning describe the symptoms and leave out an attributed cause.

stories.text:
In Puccini's opera, Tosca's lover Mario has been arrested and will be executed tomorrow. Tosca wants to get him out of jail alive and escape with him. She is virtuous, and there are things she will not do. Scarpia, the chief of police, is the key player, and what he wants from her is what she is unwilling to give. Her problem is thorny but clear: "How do I get Mario out of jail alive, without yielding to Scarpia?"

In the opera, Tosca promises to give herself to Scarpia if he saves Mario by staging a mock execution. When the time comes she kills Scarpia instead. Scarpia had also betrayed her, and Mario's execution was real. The authors call it a crisp problem with a disastrous solution, and note that it makes good tragedy. Mapped to the questions: the trouble is Mario's arrest, the owner is Tosca, the success criterion is escape, the constraint is her virtue, and the actor is Scarpia.

The authors work through the music industry around 1999. The trouble looks obvious, since people are illegally downloading millions of files. They point out that downloads are not the trouble in themselves. Revenues were still growing then, so downloads were a precursor of future revenue decline. The industry's aspiration was stated in revenue, not downloads.

On owner, they ask who 'the music industry' is. If the owner is the RIAA, a lobbying body, the solution space is limited to lobbying and advertising. If the owner is the head of a large label, the options widen to product, pricing and new business models.

On success criteria, asking the executive 'why' repeatedly goes nowhere: after a few rounds the executive gets irritated. The authors suggest a different question: "We are in the future and this problem-solving effort has been a great success. What is the date, and what do we see?" In their role-play the executive says at least three years from now, and that revenues are growing again. The success metric turns out to be revenue, not file counts or arrests.

On actors, the industry spent years pushing Congress to crack down on file-sharing. A stakeholder analysis might have shown that few members of Congress wanted to be seen persecuting teenagers and stifling technology so the industry could keep selling CDs at $14 each.

steps: Trouble: be specific. 'We must create a results-oriented culture' is a fake problem; 'Twenty percent of customer calls remain unanswered' is trouble. Keep interpretation out. 'Our product has lost consumer appeal' is interpretation; 'we lost five points of market share over the past year' describes a symptom. Ask 'Why now?'.
Owner: name the person whose job it is to take care of the symptoms. The owner decides when a problem statement is good enough.

Success criteria: ask what success looks like and by when. Decide whether to include a quantified target. The authors describe two schools of thought. An open-ended target admits uncertainty. An aspirational number, even an arbitrary one, focuses the mind and justifies resources, as long as you are ready to revisit it.

Constraints: look for three kinds. There are constraints on the success criteria from other commitments. There are constraints from the owner's resources and capabilities. There are constraints on the problem-solving process itself, such as time, budget and confidentiality.
Actors: list the stakeholders and what they want. Constraints are usually stable, while actors react to what you do.

Write the core question. It must be a question, not a statement. Choose its scope as open or closed. Check that it addresses the trouble, is phrased from the owner's perspective, would meet the success criteria if answered, recognises the constraints, and considers the relevant actors.
Iterate. The steps overlap, you will probably rewrite the question several times, and you return to the owner to test it.

limits: The authors say too many constraints can turn the problem into 'just making the trouble disappear without changing anything else', which they call mission impossible. Few problems would get solved if their owners never relaxed a constraint.
TOSCA suits problems with an identifiable owner. The authors say 'wicked' problems with no clear owner, such as the short-termism of global business, do not suit the approach described in the book.

quotes.text: Before stating the core question, a problem solver must ask five questions that Tosca's situation illustrates
quotes.source: Garrette, Phelps and Sibony, Cracked It!

quotes.text: when we define a problem so it suggests the solution, we're in great danger of blindly confirming that conclusion
quotes.source: Garrette, Phelps and Sibony, Cracked It!

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When a request to an agent is more than a small edit, fill in the five lines first: the symptom, who owns the result, what done looks like and by when, the constraints, and who else is affected. Then write the request as a question the agent can answer. Ask the agent to say which of the five is missing.

concepts.concept: Delegation vs abdication; position contracts; monkeys; delegate and elevate
concepts.name: Delegation, not abdication

card.title: Delegation, not abdication
idea: Gerber separates management by delegation from management by abdication. In abdication, the owner hands work to someone and runs. The owner has not given the person standards, the result they are accountable for, or any sense of where the business is going. Gerber describes the cause as desperation: the business has grown beyond what the owner can personally control, so the owner passes the accountability down and hopes it will be handled.

His remedy is a position contract. It is a summary of the results the position must achieve, the work its occupant is accountable for, the standards by which results are judged, and a line for the signature of the person who agrees to those accountabilities. Gerber stresses that it is a contract, not a job description. Accountability, he points out, literally means 'stand up and be counted'.

Wickman adds a pair of tools for the delegator's own load. Delegate and elevate: when your work needs more than 100 percent of your time, hand off the extra to the right person in the right seat so you move toward your Unique Ability. Monkey management: do not take on the problems your direct reports bring you.
why: Gerber says a person like Harry needs more direction than an owner who works as a technician can give. Harry needs to know why he is doing what he does, the result he is accountable for, the standards for evaluating his work, and where the business is heading. Without a manager the business goes into a tailspin.

Wickman's reason for delegating is capacity. Someone running at 120 percent is holding the organisation back and heading for burnout. He says you cannot keep doing another person's work or taking on their monkeys.

stories.text: A business owner hires his first employee, Harry, a sixty-eight-year-old bookkeeper with twenty-two years of experience in a company like the owner's. The owner hands over the books and, as Gerber puts it, 'runs'. For a while life gets easier. The owner uses Harry to answer the phone, then for shipping and receiving, then for a few customers. When Harry comes to say what he needs, the owner tells him to handle it, since how does not matter as long as he does not bother the owner with details. When Harry says he needs more people, the owner tells him to hire them. Then a customer calls to complain, and the story turns. Gerber's name for this is Management by Abdication rather than by Delegation.

Brothers Jack and Murray Hopeful start Widget Makers and share the work, taking turns at opening up, making widgets, helping customers and doing the books. When there is more work than they can handle they hire Jerry, their nephew, and later Herb, Jack's wife's brother, and everyone keeps taking turns. Then widgets start coming back, the books look funny, tools go missing, and people bump into each other. Gerber asks the questions nobody can answer. If everybody is doing everything, who is accountable for anything? If Jack and Murray are both in charge, what happens when Jack tells Jerry to do something that Murray will not allow?

Their fix is to draw an organisation chart for the company as it will be when fully realised, since the work is the same and only the faces change, and then to write a position contract for each position. One of them must be the chief operating officer. They choose Jack, who signs the COO position contract. When they finish, Jack has eight positions and Murray three, so they rebalance to six each.

Tyler Smith of Niche Retail started the company with his partner Brad Sorock, with Tyler as integrator and Brad as visionary. In the first year Tyler handled all sales, operations and finance himself. A ping on his phone told him of an order, and he went to his basement to print it, package it, ship it, process the payment, order from the supplier and pay the bills.

As the company grew he reached full capacity and handed things off one at a time. His wife, Stacey, helped him pack boxes. He hired someone to ship orders and let go of that function. A move to a 2,000-square-foot warehouse created the need for an operations manager. He hired a bookkeeper. At a 10,000-square-foot warehouse the company needed a CFO, a COO, and a head of site stores and marketing. Wickman writes that the growth continued to an 80,000-square-foot warehouse, and that Tyler delegated and elevated each time he reached capacity, avoiding burnout.

steps: Draw an organisation chart for the company as it will be when fully realised, with every position that work needs.
Write a position contract for each position: results to be achieved, work the occupant is accountable for, standards of evaluation, and a signature line.
Name one person as accountable for each position, and check the load across positions.

Wickman, monkeys: a direct report who brings a problem must leave with it. Wickman says that if the person can't or won't, you hired the wrong person.

limits: Gerber's warning is that accountability cannot itself be handed off. In a scene in the book, he tells an owner named Sarah that she cannot delegate her accountabilities, and that she must set the standard for how managers are expected to produce results.
Wickman says delegating works only with the right person in the right seat. If you do not have that, you will never feel completely comfortable letting go.

concepts.concept: Thresholds set in advance that force stop or rethink; category decisions
concepts.name: Trip wires

card.title: Trip wires
idea: A trip wire is a decision made in advance about what you will do when a specific quantifiable time, amount or circumstance is reached. Parrish calls trip wires a form of precommitment. His example is a team climbing Everest that agrees to abort the summit attempt if it has not reached a certain location by a certain time. If the team fails to, it turns back, with no argument. The members do not try to decide in the middle of fatigue and oxygen deprivation, because they decided earlier.

Parrish says trip wires cover negative signs, which are red flags that something is going seriously off course, and the absence of positive signs. When signs are positive you stay the course. When they are murky, that is when trip wires help. If neither the negative nor the expected positive signs appear, he says it is time to re-evaluate: ask whether the most important thing is still the most important thing, whether you were wrong, and what it will take to reach your goals now that you have moved further in time but not in progress.

Duke approaches the same problem from decision-making. After a bad outcome you can go on 'tilt', a hot emotional state that damages decisions. She gives the sunk cost fallacy as an example: you keep going on a project that an outside observer would say you should drop. Her advice is to come up in advance with the conditions under which you would quit, write them down, and commit to changing course when they arise. She says this is particularly effective in a team setting. She also describes category decisions, a one-time advance choice about which options you may or may not take.
why: Parrish's reason is that fail-safes make sure a decision is executed as planned. He adds that when the whole team understands the markers of success and failure, people are empowered to act the minute things veer off course.

Duke's reason is that it is easier to work out the right response before things go wrong than after. Imagining bad outcomes in advance also lowers their emotional impact, because the thought shifts from 'I can't believe this happened' to 'this happened but I knew it was a possibility'.

stories.text: Parrish uses Ulysses. Sailing past the island of the Sirens, Ulysses wanted to hear their song without risking the crew. He stuffed the crew's ears with beeswax and had them tie him to the mast so that whatever he said or did he could not change the decision already made. He told them that the more he struggled, the tighter they should bind him. Parrish adds that he is not saying Ulysses made a great decision, since better thinking would have avoided the island. His point is the execution fail-safes.

Duke imagines a medical device company planning to sell a device in a new overseas market. The team's premortem finds that the country is considering new regulations that would ban the device, and the team estimates the probability of the regulations taking effect as high. In that case, she says, you might decide against selling in that market until the uncertainty resolves. She sets this in a longer process: record the premortem and a backcast in a Decision Exploration Table with likelihoods, then use the output to modify the decision, plan reactions to future outcomes so they do not take you by surprise, and look for ways to reduce the impact of bad outcomes.

method.intro: Parrish's steps for setting a trip wire, with Duke's additions.
steps: Choose a measure that can be checked: a time, an amount, or a circumstance.
List the negative signs you would see if things were going wrong, and the positive signs you expect if they are going right.
Decide in advance what you will do when the wire is hit. Parrish's example is to turn back or re-evaluate.
Make sure everyone on the team knows the markers and has the authority to act on them.

Duke: for risks of repeated temptation, make a category decision once, such as 'I invest only in...'. She notes that you will not always land on the right side of the category, but it reduces how often you stray.
Duke: write down the conditions under which you would quit, and commit to changing course when they occur.

limits: Duke says category decisions are not perfect. In any given case you might make a decision that falls on the wrong side of the category. She argues they still cut the probability that you stray, and the gains add up.
Parrish notes that trip wires matter most in murky situations. When signs are clearly positive, you know to stay the course.

concepts.concept: Escalate without giving up ownership; permit, drop a pin; daily updates
concepts.name: Escalating without letting go

card.title: Escalating without letting go
idea: Wiseman describes a way of asking for help while keeping ownership. When people escalate a problem to management, she writes, it often comes with an implied transfer of ownership. A Stanford Health Care manager described one employee whose emails "essentially say, 'Hi, this is a problem. Goodbye.'" The Impact Players Wiseman studied called in reinforcements from leaders and colleagues and kept the accountability. The message, she writes, was "I need your guidance or action so I can move this forward."

Two practices keep the manager informed. Take out a permit: agree with your manager where you are headed and why, and which parts of your core job you need to keep doing well. Drop pins: check in often with short updates, and find out how priorities are shifting so you stay on the agenda. Wiseman compares the first to a hiker who tells the authorities a destination before going into the backcountry, and the second to a hiker with a satellite tracker.

Dalio sets a duty to escalate. Escalating means saying you do not believe you can successfully handle a situation and that you are passing the Responsible Party job to someone else. The person you report to then chooses whether to coach you through it, take control, have someone else handle it, or do something else. Dalio wants escalation seen as a responsibility and not as a failure, and wants people to speak up when they cannot meet agreed deliverables or deadlines. He also asks each person who reports to him to take ten to fifteen minutes a day to write what they did, the issues that concern them, and their reflections. By reading and comparing those updates he can see how people work together and which threads to pull.
why: Wiseman's survey of 170 managers found that their most frequent frustration was people bringing problems without first trying to find solutions. One manager compared it to a cat that drops a dead rat at your front door. Another top frustration was surprises. She calls them surprise parties that make the manager look bad. In her credibility ranking, escalating problems without offering solutions, making your manager chase you, and surprising managers with bad news all damage credibility.

On why people avoid asking for help, she cites Heidi Grant: the social threats involved, such as uncertainty, risk of rejection and diminished status, activate the same brain regions as physical pain. She adds that people are neurologically wired to want to help, and that a responsible request brings out the best in both sides.

stories.text: Fiona Su is a planning manager at Google's Media Lab. Her manager, John Tuchtenhagen, who heads media for North America, says she produces the output of at least two people. When she is told no, she asks why and starts from no to find a path forward. When she runs into trouble, she tells John that this one is over her head and she needs help. She involves him more as a consultant than as a new owner. John says, "She knows how to bring me in and bring me along," and, "Fiona never blindsides me." He is eager to help because he gets to contribute without taking back responsibility.

A NASA engineering manager described an engineer he called Ed, a Steady Eddie type. Ed did what was asked, gave updates gladly and submitted his work on time. When colleagues reviewed it, more work was usually needed because of integration issues or bugs. Ed would say he was already working on another project. When the mission became complicated he bumped issues up to his boss, often saying, "This one is above my pay grade." Wiseman compares him to a tennis partner who takes the easy shots and calls "Yours!" on the hard ones. Ed's work always got done and was fit for the mission, but the manager notes that it was not Ed who got it across the finish line.

method.intro: Wiseman's practices, with Dalio's escalation rule.
steps: Take out a permit. Agree with your manager where you are headed and why, and which parts of your core job you will keep doing well.
Drop pins. Check in at intervals and find out how priorities are changing, in addition to reporting your own work.
Call in reinforcements. When stuck, bring in the leader as a consultant and say what guidance or action you need to move forward. Keep the accountability.
Negotiate the necessities up front, so the support you will need is arranged before you need it.
Dalio: escalate as soon as you see you cannot meet a deliverable or a deadline, so the person you report to can decide how to respond.

card.tension: Wiseman and Dalio describe escalation differently. In Wiseman's version the person escalates to get help and stays accountable, with the leader acting as a consultant. In Dalio's version escalation means passing the Responsible Party job to someone else, and the boss decides whether to coach, take control or reassign it. Read together, Dalio's rule fits a responsibility you doubt you can carry. Wiseman's fits an obstacle that needs a leader's authority or time while the work stays yours. This reading is ours and neither book states it.
limits: Wiseman notes that escalation can carry an implied transfer of ownership. If the person only reports the problem and leaves, the manager inherits it.

concepts.concept: Expert support on real work, withdrawn as skill grows
concepts.name: Scaffolding and fading

card.title: Scaffolding and fading
idea: Beane borrows scaffolding from education research. Jerome Bruner, David Wood and Gail Ross coined the term in the late 1970s for parsing out challenge over time so that learners stay engaged. Vygotsky had earlier named the middle zone between what a learner can do alone and what is out of reach the zone of proximal development. Decades of research, Beane writes, show that students given the hardest tasks they can handle, with guidance, learn more and build more confidence than students who struggle alone. He cites Benjamin Bloom, who showed that an average student held to this standard through one-on-one tutoring improved to the 95th percentile.

Fading is the other half. Allan Collins, John Seely Brown and Susan Newman used the term in 1986. As the learner builds skill, the expert backs away and lets the learner handle what they can and should handle themselves.
why: Taking on more challenge with an expert's help also means stepping into territory that is much harder than you could manage alone, which raises the risk that you feel more incompetent. Beane names frustration management as the scaffolding tactic that matters most. The expert can act in advance by indicating the payoff of the coming struggle, and afterwards by reminding the learner how far they are stretching. His baseball example: before, "Want to play on the varsity team in high school? You have to be able to hit pitches at least this fast." After a first hit that went nowhere: "Great. You can now officially hit a foul ball in the majors."

stories.text:
Andre took six years to work his way up to deputy chef at a three-star Michelin steakhouse. In his early days he worked under a deputy chef, Jane. Before he began apprenticing for her role they met, and she laid out a plan. He would do easier, more peripheral tasks first, taking his lead from her, and they would debrief over a break. Then she threw more difficult work at him, a bit more than he thought he could handle, and he knew she would not come to his rescue at game time.

After he mastered prep and showed interest in inventory, she introduced him to her purchasing guy and the appliance maintenance tech. The week after that it was the stations upstream and downstream of his. Then he set his own stretch goal of cutting his prep time by 25 percent and got her approving nod when he hit it. Sooner than he expected Andre was taking the lead and Jane took a back seat.

Years later Andre does the same for a prep cook learning to fillet salmon. He starts her on skinning and deboning and stands by to watch for serious errors and give feedback, since Copper River salmon is expensive. Once she gets the hang of it, he challenges her to use smoother motions, fewer cuts and less waste, and then he steps away. The old scaffolding fades, new scaffolding goes in for new challenges, and the prep cook takes on more and more responsibility.

method.intro: Features of good scaffolding that Beane draws from the research.
steps: Give the learner the hardest tasks they can handle with your help. Start with the basics and progress to complicated tasks.
Manage frustration. Say in advance what the struggle is for, and point out afterwards how far the learner has stretched.
Make sure expert and novice share a solid understanding of the goal. Beane says scaffolding works well only then.
Tune the help to the individual. Learners differ in capability, goals and preferences, and an expert who ignores this can overextend one learner and bore another.

Match directiveness to the task. When the task is well structured and the next struggle is predictable, guidance can be more directive and closed-ended. When the task is unstructured, guidance has to be less directive and more open-ended.
Fade. Scaffolding is temporary. When the learner gets better, back away.

limits: Beane says good scaffolding depends on an expert who understands each learner's capabilities and goals. Without that, the support is badly tuned.

concepts.concept: GUIDE questions instead of instructions
concepts.name: The GUIDE model

card.title: The GUIDE model
idea: Webb's coaching advice is to replace the instinct to instruct with the instinct to inquire. A good question makes the other person think. She writes that it is as though you are running a command in their brain that triggers a search for insight. The question she wants invites the colleague to explore their thinking out loud. She rules out a disguised suggestion such as "Have you thought about doing X or Y?" and a yes or no prompt such as "Did you try asking them?" Her example of a good question is "So tell me, how are you thinking about this?"

GUIDE is an acronym for five steps. Goal: ask them to get clear on what they are trying to achieve. Understanding: explore how they see the issue. Ideas: surface their ideas before you add yours. Deepen: sharpen their thinking through constructive challenge. Enable: make sure they are ready to take action.
why: Webb gives reasons for several steps. Explaining something out loud improves a person's understanding, shows you how clearly they see things, and raises the quality of the conversation when they feel listened to. Putting your own idea second leaves the colleague in ownership of the issue, and through the IKEA effect people are more committed to ideas they helped shape. The colleague may also have information you do not, such as the view from the front line or the customer. When leaders ask whether they are supposed to pretend not to know the answer, she says no pretending is required, only sequencing: "Always go second."

The last step draws on implementation intentions, which means planning the action, anticipating the obstacles and deciding in advance how to respond. Webb says studies suggest this can triple the likelihood of success.

stories.text:
Webb builds a sample conversation from a story told by Shellye Archambeau about a supply chain challenge at one of her companies. A colleague brings a concern about an external supplier.

Goal. The colleague says the real goal is to make sure the new product launch is not derailed by the supplier situation, ideally with an alternative supplier of trusted quality and without blowing the budget or delaying the timeline. The coach plays back what was said: reliability is key, with cost and speed also important.

Understanding. Eighty percent of supply comes from a partner that has had financing issues, and there have been two late shipments. The colleague has contacted a solid backup supplier who is interested but has not worked with their specifications.

Ideas. The colleague proposes staying on top of the current supplier or onboarding the second supplier. The coach asks, "Any other ideas? I have one, but let me let you finish your thought first," and waits. The colleague then suggests deferring part of the launch to reduce early exposure. The coach says they were thinking the same and shares their thought second.

Deepen. The coach asks what would have to be true for each option to work. The colleague finds both unrealistic as they stand. When the coach asks what they are assuming, the colleague notices an assumption that the choice was either-or, and proposes a hybrid: one more push with the current supplier, the second supplier in parallel, and a softer launch timeline.

Enable. Next steps are rough quotes from the second supplier and a map of how the launch schedule could change. The hardest part will be getting colleagues to agree to defer part of the launch. The support needed is a quick check of the financial assumptions before pitching Sales, due by end of day tomorrow. Archambeau ends such conversations with, "Listen, I knew you could figure this out."

steps: Goal. "Let's take a step back for a moment—what's your real goal here?" If they are overwhelmed, narrow it: "What aspect of this issue would be most helpful for us to talk through right now?"
Understanding. "What do you understand about the situation?" Follow up with "What have you tried so far, and what did you learn from that?" Summarise what they say in their own language.
Ideas. "What ideas do you have about the way forward?" Wait. Then add yours alongside theirs: "You mentioned X and Y as options. Another possibility could be Z. How does that compare?"

Deepen. Test one idea with "What would have to be true for that to work?" To choose between options, ask for the criteria of an ideal solution and rate the options against them. Build on their thinking with "Here's what I like about your idea..." and "Here's what would make me like that idea even more..." To reduce blind spots, ask what they are assuming and what the opposite would be.
Enable. "What are your specific next steps?" "What support or input do you need, from me or others?" Then: "What's likely to be the hardest part, and what will help you find a way through that?"

limits: Webb says being coached is not easy: you ask a colleague to think deeply, come up with new ideas and commit to action. If the change feels big, she suggests telling your team you are adopting a coaching style, since the changes have more impact when they understand why you are giving them space to think.

concepts.concept: Tension: specify everything (Gerber, Agrawal) vs leave room for judgment (Beane, Nguyen)
concepts.name: Specify it or leave room?

card.title: Specify it or leave room?

sources.authors: Ajay Agrawal, Joshua Gans, Avi Goldfarb

idea: Four books split on how much to write down in advance. Gerber and Agrawal, Gans and Goldfarb argue for rules and procedures. Beane and Nguyen argue for leaving room for the judgment of the person doing the work.

The case for specifying. Gerber wants a systems-dependent business run from operations manuals. Agrawal et al. say standard operating procedures cut cognitive load and add reliability: when people follow rules, they can do their parts without costly communication such as meetings.

The case for room. Nguyen compares old-school recipes, made of principles that call for experience, with modern recipes made of algorithms that nearly anyone can execute. Fuzzy principles let an expert use sensitivity that a mechanical rule cannot hold. Beane reports that experts trust and respect novices who show initiative beyond the rules, and he warns that following rules and meeting quotas can stall skill.

stories.text: The construction industry breaks the whole process into simpler tasks. A construction schedule lists every task line by line and day by day, in order. The outcomes of those tasks are planned in advance, and no one on site has to think about more than their own task. When a task is done the worker marks a check and moves on. Agrawal et al. say such rules generate reliability and reduce the need to coordinate actively. The decisions are made up front and put into the plan. The cost is that a plan is expensive to change, and a big issue can derail it. A fixed set of SOPs makes it hard to change and adapt.

Gerber describes Ray Kroc and McDonald's. He says Kroc understood that the franchisee, left to his own devices, would most assuredly not make it work, so the business had to work in order to be sold. Kroc therefore set out to create what Gerber calls a systems-dependent business and not a people-dependent business, one that could work without him. Among Gerber's rules for such a franchise prototype: it will be operated by people with the lowest possible level of skill, and all its work will be documented in operations manuals.

Nguyen learned to cook from modern, algorithmic recipes. When he asked his mother to teach him her hot and sour catfish soup, she gave him a ramble of judgment calls. He was to taste the tomato and pineapple first. If both were sweet he would add vinegar, and if both were sour he might add brown sugar. She would not say how much, since it depended on how things tasted that day. He also had to smell the catfish to tell whether it was a clean farmed one or a funky wild one. He told her, to his eternal shame, to give him a real recipe. He later saw that she had given him something profoundly real.

He contrasts an old recipe for egg bread (about ten handfuls of flour, a bit of yeast, bake until golden brown with a nice hollow ring when knocked) with a modern one with exact amounts, temperature and time. The modern one is accessible to a novice. The old one is miserably cryptic to a novice and a useful guide for an experienced baker.

Sociologist Michael Burawoy took a job as a machine operator in a Chicago machine shop in the 1970s, hoping to earn the machinists' trust so he could learn from them. He joined an informal game they called 'making out', which meant producing more than the quota and hiding that output from management. He worked extra hard, and his coworkers confronted him and said he would make them look bad. Their game was about quality, safety and solidarity among workers too. The real informal rule, in Beane's words, was that you don't race ahead unless the group does it together, strategically. Beane uses the story to show that the standards for skill and conduct are rarely stated and can conflict with each other.

card.tension: Nguyen states the trade-off directly. Mechanical procedures are repeatable and accessible, and they work best on things that are naturally public and observable. Fuzzy principles need the trained judgment of an experienced person, who can then use all of their experience and sensitivity. They are harder for the public to inspect, and different experts may do different things. Agrawal et al. add that rules are decisions made in advance, and that making a decision costs more than following a rule, so it pays when the consequences are significant and the cost of information is small. Putting the two together, specification fits work where reliability and coordination at scale matter and the situation can be observed by anyone. Room for judgment fits work where the situation needs an expert's sensitivity, or where the person is still building skill. The last sentence is our synthesis.
limits: For specifying: a fixed set of SOPs is hard to change, and a big issue can derail the plan (Agrawal et al.).
For leaving room: fuzzy principles are harder for others to inspect, and different experts may end up doing different things (Nguyen). A total novice finds an old-school recipe miserably cryptic.

concepts.concept: Curse of knowledge and illusion of transparency; 45% know what's expected
concepts.name: The curse of knowledge

card.title: The curse of knowledge

sources.authors: M. Neil Browne, Stuart M. Keeley

idea: The curse of knowledge is the assumption that what is clear to you is equally clear to others. Browne and Keeley define it this way: we cannot recall what it is like when we did not know what we now know. Webb adds a second effect, the illusion of transparency. People also overestimate how clearly their hopes, feelings and intentions come across.

Webb opens her chapter on communication with a survey figure: only 45 percent of employees agree with the statement "I know what is expected of me." She gives three reasons the gap opens. First, the curse of knowledge and the illusion of transparency. Second, listeners rarely take in everything the first time. Selective attention means they miss some of what you say without realising it, and working memory limits make it hard to take in a lot of new information at once. Third, people grasp and retain information better when it feels psychologically rewarding and relevant, so if they cannot see how what you say matters to them, it is less likely to stick.
Browne and Keeley note that critical thinkers, like everyone else, struggle with the curse of knowledge.

stories.text: Webb describes leaders she has coached who say "I don't know why they're not getting it." Rob Allen is CEO of Intermountain Health, which has sixty thousand employees, and he led a simplification drive across its operations. Early on he worried his message was not landing: "I felt like my words were going out into the organization and people would say, 'Yes, okay'—but then carry on as they always had." He adjusted by tailoring the message, with different angles for nurses and doctors, and by sharing personal stories and data.

Webb's example of an unclear request: "I want people to be more customer-focused." Each colleague makes their own best guess, and the guesses can differ widely. One person may reach out to more prospective customers while another builds stronger relationships with existing customers. Her own version of the problem comes from a government leadership program she worked on with her manager, Suzanne. Webb powered ahead on the program design without asking anyone on the team for input. She had assumed the best way to impress Suzanne was to present her work as a finished product. Suzanne told her that two senior colleagues had relevant expertise in how government worked, and that she could and should ask for more help.

Browne and Keeley use a scene from The Big Bang Theory. Sheldon says, "I need your help in a matter of semiotics." Penny asks, "What?" Sheldon answers, "Semiotics, the study of signs and symbols as a branch of the philosophy related to linguistics." Penny replies, "Okay, honey, I know you think you are explaining yourself, but you're really not." The authors say Sheldon's egocentrism gets in the way of a conversation that thinking about who Penny was might have made possible.

method.intro: Webb's remedies, from the chapters on change and communication and on coaching.
steps: Write a From-To statement. The from is what people do today ("The way things have been done in the past is..."), and the to is what you want to see ("The way I'd like us to do them in the future is...").
Spell things out more clearly and fully than seems necessary, and repeat them.

Ask the other person to say what they understand. In the GUIDE model, Webb recommends "What do you understand about the situation?" because explaining out loud improves understanding and shows you where it is thin.
Invite questions about anything they are unsure of, and appreciate them when they ask.

concepts.concept: System 1 builds a coherent story from what it has; both sides feel sure
concepts.name: What you see is all there is

card.title: What you see is all there is
idea: Kahneman abbreviates the rule as WYSIATI: what you see is all there is. System 1, the fast and automatic mind, builds the best story it can from the information that is active in the moment. It cannot allow for information it does not have. The measure of success for System 1 is the coherence of the story, and the amount and quality of the data behind the story are largely irrelevant.

One result is that confidence follows coherence. Kahneman writes that people's confidence depends mostly on the quality of the story they can tell about what they see, even if they see little. He also says that knowing little makes it easier to fit everything you know into a coherent pattern.

The same mechanism applies to a task handed from one person to another. Each side reads the same words and builds a complete picture from them, and each feels sure of it. This application is our reading, and the books discuss the mechanism.

stories.text: Kahneman asks the reader: "Will Mindik be a good leader? She is intelligent and strong..." An answer comes quickly, and it is yes. Then he asks what if the next two adjectives were corrupt and cruel. He points out what the reader did not do: they did not ask what they would need to know before forming an opinion about someone's leadership. System 1 delivered the best story from two adjectives, with great cognitive ease.

Amos Tversky and two Stanford graduate students gave participants legal scenarios. In one, plaintiff David Thornton, a forty-three-year-old union field representative, was visiting Thrifty Drug Store #168. A store manager told him he could no longer speak with union employees on the floor and would have to use a back room while they were on break. The union contract allowed that, but it had never been enforced. Thornton objected and was told to comply, leave, or be arrested. He said he would rather be arrested. The manager called the police, he was handcuffed for trespassing, and all charges were later dropped. He sued for false arrest.

All participants read the background. Some then heard only the union lawyer, some only the store's lawyer, and some heard both sides like a jury. The lawyers added nothing that could not be inferred from the background, and participants knew the setup and could have generated the other side's argument. One-sided evidence still had a pronounced effect on judgments. People who saw one-sided evidence were also more confident than those who saw both sides.

In the 'f' exercise, run by Professor Roger Fisher and colleagues at Harvard Law School's Program on Negotiation, and now by many negotiation professors, a room of people is shown a sentence on a screen and asked to count the number of 'f's, silently. Most are confident of their count. The presenter asks how many recorded 8, 9, 10, 11 or more, and clusters of hands go up for each number. Before the right answer is revealed, the presenter asks who still feels confident in their original answer. Inevitably the majority do, despite learning that many others looking at the same sentence counted something different.

Aaron adds that people in more powerful roles may be the most confident. The powerful are less likely to consider another person's perspective and less likely to remember that others lack their privileged knowledge.

method.intro: Kahneman's own remedy, which he calls simple in principle.
steps: Recognise the signs that you are in a cognitive minefield.
Slow down.
Ask for reinforcement from System 2, the slower, deliberate mind.

Ask the question Kahneman says the reader skipped with Mindik: what would I need to know before I form an opinion? System 2 is also capable of following a list of boxes that must be checked before a decision, as when buying a home and deliberately seeking information you don't have.

limits: Kahneman writes that this sensible procedure is least likely to be applied when it is needed most. He also says System 1 is not readily educable, and that his own intuitive thinking is as prone to overconfidence as before he studied it.
He adds that most of the time the coherent story we put together is close enough to reality to support reasonable action.

quotes.text: System 1 is radically insensitive to both the quality and the quantity of the information that gives rise to impressions and intuitions.
quotes.source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

quotes.text: The confidence that individuals have in their beliefs depends mostly on the quality of the story they can tell about what they see, even if they see little.

concepts.concept: Stating your view first makes others echo it; collect views privately
concepts.name: Don't give your opinion first

card.title: Don't give your view first

sources.book: A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI
sources.authors: Rafael M. Batista, Thomas L. Griffiths

idea: Duke's rule: when you ask for advice, do not start with your own opinion. Beliefs are contagious. Offering your view first significantly increases the chance that the other person will state the same belief back to you, so what they tell you may not match what is in their head. Agreement feels good and disagreement feels bad. Duke also notes that people often ask for your view before giving theirs, to avoid accidentally disagreeing with you.

Batista and Griffiths extend the worry to AI chatbots. They argue that sycophancy distorts reality by returning responses biased to reinforce existing beliefs. A learner who is shown data sampled from their own hypothesis becomes more confident without getting closer to the truth.
why: Duke says the pull is stronger in groups. Even when members hold information that goes against the group's consensus, they often do not share it. Opinions from higher-status people are the most contagious, and the halo effect leads people to weight the opinions of highly successful people across the board, including in areas where they have no expertise.

Batista and Griffiths report an experiment with 557 participants on a modified Wason 2-4-6 rule-discovery task. Unmodified LLM behaviour suppressed discovery and inflated confidence about as much as explicitly sycophantic prompting did. Unbiased sampling from the true distribution produced discovery rates five times higher. They cite work by Wang et al. in which simple opinion statements such as "I believe the answer is X" induced agreement with incorrect beliefs at rates averaging 63.7 percent across seven model families, from 46.6 percent to 95.1 percent.

stories.text: Solomon Asch asked people which of several lines matched a reference line. Asked independently, over 99 percent said the middle line on the right. In the group version, the first people to answer were plants, told to give the same obviously wrong answer. After hearing them, 36.8 percent of the real subjects went along with the wrong answer. Duke asks what the influence must be on subjective matters such as whether a job candidate is a good cultural fit.

Garold Stasser and William Titus gave four-person groups the task of choosing the best of three candidates for student body president. The dossiers were designed so Candidate A was the most favourable. Each member reviewed a dossier, gave a private preference, and then the group met to choose. Members of the complete-information groups all had every fact, and most preferred A. In the partial-information groups, the facts were scattered across members' dossiers, so most members did not prefer A before the meeting. Everyone had been warned that their dossier might be incomplete. If members had shared everything, they would have had the same information as the other groups and presumably chosen A. They quickly formed a consensus around their pre-meeting preferences. Once a consensus appeared, members holding divergent information were unlikely to share it, and the groups almost always chose one of the other candidates.

Dan Levy, Joshua Yardley and Richard Zeckhauser of the Harvard Kennedy School studied how classes answer questions. When students raised their hands, they herded: as soon as a consensus appeared, students joined it, creating supermajorities. When students answered with electronic clickers and could not see others' answers, the supermajorities broke up. Private answers gave the instructors a better picture of what students knew and preferred.

steps: Before any group discussion, ask each person to send their opinion and their rationale on their own. Duke's examples include a hiring committee emailing their preferred candidate, and a legal team giving a settlement figure with upper and lower bounds.
Compile the answers and share them with the group before the meeting.
Say what form the feedback should take (a forecast, a rating, yes or no answers) so the answers can be compared directly.
Anonymise the first round, so lower-status views get a hearing. Duke notes that opinions cannot and should not stay anonymous forever, since an expert's view should count in their field.
For lower-stakes decisions, use the quick version: everyone writes an opinion and rationale on paper, one person reads them out, and if people read their own aloud, the most junior member goes first.

Give advisers the information they need. Build a checklist of what you would want to know if someone asked you for feedback on this kind of decision, usually goals, values, resources and details of the situation. Duke warns: junk in, junk out.

limits: Duke says the full process takes time, and a team could not run it on every decision. For lower-impact, easier-to-reverse decisions, she recommends the quick version.
Anonymity has a cost. Duke says that on a question in someone's field, their opinion should carry more weight, so anonymity cannot last.

quotes.text: The problem with offering your opinion first when soliciting someone's advice is that it significantly increases the likelihood that they will express the same belief back to you.
quotes.source: Annie Duke, How to Decide

quotes.text: sycophancy distorts reality by returning responses that are biased to reinforce existing beliefs
quotes.source: Rafael M. Batista and Thomas L. Griffiths, A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When you want an agent to review or choose, leave your preferred answer out of the prompt. Ask for options, the reasons for each, and what would change its mind. For a second opinion, give a fresh session only the artifact and the question, with none of your reasoning. Ask for the strongest case against the plan.

concepts.concept: Detail lost as intent passes down; chefs vs cooks; go to the source
concepts.name: Signal loss

card.title: Signal loss
idea: Parrish says the further information is from its original source, the more filters it has passed through. Details are abstracted, and the signal is lost. He names several causes. Information passes through people's levels of understanding, political interpretation and biases, and their incentives complicate it further. Abstractions also cannot carry all the detail of what they represent, and the person who makes an abstraction decides what is useful according to their own interests.

His metaphor for the second is a road map. A map shows roads, rivers and boundaries and leaves out rocks, plants, weather and much else. The word 'abstract' means 'to pull away from'. A map built for drivers will not tell you about population density or geology. Summaries, highlights and descriptions from a secondhand source leave out information that may matter for your decision.
why: Parrish says living on abstractions is like a diet of junk food. It has less information content, and real knowledge is earned while abstractions are borrowed. Relying on them also gives the ego default room to work: you feel confident about what to do without really understanding the problem. He also notes that when decisions look senseless to you, the other person is probably working from different information.

The person closest to the problem often has the most accurate information about it. What they tend to lack is the broader perspective. His example: a McDonald's line worker knows how to fix a recurring problem better than someone analysing data, but does not know whether the problem exists everywhere or whether the fix would cause harm if rolled out globally.

stories.text: Parrish worked for a CEO of a large company, and nothing crossed the CEO's desk without going through him. One morning he saw an email from a direct report flagging a technical problem affecting operations. He told the CEO what he had heard. The CEO asked, "Where did you get this information?" Parrish said he had heard it from the VP in charge of the division. The CEO's face showed disappointment. After a silence he said softly that his decisions could only be as good as his information. He was not getting the raw information, and he knew people in the organisation had an incentive to convey things in a way that covered up mistakes or made themselves look good.

United States general George Marshall always went to the source. During World War II, the War Department ran into a difficult situation with the Air Force in the Pacific: pilots were refusing to fly. Reports Marshall received suggested something was wrong with the planes. It was not a matter of parts. Marshall asked whether the pilots wanted the planes modified, and had one stripped of armour to cut its weight, because American planes were heavier and less maneuverable than Japanese Zeros. That was not the problem. Talking to the commander gave him no insight, so he sent someone "to look around and see things that weren't being reported—not just what they were yelling about." No one likes the person sent from the head office, and everyone is suspicious.

The person he sent found that the ground crews had no protection from mosquitoes. They worked on the planes at night under electric lights that attracted insects, and many mechanics were so full of malaria or antimalarial medication that the pilots no longer trusted their work and refused to fly. Headquarters, in mosquito-protected areas, was focused on ammunition, parts and food. Marshall overrode part of the tonnage allocated to combat supplies and got mosquito nets.

Parrish cites Tim Urban's picture of chefs and line cooks. Both can follow a recipe, and when things go to plan there is no difference in process or result. When things go wrong the chef knows why, and the line cook often does not. The chef has built depth of understanding through years of experience, experimentation and reflection, so the chef can diagnose the problem.

He also cites Leonardo da Vinci's journals, which contain notes on how to get the right information, such as "Get the master of arithmetic to show you how to square a triangle" and "Get a master of hydraulics to tell you how to repair a lock, canal and mill in the Lombard manner."

method.intro: Parrish's safeguards for getting what he calls HiFi information.
steps: Go to the source whenever you can. In his words: "Whenever possible, you need to learn something, see something, or do something for yourself."

Run an experiment, a low-risk way of gathering important information. His example is Tuft & Needle, which took orders on a landing page before it had a product, then refunded the orders and started the company.
When you must rely on someone else, evaluate their motivations and incentives, and consider the lens through which they see the situation.
While gathering information, hold back your own judgment. Ask questions, keep your thoughts to yourself, and stay curious.
Before executing a decision, check that the people carrying it out know the goals, the most important objective, and the signs and trip wires (see the commander's intent card).

limits: Parrish says the best information is sometimes the least transmissible. Even the person closest to the problem has a limited view: the line worker knows the local fix and lacks the broader perspective.
