concepts.concept: People accept a plan without adopting its goal (Ackoff's dam and violin)
concepts.name: Agreeing without sharing the goal

card.title: A plan accepted without its goal
idea: Ackoff's Fable 2.5 shows a plan that people said yes to without adopting the planners' goal. His moral: the reason for one person's giving may not be the reason for another's receiving. He says the cultural gap that keeps problem solvers from understanding the objectives of others can occur even within small and apparently homogeneous organisations.

Ackoff's protection is participation. Where solutions depend on the reactions of others, taking part in the problem-solving process is the best protection against unexpected responses. He adds that failing to consult people with a stake in our decisions is often seen as an act of aggression, because it often is, and that inviting participation is an act of conciliation and a demonstration of care and concern.

stories.text:
A Mexican government agency responsible for water resources decided to build a dam and use it to irrigate a large farming area, whose productivity it believed could be doubled. When the plans were done it sent representatives to the rural areas to explain the project to the peasants and ask whether they wanted it. The answers were uniformly yes. The dam and irrigation system were built at great expense and failed to produce the expected increase in productivity.

The puzzled experts went to find out why. The peasants had reduced the amount of land they cultivated, which gave them more time to work in nearby towns or do nothing. They felt the extra work needed to use all their land was not worth the small increase in income. One expert asked a consultant why the peasants had not said this before the dam was built.

The consultant could have said, "Because you didn't ask the right questions. You incorrectly assumed you knew the answers." He did not. He asked the expert whether he played the violin. The expert said no. Then the consultant asked what he would do if offered a Stradivarius. He said he would accept it. The consultant asked why, since he could not play it. The expert got the point.

method.intro: Bungay Stanier gives a way to ask about someone's aims without starting a defence. His reasons: a question starting with 'Why' puts people on the defensive, and asking why usually means you are trying to solve the problem yourself.
steps: When you are tempted to start a question with 'Why', rephrase it to start with 'What'.
Instead of "Why did you do that?" ask "What were you hoping for here?"
Instead of "Why did you think this was a good idea?" ask "What made you choose this course of action?"
Instead of "Why are you bothering with this?" ask "What's important for you here?"

card.tension: Maister (see the what-why-how card) says a supervisor should spend a lot of time on the why of the work, meaning its purpose. Bungay Stanier says to avoid asking a person 'why' questions in a focused conversation. The two use 'why' differently. Maister is about telling people the purpose of the work. Bungay Stanier is about the wording of questions you put to someone about what they did.

quotes.text: The reason for one person's giving may not be the reason for another's receiving.
quotes.source: Russell L. Ackoff, The Art of Problem Solving

quotes.text: A failure to consult others who have a stake in our decisions is often seen as an act of aggression, because it often is.
quotes.source: Russell L. Ackoff, The Art of Problem Solving

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: An agent that accepts a plan has not necessarily taken on its goal. Put the goal in the prompt, then ask the agent to say what the goal is and why its approach serves it. When you question a choice it made, ask "What were you trying to achieve here?" and avoid "Why did you do this?"

concepts.concept: Named models as compression; latticework; man with a hammer; cargo cult
concepts.name: Mental models as compression

card.title: Named models as compression
idea: A named mental model is a compressed idea. It packs a structural understanding from physics, economics, psychology or another field into one term. Super Thinking calls these "super models". Someone who has internalized a model can skip the low-level working and start from the higher-level analysis.
The comparison the book uses is multiplication, which is a shortcut for repeated addition. A thinker who knows the named model does not have to rebuild the reasoning from scratch each time.
why: Munger argues for holding many models from many disciplines, arranged as a latticework, so that experience hangs on several lenses at once. With several lenses a situation has fewer blind spots, and no single tool gets over-used.

stories.text: The book cites linguist Peter Gordon's study of the Pirahã, a people of the Amazon rain forest in Brazil, as recounted by Brian Butterworth in The Guardian on October 20, 2004. The Pirahã have no words for specific numbers beyond "a smaller amount" and "a larger amount". On matching tasks their accuracy dropped sharply once there were more than three objects.

The authors take the physics model of "critical mass" and apply it to a business that rents out dormant power tools. The model moves the thinking straight to two questions: how dense the supply of tools must be in a neighborhood, and what level of demand the business needs. They also quote Munger's 1994 speech at USC Marshall, where he says that 80 or 90 important models carry about 90 percent of the freight in making someone worldly-wise.
Munger warns against the "man-with-a-hammer" syndrome. A person who knows one model treats every problem as a case for that model, like a chiropractor who forces every problem to fit one treatment.

method.source: Super Thinking and Poor Charlie's Almanack
steps: Take in the big ideas across disciplines: physics, biology, chemistry, economics, psychology.
Array direct and vicarious experience on this latticework.
Identify the model that fits the situation, and use it to reason at a higher level.
Test your understanding by explaining each model to a partner and by writing it down.

limits: Using a model without understanding its mechanics produces "cargo cult" thinking: the form is imitated and the substance is missing. The test in the method (explain it, write it down) is there to catch that. Holding only one or two models leads people to bend reality to fit them.

quotes.text: When you don't use mental models, strategic thinking is like using addition when multiplication is available to you.
quotes.source: Weinberg and McCann, Super Thinking

concepts.concept: Leaders' shorthand means different things to each listener
concepts.name: Pet phrases

card.title: Pet phrases and management shorthand
idea: Leaders pick up pet phrases that compress an instruction into a few words: "We need to understand the physics of...", "We need proof points for...", "We need to close the loop on...". The leader has a full description behind the phrase. The listeners each fill it in with their own.
why: Webb points to the curse of knowledge and the illusion of transparency. The speaker assumes the meaning is obvious and does not notice that colleagues are guessing. The result is a team that works to different standards while everyone believes they agree.

stories.text: Webb describes her client Rob and other executives who repeatedly used phrases such as "We need to understand the physics of...", "We need proof points for..." and "We need to close the loop on...". When she talked with their teams, people held very different assumptions about what "understanding the physics" would require.

steps: Audit your recurring phrases and write down what each one means to you.
Ask colleagues: "When I say [phrase], what do you think I mean?"
Share explicit definitions so the team works to one standard.

concepts.concept: Proximate genus and specific difference; vagueness vs ambiguity
concepts.name: Defining terms

card.title: Defining terms
idea: McInerny holds that clear thinking depends on matching words to ideas, and ideas to reality. Logic works at the level of the statement, because only statements can be true or false. A statement is built from words, so a loose word weakens it.

His tool is the logical definition. You place a term in its immediate general class (the proximate genus) and then name what sets it apart within that class (the specific difference). The result removes two problems. Vagueness is a blurred referent: it is unclear what the word points at. Ambiguity is several possible meanings: it is clear what the word could point at, and there is more than one candidate.
why: Ideas are subjective evocations of objective facts. McInerny contrasts simple ideas such as "cat", which map one-to-one to a physical thing, with complex ideas such as "democracy", which map one-to-many: constitutions, events, laws, institutions. The more complex the idea, the more a precise word matters, and the more a listener has to guess when it is missing.

stories.text: To show the proximate genus, McInerny uses Aristotle's definition of man as "the rational animal". "Animal" is the proximate genus and "rationality" is the specific difference. He compares this to putting toys in the toy box instead of in the room, the house or the city, in Lansing, Iowa: the nearest container is the one that gives the precise location.
A trail sign reads "BEAR TO THE RIGHT". It could tell hikers to take the right-hand path, or it could warn them that a bear is on that path. McInerny uses it as his example of ambiguity.

steps: Place the term in its proximate genus, the immediate class it shares a nature with.
Identify its specific difference, what sets it apart within that class.
Express the thought in complete declarative sentences and spell out the needed background.
Avoid vague words, ambiguous terms, evasive euphemisms and double negatives.

limits: A logical definition states the exact nature of a thing. When you do not yet know a thing well enough for that, McInerny accepts a looser "definition by description", which catalogs observable characteristics.

quotes.text: Putting the right word to an idea is not an automatic process, and sometimes it can be quite challenging.
quotes.source: McInerny, Being Logical

concepts.concept: Every metaphor highlights some aspects and hides others
concepts.name: What a metaphor hides

card.title: What a metaphor hides
idea: Lakoff and Johnson argue that thought and everyday language are metaphorical. Metaphors let people grasp abstract concepts through physical experience, such as spatial orientation. Because a metaphor presents some aspects of a concept, it leaves others out. Highlighting makes an abstract idea manageable, and hiding distorts the full picture.
why: Michael Reddy's "conduit metaphor" structures how English speakers talk about communication: ideas are objects, words are containers and communicating is sending. The metaphor makes some features of communication easy to see and others hard to see.

stories.text: Lakoff and Johnson report Reddy's finding that the conduit metaphor ("It's hard to get that idea across", "I gave you that idea") accounts for over 70 percent of the expressions used to talk about language in English.

They examine ARGUMENT IS WAR: "attack a position", "demolish an argument", "his claims are indefensible". This metaphor highlights the combative side of debate. It hides the cooperative side, taking turns and reaching mutual understanding.

Galef notes that militarized metaphors for argument ("defending beliefs", "shooting down claims") reinforce what she calls the soldier mindset, which aims at winning. She contrasts it with the scout mindset, which aims at mapping reality accurately.

limits: Metaphorical structuring is always partial. If it were total, one concept would be the other. In "TIME IS MONEY", time can be spent and saved like money, but a unit of lost time cannot be retrieved the way money can.

quotes.text: The very systematicity that allows us to comprehend one aspect of a concept in terms of another... will necessarily hide other aspects of the concept.
quotes.source: Lakoff and Johnson, Metaphors We Live By

concepts.concept: Simplifiable jargon and legalese hide errors; Garner's rules
concepts.name: Plain language

card.title: Plain language

sources.authors: Carl T. Bergstrom and Jevin D. West

idea: Jargon and legalese are compressed terms that fail outside a circle of experts. Garner's point is that they also hide problems: drafting errors, ambiguities and a lack of substance sit behind words that sound authoritative. Rewriting in plain words forces the problems into view.

Bloated phrases, doublets and triplets ("null and void") and archaic terms add words and no precision. Professionals use jargon to signal identity and authority, and lay readers find it pompous or unintelligible.
why: Plain language is more precise than traditional legal writing, because it uncovers the ambiguities, gaps and errors that the traditional style tends to hide. Bergstrom and West make a related point from the reader's side: Bruno Latour's "black boxes" are technical terms and mathematics that intimidate an audience and keep claims from being examined.

stories.text: Garner quotes an old law-firm email disclaimer full of legalese, including the phrase "hereinabove and/or hereinbelow", which sounds absurd to anyone outside the profession. He also reports judges' reading likes and dislikes, collected at a seminar with almost every judge in the state of Delaware taking part. Verbosity, legalese, run-on sentences and Latin were among the dislikes.

Aaron describes corporate counsel explaining a spin-off agreement to a marketing vice president: "The contractual language... may give rise to a non-frivolous preliminary injunction motion... parol evidence rule is likely to preclude testimony...". The VP was lost until someone translated it into plain English.

method.intro: Garner's rules for removing jargon:
steps: Eliminate simplifiable jargon and replace legalisms with everyday words ("before" for "prior to", "under" for "pursuant to").
Drop doublets and triplets. If one word covers the meaning ("transfer" for "alienate, transfer, and convey"), use it alone.
Call parties by their names, not by labels ending in -or and -ee ("mortgagor/mortgagee").
Avoid newly invented acronyms.

limits: The rules target simplifiable jargon. Real terms of art with no everyday equivalent, such as habeas corpus, stay.

quotes.text: From the draftsman's point of view, complexity intensifies the risk of error in the drafting and the risk of different interpretations in the reading
quotes.source: Siviglia and Kimble, quoted in Legal Writing in Plain English

quotes.text: plain language is more precise than traditional legal and official writing because it uncovers the ambiguities and gaps and errors that traditional style, with all its excesses, tends to hide.
quotes.source: Joseph Kimble, quoted in Legal Writing in Plain English

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: a lot of people talk about this idea of a company brain, right, or a context graph. I feel like those terms are unnecessarily complex uh or even abstract.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Ask the agent to restate a plan or a design in plain words before you approve it. If it cannot do that without the jargon, the plan has a gap. Do the same with your own task descriptions: replace the abstract label with the concrete thing it refers to.

concepts.concept: Tension: exact numbers for probabilities (Duke) vs fuzzy terms for values (Nguyen)
concepts.name: Precise or fuzzy?

card.title: Precise or fuzzy?
idea: Two books disagree about how exact language should be, and the disagreement depends on what is being described.

Duke is writing about probabilities. Verbal terms such as "likely" or "real possibility" hide how much two people differ, so she asks for percentages. Nguyen is writing about values. He argues that turning rich values into precise, mechanical terms and scores eliminates the room in which subtle values develop. In his account this is value capture.
why: Duke: "when you use these blunt terms, you and the other people in the conversation are often speaking different languages without even knowing it." A person who thinks something has a 30% chance, talking to a person with reliable information that it has 70%, needs that disagreement to come out. Vague words let both nod in agreement.

Nguyen: simplified metrics decide where you look. They travel across contexts and aggregate at scale, and they hide error because they point your attention at what they measure. Precise value language would suit a world in which we already knew what is important. Where we do not know, it closes off exploration.

stories.text: Andrew and Michael Mauboussin surveyed 1,700 people on the probability they associate with common verbal terms. The spread was wide. "Real possibility" ranged from about 20% to 80%. Duke has readers repeat the exercise with a four-person survey and expect to find the same disagreement.

In Garold Stasser and William Titus's experiment, four-person groups chose which of three candidates was best suited to be student body president. Researchers gave each member a dossier with positive and negative attributes of the candidates, built so that candidate A was the most favorable on all the information. Group members often did not share information that went against the group's view.

Wendy Nelson Espeland and Michael Sauder studied the U.S. News & World Report law school rankings (Engines of Anxiety). Before the rankings, law schools pursued different missions such as social justice, legal theory and corporate placement, described in words in Barron's guide. Once the rankings took over, schools dropped distinct missions and reshaped admissions and budgets to improve their score.
A pastor whose church set up an internal leaderboard for baptism rates stopped long-term spiritual care and moved to crowd-pleasing sermons that raised his ranking.

method.source: How to Decide and The Score
method.intro: For probabilities (Duke):
steps: Replace verbal terms with percentages.
Collect estimates independently and in writing.
Compile them anonymously, then compare.

For values (Nguyen), step back regularly from external metrics and check whether they match what you care about ("reflective control"). Keep "fuzzy values" such as fun, wisdom and connection with imprecise edges.

limits: McInerny (Being Logical) allows "definition by description" when an exact definition is not yet possible. Nguyen accepts that mechanical scores work for well-bounded games, for simple coordination and for large, easy-to-measure goods, and he names reducing poverty, decreasing CO2 emissions and increasing vaccination rates. He concedes that fuzzy rules make oversight at scale harder.
card.tension: Use numbers when you are estimating how likely something is and several people need to compare their beliefs. Keep the language open when you are describing what something is worth. The books address different objects, so they disagree less than they first seem to.

quotes.text: When you use these blunt terms, you and the other people in the conversation are often speaking different languages without even knowing it.
quotes.source: Duke, How to Decide

quotes.text: Fuzzy language is a cue for the person executing the rule to exercise their own judgment.
quotes.source: Nguyen, The Score

quotes.text: Precise values embody a closed-minded spirit about what's important in the world.
quotes.source: Nguyen, The Score

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When you ask an agent to judge something uncertain (will this migration break callers? is this test coverage enough?), ask for a percentage and the reasons, so you can see how sure it is. When you describe what "good" means for a design or a piece of writing, leave the standard in words and examples and do not reduce it to a score the agent will optimise.

concepts.concept: Formulas that look rigorous but aren't; check units and magnitudes
concepts.name: Mathiness

card.title: Mathiness

sources.authors: Carl T. Bergstrom and Jevin D. West

idea: "New-school bullshit" uses the language of mathematics, science, algorithms and statistics to give dubious claims an air of rigor. Mathiness is the version in formulas: expressions that look and feel like math and ignore the logical coherence of real mathematics.
why: Equations borrow the authority of quantitative fields. The authors describe an algebraic "shock and awe" that intimidates readers who feel unqualified to challenge it.

stories.text: The VMMC Quality Equation from healthcare quality management reads Q = (A × O × S) / W, with Q for Quality, A for Appropriateness, O for Outcomes, S for Service and W for Waste. It claims specific multiplicative relationships between quantities that are ill-defined and cannot be measured. Q = (A + O + S) / W would convey the same directional trends, which shows the formula is arbitrary.

The Trust Equation, from a 2005 book of that title, reads Trust = (Credibility + Reliability + Authenticity) / Perception of self-interest. As self-interest approaches zero, trust becomes infinite. A coin flip used to choose stocks has no self-interest, yet nobody trusts it infinitely. Because the terms are added, the formula also predicts high trust for someone with high authenticity and zero credibility.

Bergstrom picked up a packet of instant hot cocoa in a hotel lobby that said "99.9% caffeine-free". A 20-ounce Starbucks coffee contains 415 mg of caffeine, about 21 mg per fluid ounce, and a fluid ounce of water weighs about 28 grams. Drip coffee is therefore about 0.075 percent caffeine by weight, which makes regular coffee "99.9% caffeine-free" as well.

steps: Examine the data going into the black box for bias or flaws.
Sanity-check the output for plausibility.
Apply dimensional analysis: track the units through the equation.
Think in orders of magnitude: estimate claims to the nearest power of ten.

limits: The target is specious quantitative claims. Modeling that rests on sound data and logic is not in scope.

quotes.text: Mathiness refers to formulas and expressions that may look and feel like math—even as they disregard the logical coherence and formal rigor of actual mathematics.
quotes.source: Bergstrom and West, Calling Bullshit

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Treat a score, an estimate or a formula in an agent's report the way you would treat one in a vendor deck. Ask what went in, what units it has and whether the order of magnitude is plausible. An agent that reports "confidence 0.92" has not told you how it was computed.

concepts.concept: Paltering and weasel wording; restate with someone responsible
concepts.name: Weasel words and paltering

card.title: Weasel words and paltering

sources.authors: Carl T. Bergstrom and Jevin D. West

idea: Paltering means misleading someone with statements that are literally true, by relying on what the statement implies. Weasel wording is the use of passive voice, euphemism and hedges ("mistakes were made", "people are saying") to spread responsibility around so that nobody holds it.
why: Communication depends on meaning that goes beyond the literal words; this is Grice's implicature. Outright lying is punished socially. A speaker can mislead while keeping deniability by using the gap between what is literally true and what is implied.

stories.text: Bill Clinton told Jim Lehrer on the NewsHour that "there is no sexual relationship [with Monica Lewinsky]". He later defended it as literally true because of the present tense of "is".

After a 2019 NBC News investigation found that global manufacturers likely used materials produced by child labor in Madagascar, where children worked mica mines in the blazing sun for forty cents a day, a Fiat Chrysler spokesperson said the company "engages in collaborative action with global stakeholders across industries and along the value chain to promote and develop our raw material supply chain."

The authors give everyday cases. Toothpaste that reduces plaque "by up to" 50 percent is false only if it works better than that. A politician says "people are saying" that an opponent has ties to organized crime. A manager says "mistakes were made" to go through the motions of an apology without blaming anyone.

steps: Analyze the implicature: compare the literal statement with what it implies.
Ask the journalist's questions: who is making the claim, how do they know, and what are they selling?
Translate to plain language: remove euphemism and passive voice, and restate the claim with a clear person responsible.

quotes.text: If I deliberately lead you to draw the wrong conclusions by saying things that are technically not untrue, I am paltering.
quotes.source: Bergstrom and West, Calling Bullshit

quotes.text: weasel wording uses the gap between literal meaning and implicature to avoid taking responsibility for things
quotes.source: Bergstrom and West, Calling Bullshit

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Agent status reports can palter without intent: "the tests pass" can mean the tests that were run, or the ones that remained after the agent edited them. Ask for the exact command that ran, its output and who or what changed which files. Rewrite vague claims in the active voice ("the agent deleted two tests") before you accept them.

concepts.concept: Answer first, grouped and ordered support; SCR opening
concepts.name: The pyramid principle

card.title: The pyramid principle
idea: Minto's structure puts the answer first. A document opens with one summarizing idea, the governing thought. Below it sit grouped ideas that answer the questions the level above raises (Why? How?). The groups should be mutually exclusive and, together, cover the point.
The mind imposes order on information by grouping it into pyramids. Synthesis means thinking one level of abstraction higher: from a set of facts to the single idea that states how they relate.
why: Working memory holds roughly seven items (Minto cites George A. Miller's "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two": five to nine items, and Minto adds "I'm a five myself"). Grouping replaces many items with one summary and cuts the load while keeping the details retrievable. When the summarizing idea comes first, the reader does not have to hold the details and work out the connection at the same time.

stories.text: A husband going out for a magazine is given a shopping list: grapes, milk, potatoes, apples, eggs, butter, oranges, sour cream, carrots. Nine loose items exceed working memory. Grouped as dairy (milk, eggs, butter, sour cream), fruit (grapes, apples, oranges) and vegetables (potatoes, carrots), the three categories prompt recall of all nine.
In Wolfgang Köhler's experiments with six dots, observers see two groups of three because of proximity, not six separate points.

G.K. Chesterton's essay on keeping pigs as pets shows the vertical question-and-answer pattern. Pigs should be pets. Why? Pigs are fat and beautiful. Why is fat beautiful? In English tradition fat symbolizes power joined with kindness.

Minto's Big Chief hamburger emporium gets many deliveries and asks for a revised beverage billing system: hold the delivery tickets, record them on computer tape and mail one check a month. The situation is the request. The complication is that management asks whether it makes sense. The question is whether it does. The answer is to reject it, because of fraud and audit risks.

method.intro: The three rules of the pyramid, then two ways to build one.
steps: Ideas at any level summarize the ideas grouped below them.
Ideas in a group are the same kind; one plural noun can describe them.
Ideas in a group are logically ordered: deductive (major premise, minor premise, conclusion), chronological (time or cause and effect), structural (a whole into parts) or comparative (by importance).

Top-down: draw a top box with subject and predicate. State the situation and complication so the reader's question is clear. Put the answer in the top box. Derive the key-line sub-questions (Why? How?) and answer them on the line below, inductively or deductively.
Bottom-up, when the top is unclear: list every point you want to make, work out how they relate, and draw a summarizing conclusion one level higher.

Opening storyline (SCR): state the situation the reader will accept as true, then the complication, then the question it raises, then the resolution. Vary the order by audience: resolution first for busy executives, situation and complication first to build buy-in.
Conn and McLean use a variant, Situation-Observation-Resolution, for what McKinsey calls the "one-day answer": a project summary that can be written at any stage.

limits: Thoughts stay hazy until they are written down, so a pyramid is not built perfectly in one pass. The structure is found bottom-up by grouping or top-down by asking questions and answering them. The round2 text also says that leading with the resolution can set off defensiveness in a hostile audience; that limit was not found in Minto.
card.tension: See the card "Conclusion first, or step by step?" for a case where Aaron and Berger advise against leading with the answer.

quotes.text: The clearest sequence is always to give the summarizing idea before you give the individual ideas being summarized.
quotes.source: Minto, The Pyramid Principle

quotes.text: All mental processes (e.g., thinking, remembering, problem solving) apparently utilize this grouping and summarizing process, so that the information in a person's mind might be thought of as being organized into one giant conglomeration of related pyramids.
quotes.source: Minto, The Pyramid Principle

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Ask the agent to report with the answer first, then the support in groups: the conclusion, the three reasons, then the detail. Open a task brief with situation, complication, and the question you need answered. Ask for the structure before the full draft, so you can fix the top of the pyramid while it is still cheap.

concepts.concept: Write it all down, then group under 3–4 headings
concepts.name: Dump and chunk

card.title: Dump and chunk
idea: Dump and Chunk is a two-step technique in Webb's FUSE framework. First, unload swirling thoughts from your head onto paper. Second, group them under a small number of themes. The aim is to simplify a complex problem.
why: Working memory handles about four to seven chunks at once. Thoughts that stay in the head keep circling. Once they are written down they stop competing for space, and grouping under three or four headings lets the brain treat a lot of information as three or four items.

stories.text: Antony Mayfield, founder and CEO of the digital agency Brilliant Noise, uses Dump and Chunk under pressure. He writes or mind-maps his thoughts and groups them under three or four themes, such as timing, type of work and objectives. This lets him see patterns, connections and missing steps.
Michael Roberts, CMO of a large financial services company, carries blank paper so he can write a brain dump by hand when he is taking in a lot of new information.

steps: Dump: write out all thoughts, worries, facts and half-formed ideas without judging them, ideally by hand.
Parking lot: put off-topic thoughts on a separate list for later.
Chunk: group the notes under three or four headings, such as sub-questions, themes or paths forward.
Reverse chunk: if you start from a huge question, split it into three or four smaller sub-questions.

quotes.text: Research on working memory has found it's easier for us to handle large amounts of information if we arrange it into a smallish number of chunks.
quotes.source: Webb, Leadership Intelligence

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Before you write a prompt for a large task, dump everything you know about it into a scratch file, with constraints, worries and half-ideas. Group the notes into three or four headings and use those as the sections of the brief. You can also give the dump to the agent and ask it to propose the chunks, then correct them.

concepts.concept: Atkins's seven steps: set-up to delivery; short sentences
concepts.name: The art of explanation

card.title: The art of explanation
idea: Atkins, a BBC journalist, describes a seven-step process for explaining something. It removes obstacles to understanding by distilling the material, grouping it into strands and ordering the strands before delivery. The result is a dense message with nothing in it that distracts.
why: Audiences are overloaded and attention is short. Cutting unnecessary detail, long sentences and competing inputs keeps attention and gets more useful information into each minute.

stories.text: While reporting on the 2015 Greek debt crisis, Atkins kept three lists to handle the complexity: what he understood, what he struggled with, and the uncertainties that were emerging.
When editing an explainer Atkins uses a "dial test": he cuts anything wordy or non-essential that might make attention drift.
Session guitarist Dean Parks describes the 1977 Steely Dan sessions for the album Aja, where Becker and Fagen worked past the "perfection point" until the playing sounded natural, almost improvised.

steps: Set-up: define the purpose, the audience, the questions they will have and what they do not yet understand.
Find the information: gather facts from direct, reliable sources into an "info dump".
Distil: strip the material down to the smallest essential nuggets (the "ball mill").
Organise: group the nuggets into strands, choose a narrative frame (chronological, zoom out, block by block) and choose strong openers and closers.
Link: connect the strands with joining phrases and hooks.
Tighten: use short sentences (for speech, about fifteen words at most), put subjects early, cut filler and get a second opinion.
Deliver: say it out loud to iron out creases until it flows.

quotes.text: Simplicity is the key to understanding. Short words in short sentences present the listener or reader with the fewest obstacles to comprehension.
quotes.source: BBC journalist Allan Little, quoted in The Art of Explanation

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When you need the agent to explain a diff or a design to you, state the audience and what they do not yet know, and ask for short sentences with the main point first. Ask it to cut anything the reader would not miss. Read the explanation aloud or ask yourself whether you could repeat it to a teammate.

concepts.concept: Pitch as press release and FAQ in plain "Oprah-speak"
concepts.name: PR/FAQ in plain words

card.title: PR/FAQ in plain words
idea: Flyvbjerg and Gardner cite former Amazon executive Ian McAllister on Jeff Bezos's PR/FAQ. A new project is pitched as a press release plus an FAQ, written in plain "Oprah-speak". The format is meant to stop fuzzy thinking and unsupported assumptions from hiding behind jargon.
why: Plain wording leaves nowhere for fuzzy thinking or unsupported assumptions to hide.

steps: Pitch the new initiative as a press release and an FAQ before work begins.
Write both in plain language.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Before you hand a large feature to an agent, write the announcement you would publish when it is done and the five questions a skeptical user would ask. If you cannot answer them in plain words, the brief is not ready.

concepts.concept: Question and answer in under 75 words on page one; no left-branching
concepts.name: The deep issue

card.title: The deep issue
idea: Garner's advice for analytical and persuasive writing starts with a "deep issue" on page one. It is a concrete summary of fewer than 75 words that combines the rule or factual premise, the question and the answer with the reasons. Below it, material is ordered logically or by descending importance, and every paragraph is built around a topic sentence.
why: Traditional legal and technical writing has verbosity, a disorganized "all-middle" structure and left-branching sentences that delay the main verb. Putting the question, the answer and the reasons first matches how readers process text, and it exposes ambiguities that legalese hides.

stories.text: Garner ran judicial-writing seminars in which judges listed what they liked and disliked reading. Verbosity, legalese and run-on sentences were among the dislikes. The seminar included almost every judge in the state of Delaware.
Betty S. Flowers' "Madman, Architect, Carpenter, Judge" model of the writing process says the Architect organizes the Madman's uninhibited ideas into an outline before drafting begins.

A court rule puts a list of five kinds of served papers, about 70 words long, before its main verb, "must be served". This is left-branching: the reader has to hold all the conditions before learning what is required.

steps: Deep issue: write a true summary on page one in fewer than 75 words, combining the rule or factual premise, the question, and the answer with its reasons.
Order logically: facts chronologically. In contracts and statutes, main obligations and general rules first, exceptions and narrow points after.
Divide and head: split the text into subparts with informative headings.
Center paragraphs: topic sentence first, no more than about 150 words on average, with explicit links between sentences.
Avoid left-branching: put the subject and the main verb early.

quotes.text: [T]he choice between precision and clarity is usually a false choice.
quotes.source: Joseph Kimble, quoted in Legal Writing in Plain English

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Start every task description with a summary of under 75 words: the situation, the question and what a good answer looks like. Ask the agent to open its report in the same way. Keep the subject and verb of each instruction early in the sentence, and list conditions after the instruction.

concepts.concept: Easy text feels true; strain triggers scrutiny
concepts.name: Cognitive ease

card.title: Cognitive ease
idea: Kahneman describes cognitive ease as a state in which System 1 processes a message smoothly. Clear type, simple words, high contrast and familiar, coherent associations all produce it. A message that is easy to process feels pleasant, trustworthy and true. Cognitive strain, the opposite state, wakes System 2, which brings more skepticism and more careful checking.
why: System 1 rates every input on a scale from easy to strained and treats ease as a sign of truth, safety and validity. Effortful material engages System 2's slower thinking.

stories.text: Danny Oppenheimer wrote a paper titled "Consequences of Erudite Vernacular Utilized Irrespective of Necessity: Problems with Using Long Words Needlessly". It found that familiar ideas expressed in pretentious language lead readers to rate the author as less intelligent and less credible.

Forty Princeton students took Shane Frederick's Cognitive Reflection Test. Of those who saw it in normal font, 90% made at least one mistake. Of those who saw it in a barely legible font, 35% did, because the strain activated System 2.
Reports from fictitious Turkish brokerage firms carried more weight when the firm's name was easy to pronounce (Artan) than when it was hard (Taahhut).

In Robert Zajonc's mere-exposure study in Michigan student newspapers, made-up Turkish-sounding words (kadirga, saricik, biwonjni) were later judged to mean something good after they had been shown repeatedly.
Rhyming aphorisms ("Woes unite foes") were rated as more insightful than non-rhyming versions ("Woes unite enemies").

method.intro: To write for cognitive ease:
steps: Maximize legibility: clear fonts and high contrast.
Use short, familiar words.
Link statements coherently to beliefs the reader already holds.
Make the message memorable with rhythm, rhyme or an easy name.

limits: Ease works against you when you want readers to think hard, catch errors or resist a plausible intuition. In those cases deliberate strain forces scrutiny.

quotes.text: If you care about being thought credible and intelligent, do not use complex language where simpler language will do.
quotes.source: Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: A fluent agent answer feels correct for the same reason. Treat smooth, confident prose as no evidence of accuracy, and check the claims that matter. When you review agent work, change how it looks (read the diff in a different order or tool, ask for a table) to create some strain.

concepts.concept: Analysis without a point of view (APK)
concepts.name: The anxious parade of knowledge

card.title: The anxious parade of knowledge
idea: Conn and McLean report that at McKinsey the failure of presenting analysis with no point of view was called the "anxious parade of knowledge", or APK. The team shows everything it found and never says what it concludes: reams of data and unfinished models that do not become a coherent story.
why: Memory cannot hold an unstructured dump. When the writer does not break the issue down or state a governing thought, the audience has nothing to organize the material around.

stories.text: Conn and McLean describe the APK as one of the causes of failure at the later stages of problem solving: giant models that are not quite finished, and large amounts of data produced without a clear point of view.

steps: Break vague problems into SMART criteria and logic trees before analyzing data.
Check horizontal logic: storyboard so that the slide titles, read in order, form one continuous argument.

quotes.text: in McKinsey this was called the anxious parade of knowledge, or APK
quotes.source: Conn and McLean, Bulletproof Problem Solving

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When an agent returns a long list of findings, ask it for the single conclusion and the three facts that support it. Ask it to state what it thinks should be done. A report with no position leaves you to do the analysis again.

concepts.concept: Thesis, antithesis, synthesis: answer the strongest counterargument
concepts.name: Thesis, antithesis, synthesis

card.title: Thesis, antithesis, synthesis
idea: Garner recommends a three-part argument for persuasive writing. State your case (thesis). Confront the strongest counterarguments (antithesis). Show why your case prevails (synthesis). He calls this the dialectical method.
why: A writer who ignores counterarguments loses credibility, and a critical reader resists. Dealing with the opposing view in the middle of the argument shows thoroughness and candor, and it disarms objections before the reader raises them.

stories.text: In the 1998-99 Clinton impeachment, Garner notes, an advocate for Clinton had to concede that the conduct was bad before arguing that it did not meet the threshold of high crimes and misdemeanors. An advocate on Kenneth Starr's side had to concede that high crimes require severe wrongdoing before arguing that perjury and obstruction met it.

steps: Thesis: state the rule and show how the facts support your proposition.
Antithesis: acknowledge the strongest counterarguments or unfavorable facts in the middle.
Synthesis: rebut them by showing why the rule, policy or evidence overrides them.
Restate the conclusion.

limits: Giving the opponent's arguments too much space before answering can validate them and confuse the reader.

quotes.text: You must weigh and address all serious ones, and the dialectical method of arguing is the best tool for this.
quotes.source: Garner, Legal Writing in Plain English

quotes.text: At its simplest, its form is thesis-antithesis-conclusion.
quotes.source: Garner, Legal Writing in Plain English

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Ask the agent to argue for its proposed design and then to state the strongest case against it, and say why the proposal still holds. Do this before you accept a plan. If the agent cannot name a serious objection, ask it to try again.

concepts.concept: Layered, visual, user-tested legal documents
concepts.name: Legal design

card.title: Legal design

sources.authors: Marcelo Corrales Compagnucci, Helena Haapio, Margaret Hagan and Michael Doherty (eds.)

idea: Legal design applies human-centered design to legal documents, decisions and systems. It turns material written "by lawyers for lawyers" into something that the people it affects can understand and use.
why: Dense legalese goes unread or is misunderstood, which leads to breaches, congestion and injustice. Visual patterns, layered information and clear typography improve comprehension and let people act on their own.

stories.text: Creative Commons licenses come in three layers: machine-readable code, a human-readable "Commons Deed" with icons, and the full legal code.
Robert de Rooy in South Africa produced comic-strip employment contracts for fruit pickers and other workers with low literacy.
The Center for Urban Pedagogy and designer Candy Chang made "Vendor Power!", a guide for New York street vendors with short sentences in five languages and diagrams of vendors' rights and rules.

Mariana Bernal Fandiño describes the Access to Justice Design Lab at Andes University in Bogotá. Working with the Constitutional Court of Colombia, the lab redesigned long tutela decisions with templates, timelines and summaries.

steps: Move from "unconscious drafter" to "conscious designer" with the user as the focus.
Interview and observe users in their real setting.
Apply design patterns, for example the WorldCC Contract Design Pattern Library: user-guide format, skimmable headings, numbered steps, icons and layers.
Prototype and test comprehension with real users before deploying.

limits: Simplifying without checking legal requirements can drop mandatory clauses or create ambiguity that undermines enforceability.

quotes.text: Demand is growing to transform what was drafted
quotes.source: Legal Design

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Write agent instructions and project docs for the reader who will use them. Put a short layer first (what to do, the commands to run) and the long reference after it. Test the document by giving it to a fresh agent session and watching where it goes wrong.

concepts.concept: Issue trees that don't overlap and cover everything
concepts.name: MECE issue trees

card.title: MECE issue trees

sources.authors: Bernard Garrette, Corey Phelps and Olivier Sibony

idea: An issue tree splits a problem into parts that do not overlap (mutually exclusive) and that together cover the whole problem (collectively exhaustive). The common abbreviation is MECE.
why: Jumping to an answer invites confirmation bias. Descartes' rule is to divide a problem into elementary parts, and an issue tree applies it. Parts that do not overlap avoid duplicated work. Parts that cover everything keep the real answer inside the tree.

stories.text: Librinova, a French self-publishing start-up, considers expanding into Canada through De Marque. Instead of confirming one hypothesis, the authors split the question into sub-issues: market size, partner capabilities, deal structure and other countries.

Starbucks revenue growth is split into existing customers and new customers. Existing customers are split into visit frequency and spend per visit. An "other ideas" branch catches anything the split missed.

steps: Define the problem with TOSCA (Trouble, Owner, Success criteria, Constraints, Actors) and write a core question.
Choose the tree: a component tree for exploration, a deductive tree (profit or ROIC) when the relationships are known, an inductive tree built from cases, or a decision tree for sequential choices.
Enforce MECE: no overlapping branches, and branches that cover 100% (old/new, inside/outside, these/others).
Use industry or functional frameworks as building blocks.
Prune with a 2x2 of impact against ability to influence.

limits: The method is slow and analytical, and weak for radical creative problems, where design thinking fits better. Forcing pre-packaged frameworks onto unique problems distorts them.

quotes.text: A MECE list is like a solved jigsaw puzzle: the pieces fit with no overlap, and their combination covers the whole picture.
quotes.source: Garrette, Phelps and Sibony, Cracked It!

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Before an agent starts debugging or planning a broad change, ask it to list the possible causes or areas as a tree with no overlaps and an explicit "other" branch. Then have it check one branch at a time. This keeps it from settling on the first plausible hypothesis.

concepts.concept: Tension: conclusion first (Minto) vs small steps for bad news (Aaron)
concepts.name: Conclusion first, or step by step?

card.title: Conclusion first, or step by step?
idea: Minto and Garner say to put the answer, the governing thought or the deep issue first. Aaron and Berger say a stark conclusion up front can block understanding, and that bad news should be delivered in small steps. The two positions describe different situations.
why: Minto's side: working memory holds roughly five to nine items, so a reader who has the governing thought can place each detail as it arrives. Aaron's side: on hearing life-altering news, people often enter what sociologist Douglas Maynard calls a "noetic crisis". If the client catches the negative import of the first phrase or two, emotions may stop them from absorbing the words that follow, even if they technically hear them.

stories.text: Aaron has watched many law students give actor-clients a perfectly accurate explanation of summary judgment and then, without a break in tone or speed, finish with the bad news: "that is why the other side is likely to win on summary judgment, and you will not recover anything." The actor-clients said the lawyer's matter-of-fact voice made them feel the lawyer was "strolling along a logical road" and was unaffected by its conclusion.

Aaron draws on Douglas Maynard's research on how people deliver bad news. A speaker forecasts that news is coming, delivers it in small bits with real pauses, and checks how the listener has understood it.

method.intro: Aaron's method for bad news:
steps: Deliver information in small bits, with real pauses between separate concepts and ideas.
Forecast the news before giving it.
Check how the client understands it.
Offer alternative meanings.

limits: Aaron warns that softening with euphemisms distorts reality, so the pacing must not turn into hiding the news.
card.tension: Use the conclusion-first order for a reader who wants to decide or act and who is not upset by the answer (a status report, a design review). Use paced disclosure when the answer is bad news for the listener and understanding depends on their reaction (a failed project, a lost motion).

quotes.text: The clearest sequence is always to give the summarizing idea before you give the individual ideas being summarized.
quotes.source: Minto, The Pyramid Principle

quotes.text: Deliver information in small bits, PAUSING—really PAUSING—between separate concepts and ideas.
quotes.source: Aaron, Client Science

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Ask the agent for the answer first when it reports on its own work. When you tell an agent that its work is wrong, give it the failing evidence and one correction at a time, and ask it to say back what it understands before it acts.

concepts.concept: Calculate under known risk; simple rules under uncertainty (1/N, hiatus, Ottawa)
concepts.name: Risk vs uncertainty

card.title: Known risk versus uncertainty
idea: Gigerenzer separates two kinds of situation. Under known risk, all the alternatives and their probabilities are known, as in a lottery. Under uncertainty, the probabilities are unknown or keep changing.
His rule: under known risk, calculate. Under uncertainty, use a simple rule of thumb (a one-reason decision or a fast-and-frugal tree) that ignores part of the information.
why: Under uncertainty, a complex model fits too many parameters to noisy history. It matches the past very closely and predicts the future badly (overfitting). A simple rule ignores the unreliable detail and so makes less total error. Gigerenzer calls this the bias-variance dilemma and the "less is more" effect.
Under known risk the probabilities do not move, so exact calculation is the best method.

stories.text: Harry Markowitz won the Nobel Prize for mean-variance portfolio optimization. For his own retirement savings he used a simple rule instead: 1/N, which means allocating your money equally to each of N funds. Gigerenzer adds that 1/N beat mean-variance in six of seven tests, and that the complex methods would need about 500 years of stock data to pay off.

Three companies (an airline, an apparel retailer and CDNow) wanted to forecast which customers would buy again. The simple hiatus rule says a customer who has not bought for nine months is inactive. It beat the complex Pareto/NBD model for the airline (77 percent against 74 percent) and for the apparel retailer, and tied for CDNow.

The Ottawa Ankle Rules are a fast-and-frugal tree. A doctor asks at most four questions about pain and bone tenderness and walks through four steps. The rules cut unnecessary X-rays while still catching fractures.

The turkey illusion comes from Taleb. Every feeding confirms the turkey's belief that people look after it, until the day before Thanksgiving. The turkey has treated uncertainty as if it were calculable risk.

method.source: Risk Savvy and Algorithms to Live By
method.intro: Gigerenzer's steps, then the matching tools from Christian and Griffiths.
steps: Decide whether the situation is known risk or uncertainty.
Under uncertainty, choose a simple rule that ignores non-essential information (a one-reason decision or a fast-and-frugal tree).
Look for a simple solution before building an elaborate calculation.
Christian and Griffiths add a way to build the simple model: penalize complexity so that unimportant factors are pushed to zero (the Lasso, see the regularization card).
When new data is noisy or each extra step adds little, stop early (Early Stopping).

limits: In stable, well-defined environments with known probabilities, calculation beats heuristics.
card.tension: Nudge (Thaler and Sunstein) documents people misusing simple rules in investing. A dollar invested in 1925 was worth $18 in Treasury bills by 2005 (3.7 percent a year) and $2,658 in stocks (10.4 percent a year). New plan participants put more into equities near the 2000 peak and were down to 54 percent two years later, timing the market backwards. In the Read and Loewenstein Halloween experiment, every child offered a choice of two bars at one house took one of each, against 48 percent at two adjacent houses. Nudge does not argue for mean-variance optimization. Its remedy is defaults, automatic rebalancing and life-cycle funds. Gigerenzer's resolution: optimization fits known risk, and heuristics fit uncertainty and limited, noisy data.

quotes.text: In an uncertain world, complex decision making methods involving more information and calculation are often worse
quotes.source: Gerd Gigerenzer, Risk Savvy

quotes.text: To make good decisions in an uncertain world, one has to ignore part of the information, which is exactly what rules of thumb do
quotes.source: Gerd Gigerenzer, Risk Savvy

quotes.text: Complex problems do not always require complex solutions
quotes.source: Gerd Gigerenzer, Risk Savvy

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Before you write a long, detailed instruction for an agent, ask whether the task is known risk (a stable procedure with a known right answer) or uncertainty (new, changing, noisy). For the second kind, give the agent two or three plain decision rules and the goal. Long rule lists for uncertain work tend to fit last week's cases.

concepts.concept: Rules are frozen decisions; judgment by exception; redesign when a rule becomes a decision
concepts.name: Rules are frozen decisions

card.title: Rules as frozen decisions

sources.authors: Ajay Agrawal, Joshua Gans, Avi Goldfarb

idea: A rule is a decision made in advance. Standard operating procedures and checklists hold an organization together because other people can rely on them without deciding again.

Agrawal, Gans and Goldfarb argue that rules fit when information is costly or uncertain, or when many decisions are tightly coupled and the system needs reliability. When accurate prediction becomes cheap and the stakes are high, a decision made case by case can replace the rule.
why: Rules cut cognitive load and remove uncertainty for everyone else in the system. They are also rigid, and organizations build costly scaffolding to absorb the inefficiency they cause. Once prediction is cheap, decisions can be tailored. The system around them then has to cope with less fixed reliability.

stories.text: Jerry Reinsdorf asked Michael Jordan, who was recovering from a broken foot with a 10 percent risk of a career-ending injury, whether he would take a headache pill if one pill in ten was lethal. Jordan answered that it depends how bad the headache is. A decision combines prediction (the probabilities) with judgment (how much each outcome matters).

During COVID-19, twelve large companies (the founding partners of the CDL Rapid Screening Consortium) used rapid antigen tests to decide case by case who could come to work. This replaced blanket shutdown rules.

Lavish airport terminals are expensive scaffolding. Singapore installed a garden with a five-story waterfall, Doha has a swimming pool, and Vancouver has an aquarium. The authors treat them as a cost that hides the uncertainty behind the rule that passengers arrive two to three hours early.

steps: Identify the rules, checklists and SOPs that hold the organization together.
Isolate the uncertainty behind each rule.
Use prediction (such as AI) to make that information cheap.
Check whether turning the rule into a decision disrupts interdependent decisions, and redesign the system to match.
Use judgment by exception: automate the common, well-understood cases and leave the rest to people.

limits: Turning a rule into a decision fails if the surrounding system cannot absorb the unpredictability.

quotes.text: SOPs and checklists are the detritus of hidden uncertainty
quotes.source: Agrawal, Gans and Goldfarb, Power and Prediction

quotes.text: you may need to redesign the system to account for the reduced reliability
quotes.source: Agrawal, Gans and Goldfarb, Power and Prediction

quotes.text: Rules are decisions that we make preemptively
quotes.source: Agrawal, Gans and Goldfarb, Power and Prediction

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: I try to extract out the deterministic parts and turn that into code and just leave only the parts that actually require judgment to the agent.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Look at the rules you have written for your agent (a rules file, a skill, a checklist in the prompt). For each, ask what uncertainty it was written to cover. If a check can now be run on the real case, let the agent decide with that information. Keep the fixed rule for steps where other people or systems depend on a predictable result.

concepts.concept: Formulas beat experts in noisy domains; broken-leg rule; structured interviews
concepts.name: Formulas vs intuition

card.title: Formulas against expert intuition
idea: In low-validity environments (noisy, complex, long-term outcomes such as parole, admissions, stock picking and business success), Kahneman says the final call should go to a formula. Expert intuition earns trust only in high-validity environments with stable regularities and fast, clear feedback (see the next card).
The formula can be simple. Equally weighted scores built on a few valid cues often predict well.
why: In low-validity settings System 1 builds a coherent story from whatever it has (WYSIATI, "what you see is all there is") and swaps a hard question for an easier one. The result is an illusion of validity.
Human judges are also noisy. A simple formula uses weak but valid cues and applies them the same way every time.

stories.text: Paul Meehl reviewed studies that compared clinical judgment with statistical prediction. In the later literature of roughly two hundred studies, about 60 percent show the algorithm significantly more accurate and the rest are ties. A tie favors the algorithm because it is cheaper. (Kahneman describes Meehl's original review as covering 20 studies.)
In 1953 Virginia Apgar introduced five variables, each scored 0 to 2, assessed one minute after birth. It replaced clinical impression and gave delivery rooms a consistent standard.

In the Israeli army, Kahneman replaced global intuitive ratings with six characteristics, each rated separately on factual questions and combined by formula. Predictions of combat performance improved.
Orley Ashenfelter predicted Bordeaux wine prices from three weather variables, with a correlation above .90. Experts called the approach "ludicrous and absurd", and the formula beat them.
Experienced radiologists who rate the same chest X-ray as normal or abnormal contradict themselves 20 percent of the time.

method.intro: Kahneman's rule-based selection, adapted from his army work.
steps: Choose about six independent traits relevant to the role.
Write factual questions about past behavior for each trait.
Score each trait on a 1 to 5 scale before moving to the next.
Add the scores by formula. Do not override the total with a gut feeling.

limits: Formulas fail where the environment is not stationary and the past no longer predicts the future, and where people trust mined correlations without a causal story.
Broken-leg rule: override a formula only for rare, decisive information the formula cannot contain, such as knowing that the person broke a leg today.
card.tension: Gary Klein, cited by Kahneman and by Sibony, defends intuition built through long experience, such as the fire commander who ordered his team out of a house just before the floor collapsed. Kahneman and Klein agree on where each applies. Formulas fit low-validity domains (stock picking, parole, long-term political forecasting). Intuition fits orderly domains with fast, clear feedback (firefighting, chess, intensive care). The next card covers the conditions.

quotes.text: to maximize predictive accuracy, final decisions should be left to formulas, especially in low-validity environments
quotes.source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

quotes.text: Simple equally weighted formulas based on existing statistics or on common sense are often very good predictors
quotes.source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When you must rate many items the same way (candidate documents, vendor proposals, support tickets), ask the agent to score each on a fixed list of separate criteria first, and add the scores yourself or by script. Ask for one overall impression only after the criteria are scored, so the overall impression does not shape the scores.

concepts.concept: Trust intuition only with regular environment and fast feedback; recognition-primed decisions
books: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
concepts.name: When to trust intuition

card.title: When to trust intuition

sources.book: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

idea: Real intuitive expertise needs two conditions: an environment regular enough to be predictable, and long practice with fast, clear feedback. Without both, years of practice produce confidence and no skill.
Herbert Simon defined intuition as recognition. An expert sees familiar elements in a new situation and knows the fitting action.
why: Confidence tells you how easily a coherent story formed. It does not tell you whether the story is right. Kahneman calls this cognitive ease and the illusion of validity.

stories.text: A chess master glances at a position and says "White mates in three".
Anesthesiologists learn the result of their choices within minutes. Radiologists reading mammograms rarely learn the outcome, so the same years of practice teach them far less.

Kahneman evaluated Israeli officer candidates on an obstacle course (for example, carrying a log over a wall). His predictions were barely better than chance, yet his confidence stayed high with each new candidate. He called this the illusion of validity.

stories.source: Thinking, Fast and Slow and You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
stories.text: Gary Klein tells of firefighters hosing down a kitchen fire. Soon the commander heard himself shout "Let's get out of here!" without knowing why. The floor collapsed almost immediately after they left. Afterwards he realized that the fire had been unusually quiet and his ears unusually hot. The heart of the fire was in the basement beneath them. Sibony uses the same case to illustrate Klein's recognition-primed decision model.

Art experts instantly felt that a supposedly ancient Greek statue was a fraud, although it had passed scientific tests. They were right. Flyvbjerg and Gardner also name Frank Gehry and Pete Docter as experts whose tacit knowledge guides their projects.

method.source: Kahneman and Klein, with Klein's recognition-primed decision model
method.intro: First the audit of whether to trust an intuition, then how experts use one.
steps: Is the environment regular enough to be predictable?
Has the person had long practice with fast, clear feedback?
If not both, set the confidence aside and use base rates, formulas or reference classes.
If both, use recognition-primed decision making. Pattern recognition brings one plausible action to mind.
Mentally simulate it to see if it will work here.
If it falls short, modify it. If it cannot be fixed, take the next plausible option and simulate that.

limits: Intuition fails where there are no stable regularities or where feedback is slow.

quotes.text: Valid intuitions develop when experts have learned to recognize familiar elements in a new situation and to act in a manner that is appropriate to it
quotes.source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

quotes.text: The confidence that individuals have in their beliefs depends mostly on the quality of the story they can tell about what they see, even if they see little.
quotes.source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

quotes.text: This is "skilled intuition," not garden-variety gut feelings, which are unreliable.
quotes.source: Bent Flyvbjerg and Dan Gardner, How Big Things Get Done

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When an agent states a result with confidence, treat the tone as no evidence. Ask what it checked, and whether it has had feedback on this kind of task. Apply the same test to your own hunches about what the agent will get right: trust them in areas where you have seen many results, and test them elsewhere.

concepts.concept: Penalize complexity; stop early to avoid overfitting
concepts.name: Penalize complexity

card.title: Penalize complexity and stop early
idea: A model that fits its data too well is overfitted. It has learned the noise in the data and will predict new cases badly. Computer scientists add a penalty for complexity so that a more complex model has to explain the data significantly better to justify itself. The principle is called regularization.
why: Only the factors with a big effect should stay in the model. The penalty pushes the weights of the others down to zero. The result is a simpler formula that holds up better on new data.

stories.text: The Lasso was discovered in 1996 by the biostatistician Robert Tibshirani. It uses the total weight of the factors in the model as its penalty. The authors' example is a nine-factor model of the German marriage survey data that becomes a simpler, more robust formula with just a couple of the most critical factors.

steps: Penalize complexity, for example with the Lasso, which penalizes the total factor weight.
Let the penalty push the weights of non-essential factors to zero.
Use Early Stopping when new data is noisy or gives diminishing returns. Stopping the fitting process before the model becomes too complex can give a better result than a thorough fit.

limits: The source gives no limits beyond those in the risk-versus-uncertainty card. Calculation still wins when probabilities are known and stable.

quotes.text: Computer scientists refer to this principle—using constraints that penalize models for their complexity—as Regularization.
quotes.source: Brian Christian and Tom Griffiths, Algorithms to Live By

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When a prompt or rules file keeps growing, remove a rule and see whether the output gets worse. Keep only the rules whose removal shows a clear loss. Stop revising after a few rounds when the changes stop improving results on new cases.

concepts.concept: Mechanical rules gain consistency, lose adaptability; reasoning by example
concepts.name: Mechanical rules vs principles

card.title: Mechanical rules and principles
idea: A mechanical rule gives the same result whoever applies it. That gives transparency, consistency across many people, auditability, and resistance to bias or corruption. Nguyen's example is the rule that adulthood starts at eighteen.
A principle needs trained judgment and reasoning by example. It fits context-sensitive situations, developing values and complex human goods.
why: Mechanical rules can be used by anyone without training. They are portable, cheap and easy to agree on. They cannot adapt. Applied to rich values they produce value capture and rigidity (see the value-capture card).
Mechanical procedures work best on inputs that are public and observable by everybody. Where the situation is subtler and needs discernment, they are far less accurate.

stories.text: Lorraine Daston describes algorithmic rules such as logarithm tables and navigation tables. They let unskilled "calculators" replace expensive mathematicians.
Basketball's hoop is an example of a mechanical scoring device. James Scott's Seeing Like a State describes states making complex realities legible so that they can be governed by rule.

Levi describes legal reasoning by example: see the similarity between cases, state the rule, apply it to the new case. In MacPherson v. Buick, liability moved beyond strict contractual privity. (Levi is a PDF and could not be checked.)

method.source: The Score and Thinking Like a Lawyer
method.intro: Nguyen's choice of tool, then Vandevelde's method of legal reasoning.
steps: Decide whether the domain needs mechanical rules (scale, consistency, anti-corruption) or principles (nuance, adaptability).
Exercise reflective control over whether the rules distort the underlying values.
Keep fuzzy principles in open-ended domains.
For principles, identify the applicable statutes and cases and extract the rules and the policies behind them.
Synthesize them into a coherent structure, from general to specific.
Apply them to the facts by deduction or analogy, using the policies to resolve hard cases.

limits: Mechanical rules fail outside the context they were made for. Principles fail where consistency is needed across many people nobody monitors.
card.tension: Standard procedures and tacit discretion pull in different directions. Procedures give reliability and coordination at scale. Discretion and fuzzy principles give adaptability, skill-building and a way to work in open-ended domains. Nguyen puts the trade this way: mechanical rules gain consistent repeatability but often trade away deep accuracy. Matt Beane (The Skill Code) adds that surgical residents lose practice when senior surgeons run the robot and follow the procedure alone.

quotes.text: A rule is mechanical precisely because anybody can apply it in the same way.
quotes.source: C. Thi Nguyen, The Score

quotes.text: What he asks us to sacrifice is adaptability
quotes.source: C. Thi Nguyen, The Score

quotes.text: Mechanical procedures work best with the kinds of things that are naturally public and observable by everybody
quotes.source: C. Thi Nguyen, The Score

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: that's very mechanical right you don't you don't need an agent to think about it

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Sort the steps of an agent workflow into two lists. Steps with public, checkable inputs (formatting, file naming, a migration pattern) go into a script or fixed rule. Steps that need discernment (tone, what matters to a client, whether an exception applies) stay as principles with examples of good and bad cases.

concepts.concept: Personal rules, friction, HALT; Slovic's handicappers; Stop-FLOP-Know
concepts.name: Automatic rules

card.title: Personal rules and safeguards
idea: Parrish recommends replacing repeated case-by-case choices with automatic rules and deliberate safeguards. They protect decisions from the biological defaults: ego, emotion, inertia, social pressure and fatigue.
why: A choice that depends on willpower wears down under stress, tiredness and social pressure. An automatic rule skips the deliberation in the moment. People also tend to argue with a decision and to respect a rule.

stories.text: Daniel Kahneman told Parrish his favorite personal rule: never say yes to a request over the phone. He knew that his wish to be liked made him accept commitments he did not want, so he tells the caller he will get back to them after thinking about it.

During a major report deadline, Parrish told his colleagues he would buy them all lunch if they caught him with his email open before 11:00 a.m. Not wanting to pay created enough friction to keep him focused.
Alcoholics Anonymous uses HALT: Hungry, Angry, Lonely, Tired. Do not make decisions in any of those states.

Paul Slovic's 1974 study gave horse handicappers five pieces of information per horse. They were 17 percent accurate (ten horses per race) at 19 percent confidence. When they were given more information, accuracy stayed the same and their confidence rose to 34 percent.

steps: Prevention: avoid important decisions when Hungry, Angry, Lonely or Tired.
Automatic rules: replace repeated choices with non-negotiable rules (go to the gym every day instead of deciding daily).
Friction: add effort, penalties or barriers to undesirable defaults.
Guardrails and checklists: use procedures that force a pause and a check.
Stop, FLOP, Know: stop deliberating and act when you have stopped gathering useful information, when you are about to First Lose an OPportunity, or when you come to Know which option is right.

limits: Rules fail without accountability to enforce them, and when they are applied so rigidly that they block integrative thinking.

quotes.text: Creating personal rules is a powerful technique for protecting yourself from your own weaknesses and limitations.
quotes.source: Shane Parrish, Clear Thinking

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Write the repeated decisions you make about an agent's work as standing rules in its instructions: which actions always need your approval, which files it never touches, what it reports at the end. Add friction for the one default you want to avoid, such as requiring a written reason before the agent skips a check.

concepts.concept: Aspiration levels; Happiness and Only-Option tests; Menu Strategy
concepts.name: Satisficing

card.title: Satisficing and maximizing
idea: Satisficing means taking the first option that meets a threshold you set in advance. Maximizing means searching for the best option. Satisficing wins in time-sensitive, low-impact or highly complex situations.
why: Maximizing assumes complete information and unlimited time. It brings analysis paralysis, fatigue and regret. Under uncertainty the best option cannot be identified anyway. Satisficing gives up a little accuracy for a lot of time. That time can go to high-impact choices and cheap experiments.

stories.text: Duke reports that the average person spends 150 minutes a week deciding what to eat and 50 minutes deciding what to watch on Netflix, and more on what to wear. Together this is 250 to 275 hours a year.

Gigerenzer compares two shoppers. The maximizer tries every pair of trousers in several stores and ends up unsatisfied. The satisficer sets an aspiration level (black, fits, not more than $100) and buys the first pair that meets it.
Duke calls a high-stakes choice between near-equal options a "sheep in wolf's clothing", for example a vacation in Paris or in Rome. If both options pass the Only-Option Test, agonizing adds nothing.

method.source: How to Decide and Risk Savvy
method.intro: Duke's five tools, then Gigerenzer's three steps.
steps: Happiness Test: will the outcome affect your happiness in a year, a month, a week? If not, go faster.
Freerolls: spot choices with upside and almost no downside by asking "What's the worst that can happen?"
Only-Option Test: would you be happy if this were your only option? If several options pass, flip a coin.
Menu Strategy: spend the time sorting options into good and bad, then pick quickly among the good ones.
Quit-to-itiveness: if it is cheap to quit or reverse, decide fast and experiment.
Gigerenzer: set an aspiration level, look at options one at a time, and take the first that meets it.

limits: Satisficing fails for irreversible, high-impact one-way doors with high quitting costs.

quotes.text: Sorting options is the heavy lifting of decision-making
quotes.source: Annie Duke, How to Decide

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Give the agent an aspiration level for low-stakes choices (a library, a file layout, a wording) and tell it to take the first option that meets it and move on. For one-way choices, ask it to list and sort the options first, then pick.

concepts.concept: Choice architecture and defaults; NUDGES
concepts.name: Defaults

card.title: Defaults and choice architecture

sources.authors: Richard H. Thaler, Cass R. Sunstein

idea: Choice architecture is the deliberate design of the context in which people decide. Changing the default, adding or removing friction, and building an environment that is easy to use all steer behavior without removing anyone's freedom to choose.
why: People run mostly on the automatic system, with inertia, status quo bias and a preference for least effort. Setting the default aligns inertia with the behavior you want.

stories.text: Consent to organ donation: Germany, where people must opt in, has a rate of 12 percent. Austria, where people must opt out, has 99 percent.
Schiphol Airport in Amsterdam etched an image of a fly into each men's urinal. Spillage fell by 80 percent.

Brian Wansink gave moviegoers in Chicago five-day-old popcorn. Those given a large bucket ate 53 percent more than those given a medium bucket, although they compared the popcorn to Styrofoam. In his soup study, Campbell's tomato soup bowls were secretly refilled from machinery under the table, and people kept eating.
Parrish cleared the junk food out of his pantry. He also promised to buy colleagues lunch if they caught him with email open before 11:00 a.m.

method.intro: The book's NUDGES checklist.
steps: iNcentives: make prices and costs salient.
Understand mappings: translate options into outcomes (for example, camera megapixels into print sizes).
Defaults: make the recommended option the path of least resistance.
Give feedback when actions succeed or fail.
Expect error: design forgiving systems.
Structure complex choices (collaborative filtering, elimination by aspects).

limits: Self-serving architects exploit defaults. The book's example is a magazine subscription that renews automatically and needs a phone call to cancel.
