Where preferences vary widely, required active choice is better than a default.

quotes.text: A choice architect has the responsibility for organizing the context in which people make decisions.
quotes.source: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, Nudge

quotes.text: A good rule of thumb is to assume that “everything matters.”
quotes.source: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, Nudge

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: how do I make the easy thing the right thing?

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Treat the agent's starting state as a default. Put the safe option in place before it begins: a working branch instead of main, a read-only mode, a template file with the required sections. Ask what the agent does when it makes no choice at all, and make that outcome the acceptable one.

concepts.concept: You must do the step before you can proceed; postcompletion errors
concepts.name: Forcing functions

card.title: Forcing functions

sources.authors: Richard H. Thaler, Cass R. Sunstein

idea: A forcing function is a constraint, scheduled event or procedure that makes a step required before you can go on, or that physically prevents an error. In Don Norman's phrase, which Nudge quotes, to get what you want you have to do something else first.
why: People make postcompletion errors. After they finish the main task they forget the secondary steps, such as taking the card after taking the cash. A forcing function turns the secondary step into a condition of the main goal.

stories.text: Most ATMs now return the card before they give out the cash, so people cannot leave the card behind. Gas caps are tethered to the car. Diesel nozzles are too large to fit the opening of a gasoline tank.

Ulysses had his crew plug their ears with beeswax and tie him to the mast so that he could hear the Sirens and not steer onto the rocks. Parrish calls this tying your hands. A trip wire is a related device: a precommitment to turn back at a set threshold.
Standing meetings, regular status updates and prescheduled sessions with a personal trainer work as forcing functions.

method.intro: Parrish's fail-safes for execution.
steps: Set trip wires: precommit to act at a set time, amount or circumstance.
Empower others with commander's intent.
Tie your hands with physical, financial or legal barriers.

limits: Rigid or frustrating guardrails invite workarounds.

quotes.text: Another strategy, suggested by Norman, is to use what he calls a “forcing function,” meaning that in order to get what you want, you have to do something else first.
quotes.source: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, Nudge

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: How do I make it so that the code base makes this impossible?

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Make the required step a condition for finishing. For example, the agent may not mark a task done until the test or check command has run and its output is attached. Where a step must never be skipped, enforce it in the tool settings or a script instead of asking in the prompt.

concepts.concept: Pronovost, Boeing 299, WHO surgical checklist
books: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
concepts.name: Checklists

card.title: Checklists

sources.authors: Ajay Agrawal, Joshua Gans, Avi Goldfarb

sources.book: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

idea: A checklist forces a pause, overrides defaults and verifies the required steps before complex or high-stakes work.
why: Operating rooms, cockpits and acquisitions involve more steps than unaided memory can hold. Under stress and fatigue even experts skip basic steps.

stories.text: The US Army Air Corps first rejected Boeing's Model 299 after a crash caused by pilot error. Instead of more training for the pilots, it issued a checklist. Pilots then flew the plane 1.8 million miles without an accident, and the Army ordered nearly 13,000.

Peter Pronovost wrote a five-step checklist for inserting central lines at Johns Hopkins. Nurses were authorized to stop a doctor who skipped a step. In one ICU the infection rate fell from 11 percent to zero within a year. This prevented 43 infections and eight deaths and saved $2 million.

stories.source: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
stories.text: WHO surgical safety checklists cut complications by about one-third and mortality by half. 93 percent of surgeons said they would want the checklist used if they were the patient.
Charlie Munger points to airline pilots' checklist routines and simulator training as a model for other fields.

method.intro: Pronovost's checklist for central lines.
steps: Wash hands with soap.
Clean the patient's skin with chlorhexidine.
Cover the patient with sterile drapes.
Wear a sterile mask, hat, gown and gloves.
Put a sterile dressing over the site once the line is in.
Empower nurses to stop the procedure if a step is skipped.

limits: High-status experts resist checklists as beneath them. Checklists fail when people treat them as box-ticking.

quotes.text: Checklists save lives without extra technology and little costs.
quotes.source: Gerd Gigerenzer, Risk Savvy

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Keep a short checklist the agent must complete before it hands work back: files changed, checks run, anything it did not verify. Follow the Pronovost design. Give the person or process downstream the authority to stop the work when a step is missing.

concepts.concept: Constraints focus imagination; tighten or relax one at a time (Entebbe)
concepts.name: Wise constraints

card.title: Wise constraints

sources.authors: Kenneth Cukier, Viktor Mayer-Schönberger, Francis de Véricourt

idea: Constraints bound the imagination. They narrow an unlimited space of alternatives so that effort goes to options that can work.
why: Counterfactual thinking without limits produces too many options and ends in paralysis. Constraints remove useless options and focus the effort.

stories.text: Entebbe, July 1976: 106 hostages were held in an old airport terminal. The planners dropped unworkable ideas, and Dan Shomron made surprise the hard constraint. Using blueprints from the Israeli firm that had built the terminal, they built a model and rehearsed. They drove up in a black Mercedes with Ugandan flags. 102 hostages were rescued in 90 minutes.
Peter Weinstock at Boston Children's Hospital works with special-effects artists to build lifelike mannequins on which surgeons rehearse pediatric surgery.
In 2008 Ben Bernanke relaxed the constraint against direct intervention by the central bank, which opened new options.

steps: Separate hard constraints from adjustable ones.
Tighten constraints to focus the search.
Relax a single constraint to find new options.

limits: Rigid constraints blind people when the background changes.

quotes.text: People who are exceptional at framing understand that their imagination needs bounds—cognitive curbs, mental manacles—not to interdict their vision but to guide it.
quotes.source: Cukier, Mayer-Schönberger and de Véricourt, Framers

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: the codebase is designed in a way that there's really only one way to do something

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Tell the agent the one thing that cannot change (the deadline, the data it may not touch, the format) and let the rest vary. When the agent is stuck, relax one constraint at a time and ask what that opens up. Do not drop several at once.

concepts.concept: When a measure becomes a target it stops measuring (rats, nails, rankings)
concepts.name: Goodhart's law

card.title: Goodhart's law
idea: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The wording is Marilyn Strathern's version of Goodhart's law. Campbell's law is the parallel for social indicators: the more an indicator is used to make decisions, the more it is corrupted and the more it distorts the process it monitors.
why: People optimize what is measured, by the cheapest route. The measure was only a stand-in for what you wanted, and the cheapest route often changes the stand-in without changing the real thing.

stories.text: Colonial Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail. People cut off the tails and released the rats to breed, and some people bred rats.
Universities game the U.S. News rankings. Some recruit applicants in order to reject them, and some cap classes at 19 students to stay under 20.
A car dealership paid bonuses on monthly sales volume. Salespeople gave deep discounts that hit the volume targets and reduced profit.
In the Atlanta testing scandal, 178 educators were implicated in changing students' answers.
Von Koenigswald paid Javanese locals ten cents per hominid bone fragment. They smashed the fossils into pieces to collect more payments.
Soviet planners set targets for Gosplan by quantity: cloth by length, nails by count or weight. The satirical magazine Krokodil drew a single giant nail hanging from a crane.

limits: The sources give no method for avoiding the problem.

quotes.text: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
quotes.source: Marilyn Strathern, quoted in Calling Bullshit

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When you give an agent a number to hit (tests passing, lint warnings at zero, coverage percentage), check a sample of the result by reading it, because the agent may reach the number in ways you did not intend. Pair each metric with a second check that would expose a shortcut.

concepts.concept: Simplified metrics replace rich values; reflective control
concepts.name: Value capture

card.title: Value capture
idea: Value capture is what happens when a rich, subtle value is replaced by a simplified, usually quantified version that then takes over. Nguyen gives three conditions: your values are rich and subtle or developing that way; you enter a social, usually institutional, setting that offers simplified and often quantified renditions of your values; and the simplified versions take over.
Nguyen's "Four Horsemen" of bureaucracy (scale, rules, parts and control) create the demand for portable metrics that can be read by people far from the work.
why: Institutions need numbers that travel between people who do not share context. The simplified metric is easy to compare, so it gets used in place of the value it stood for.

stories.text: Wendy Espeland and Michael Sauder studied the effect of the U.S. News & World Report law school rankings (Engines of Anxiety). Before the rankings, the only guide was Barron's, which gave each school a qualitative blurb about its own mission. Some schools aimed at corporate law jobs, some at legal theory, some at training activists or serving underserved students. After the rankings, schools put resources into gaming them, for example encouraging unlikely applicants to apply so that the school would have more people to reject. The rankings also removed the variety of missions. A school that served a historically underrepresented community, whose students typically had lower GPA and LSAT scores, would fall in the rankings, so most schools gave up their original missions.

A pastor told Nguyen that his church had become obsessed with baptism rates. The higher-ups had set up an internal leaderboard on which pastors competed on monthly baptism rates. He found himself caring less about the long-term spiritual development of his flock and more about delivering popular sermons that would raise his rate.

steps: Recognize objectivity laundering, where a number looks neutral because its judgments are hidden.
Protect fuzzy values from being reduced to a metric.
Exercise reflective control: keep asking whether the metric still serves the value.

limits: Standard metrics are needed for coordination at large scale. They fail for open-ended goods.

quotes.text: Your values are rich and subtle
quotes.source: C. Thi Nguyen, The Score

quotes.text: The simplified versions take over
quotes.source: C. Thi Nguyen, The Score

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When you reduce a quality requirement to a checkable rule for the agent (word count, a rubric score), write down the value behind it in one sentence in the same place. Review samples against that sentence, and revise the rubric when it drifts from it.

concepts.concept: Incentives that worsen the problem; maladaptive performance
concepts.name: The cobra effect

card.title: Perverse incentives and the cobra effect
idea: A rule or incentive meant to solve a problem can create incentives that make the problem worse. Doshi and McGregor explain the mechanism. When motivation comes from economic and emotional pressure and not from play, purpose and potential, adaptive performance turns into maladaptive performance: people take the shortest path to the reward.
why: The reward attaches to a measurable action and people respond to it directly. The result matches the incentive and not the purpose behind it.

stories.text: Colonial Delhi paid a bounty for dead cobras. People bred cobras for the bounty, and when the bounty ended they released them.
Call center staff were measured on calls per hour. Some hung up on customers.

A sales force on quarterly targets discounted by 20 percent at quarter end, and customers learned to wait. In a survey of nearly 1,000 salespeople, 70 percent admitted pulling revenue forward, 59 percent set aside citizenship duties, and 18 percent helped colleagues less.
Sears auto centers set sales quotas. They recommended unnecessary repairs to undercover investigators 89 percent of the time.
Microsoft used stack ranking. Engineers withheld information and kept strong performers off their teams.

Munger describes FedEx night-shift sorters who were paid by the hour and worked slowly. FedEx changed to payment per shift, and the sorters could leave when the planes were loaded. The problem went away.

limits: Financial incentives work for simple, repetitive tasks and fail for complex knowledge work.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Look at what the agent gets rewarded for in your setup, such as a passing check, a short answer or a finished status. Ask what the quickest route to that reward would be, and whether you would accept it. Reward the outcome itself.

concepts.concept: Obeying the letter, defeating the purpose; seeking the wrong goal
concepts.name: Rule beating

card.title: Rule beating and the wrong goal
idea: Rule beating is evasive action that gets around the intent of a system's rules, abiding by the letter and not the spirit. A related failure is seeking the wrong goal, which means optimizing an indicator that does not reflect the real welfare of the system.
why: A rule describes the behavior its authors expected. People who gain from avoiding it respond to the rule's wording and not to its purpose.

stories.text: Organizations with use-it-or-lose-it budgets have year-end spending sprees, so that next year's budget is not cut.
Vermont's Act 250 required a complex approval process for lots of ten acres or less. Vermont now has an extraordinary number of lots of just over ten acres.
In the 1960s European limits on feed grain imports left out cassava, so farmers switched to cassava.
Under the Endangered Species Act, some landowners killed endangered animals before surveys could find them.
Munger describes California's workers' compensation coverage of workplace stress and the fraud it attracted.

steps: Escape rule beating: design or redesign rules so that people's creativity points at the rule's purpose.
Escape the wrong goal: choose indicators that reflect the real welfare of the system, and do not confuse effort with results.

limits: The sources give no limits.

quotes.text: Rule beating means evasive action to get around the intent of a system's rules—abiding by the letter, but not the spirit, of the law.
quotes.source: Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: After you add a rule to an agent's instructions, ask how a system that wanted to comply cheaply would satisfy it. Write the purpose of the rule next to the rule, so the agent can follow the purpose when the wording and the purpose disagree.

concepts.concept: Scale breeds bureaucracy; decision fatigue (parole judges)
concepts.name: The curse of scale

card.title: Scale breeds bureaucracy
idea: As an organization grows, its rules and approval layers multiply, and it becomes slow. Munger calls this the constant curse of scale. A second cost of too many routine decisions is decision fatigue, which lowers the quality of later decisions.
why: Large units develop bad incentives and informal pacts between departments. Munger describes the unwritten rule "If you won't bother me, I won't bother you, and we're both happy." Layers of management grow that nobody needs, and decisions take a long time.

stories.text: Munger describes early AT&T and Westinghouse as examples of scale breeding bad incentives. He mentions General Electric as a company that has fought bureaucracy with skill, using decentralized units and motivation and training programs.
Danziger studied Israeli parole judges. The share of requests approved was near 65 percent after a meal break and fell toward zero before the next break.

method.intro: Munger's remedies.
steps: Organize into small decentralized units.
Build a web of deserved trust.
Put capable "learning machines" in long-term authority.
Reduce routine choices to save decision capacity.

limits: Decentralization without deserved trust invites local misconduct.

quotes.text: The constant curse of scale is that it leads to big, dumb bureaucracy which, of course, reaches its highest and worst form in government where the incentives are really awful.
quotes.source: Charles Munger, Poor Charlie's Almanack

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Count the approval steps in your agent workflow. Keep human approval for the actions you cannot undo, and remove the others. Fewer routine confirmation prompts leave more of your attention for the decisions that need it.

concepts.concept: Independent team argues the opposite with its own facts; Buffett's advisor
books: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
concepts.name: Red teams

card.title: Red teams

sources.book: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

idea: Sibony calls this Technique #19. One team (the blue team) submits a proposal. A second team (the red team) is told to prepare the opposite assessment: to defend the other point of view or to show why the proposal will fail. The red team is "a devil's advocate on steroids". It does not depend on the rhetoric of one person, because it has its own fact-finding and analysis.

The decision maker then hears two equally well-researched views. Sibony compares her to a judge who has heard both the defense attorney and the prosecutor, each of whom did the best research they could.
why: The method builds disagreement into the process, so no single person has to risk being the one who objects. It works against groupthink and against interest biases, where the people advising have something to gain from one answer.

stories.source: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
stories.text: Procter & Gamble decided to enter the bleach business against Clorox, the market leader. Its plan was to put its marketing and sales muscle behind a good product, Vibrant. P&G's managers suspected Clorox would respond. They were still surprised to find that in the test-market city, Clorox had delivered a gallon of free bleach to the doorstep of every house. Sibony says the move was expensive but predictable if you put yourself in Clorox's place, since P&G was invading the business that produced most of Clorox's profits. P&G gave up. A. G. Lafley, a former P&G CEO who told the story, took this lesson from it: "Head-on, World War I-like assaults on walled cities generally end with a lot of casualties." Sibony uses the story for competitor neglect. A variant of the red team, the war game, has the red team anticipate the adversary's reaction.

stories.source: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
stories.text: Warren Buffett recommends a version of the red team when a board studies an acquisition, especially one paid for in stock. In his words, directors who hear only from an investment bank should "hire a second advisor to make the case against the proposed acquisition, with its fee contingent on the deal not going through." His summary is "Don't ask the barber whether you need a haircut." Sibony adds that if you want to know whether you need a haircut, you ask two barbers and tell them what answer you want.

method.source: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
steps: A blue team submits the proposal.
An independent red team is told to argue the opposite view or to show why the proposal will fail.
The red team does its own fact-finding and analysis.
The decision maker weighs both briefings and forms her own opinion.

limits: Sibony says the duplication is not free. Two teams on every routine assessment would not make economic sense, and the confrontation between teams creates tension. He limits the method to high-stakes decisions. It started in the military and in intelligence agencies, where misreading evidence can have tragic consequences.
The method also fails if it becomes a ritual or if challenging the consensus is punished.

quotes.text: The red team, in essence, is a devil's advocate on steroids: rather than relying on the critical thinking skills and rhetorical talent of one individual, it has access to independent fact-finding and analysis.
quotes.source: Olivier Sibony, You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: For a high-stakes agent result, such as a migration plan or a change that cannot be undone, give a second agent the plan with one job: find the strongest case against it, using its own searches of the repo and docs. Do not show it the first agent's reasoning, so it cannot just agree. Read both reports before you decide.

concepts.concept: Imagine it failed; write reasons individually; adjust the plan
books: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
concepts.name: The premortem

card.title: The premortem

sources.book: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

idea: The premortem is Gary Klein's technique. Before a decision is final, the team imagines that it was carried out and went badly, and each person writes down why. Kahneman describes the session: when an organization has almost decided but has not yet committed, gather a small group who know the subject and say, "Imagine that we are a year into the future. We implemented the plan as it now exists. The outcome was a disaster." Everyone takes 5 to 10 minutes to write a brief history of that disaster.

Sibony's version is the same: the organizer announces that it is year X and the project was a disaster, people write down possible reasons, then take turns sharing them, and everyone must contribute. Duke describes it as imagining a specific decision that worked out poorly, then looking back from that future to the present to find the reasons it might have happened.
why: Sibony gives two reasons. First, people are much better at explaining what has happened than at imagining what may happen. The premortem uses this by putting the failure in the past. Klein calls this prospective hindsight. Second, writing reasons down and setting the rule that everyone contributes helps doubters overcome their habit of silencing themselves, which Sibony names as the root of groupthink.

Kahneman lists the same two benefits: it overcomes the groupthink that sets in once a decision appears made, and it directs the imagination of knowledgeable people toward problems. He notes that as a team converges and the leader tips her hand, public doubts are suppressed and come to be treated as disloyalty.

stories.text: Kahneman describes the premortem casually at a session in Davos. Someone behind him muttered, "It was worth coming to Davos just for this!" He later noticed that the speaker was the CEO of a major international corporation.

stories.source: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
stories.text: Smithburg, the CEO of Quaker, looked back on the failed acquisition of Snapple: "There was so much excitement about bringing in a new brand, a brand with legs. We should have had a couple of people arguing the 'no' side of the evaluation." Sibony says a premortem would have given them the license, and the obligation, to do exactly that.

method.intro: The steps below combine the three books. The Duke steps go further than the others and add a second view.
steps: Meet when the decision is nearly made but not yet executed.
Set the scene: it is a year from now (or at the end of whatever period fits), the plan was carried out, and the result was a disaster.
Each person writes their reasons alone, in 5 to 10 minutes, before any discussion. Duke asks for up to five reasons within your control and five outside it.
Everyone shares in turn. Everyone must contribute.
Compile the reasons. Sibony notes that the most valuable result is a flaw nobody had discussed, and that shared worries are worth monitoring during execution.
Change the plan, or precommit to a response. Duke pairs this with a backcast (imagining success) in a Decision Exploration Table with probabilities and impact.

limits: The premortem is useless once the decision has been executed. It also fails if people fear retaliation for what they write.
Kahneman calls it a partial remedy for overconfidence. He doubts that overconfidence can be trained away.

quotes.text: it asks us to travel in time to the future so we can look back, and it asks us to explain what “has happened” in this imagined past.
quotes.source: Olivier Sibony, You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

quotes.text: Imagine that we are a year into the future. We implemented the plan as it now exists. The outcome was a disaster.
quotes.source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

quotes.text: In a premortem, you imagine that you made a specific decision that worked out poorly or that you failed to reach a goal.
quotes.source: Annie Duke, How to Decide

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: What if I break something overnight?

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Before you let an agent run unattended on something that matters, ask a fresh agent: "It is tomorrow and this run caused a serious problem. Write down what happened." Asked to list risks, an agent tends to list generic ones and agree with your plan. Turn the three most plausible stories into checks, limits or blocks.

concepts.concept: Record what you knew and expected before the outcome
concepts.name: Decision journals

card.title: Decision journals
idea: Duke says our memories are not time stamped. A computer file shows "date created" and "date modified"; the brain does not. After you know an outcome, your memory of what you knew when you decided drifts toward the outcome. This is hindsight bias, and it shows up as "I knew it all along" or "I should have known."

Her fix is to write down, at the time of the decision, what you knew. She calls the tool a Knowledge Tracker. It has two boxes: the stuff you knew before the decision, and the stuff you know after the outcome, which is the earlier knowledge plus what was revealed only afterward. Keeping the two apart stops later information from creeping into the first box.
why: Hindsight bias distorts what you learn. If your memory says you should have seen it coming, you draw the wrong lesson, and you are harder on yourself and others than the facts justify. Duke says tracking your knowledge helps you see that some things could not have been known at the time.

stories.text: Duke's example is a decision to take a job in Boston. In one version you move and quit after six months. In the other, Boston turns out to be a winter wonderland of great outcomes. In both cases you fill in the same Knowledge Tracker with three things that informed the decision and three things that revealed themselves only afterward. Doing so separates what you could have known from what you could not.

steps: When you decide, journal the key facts that inform the decision. Duke calls this a vaccine against hindsight bias, because it prevents memory creep before it happens.
After the outcome, fill in the Knowledge Tracker: what you knew before the decision, and what revealed itself only after the fact.
Compare what happened with the written record, not with your memory.
Ask whether the information you lacked was something you could have known.

limits: A journal written after the outcome lets hindsight back in. Duke notes it is hard to stop the gut feeling that you knew it all along; the goal is to catch it more often.
card.tension: Dalio's Principles keeps an Issue Log: every mistake is logged with its root cause and an owner. Duke's journal is written before the outcome and records the state of knowledge. Dalio's log is written after a problem and records its diagnosis. They answer different questions, and the two are often used together.

quotes.text: Tracking your knowledge creates the time stamp that can get lost in the warp of hindsight bias.
quotes.source: Annie Duke, How to Decide

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Keep a short decision note next to the work: the goal you gave the agent, what you knew, what you assumed, and what you expected to see. When the result comes back, read the note before you judge it. Agent sessions are easy to rewrite in memory, so the note helps you tell a bad prompt from bad luck.

concepts.concept: Written expectations in "inactive memory"; deviations traced to four causes
concepts.name: The decision record

card.title: The decision record
idea: Ackoff says a solution needs a control system, and part of that is a decision-record: a written note of the decision, the assumptions behind it, the effects expected and when they should appear. It is kept in an "inactive memory", meaning a record that does not change. Ackoff says human memories are too active for this purpose, because they restructure the past.

He puts it plainly: memory erases mistakes and so prevents learning from them. The record is used to check the assumptions regularly and to compare the actual effects of the decision with what was expected.
why: Without a written record, people adjust their memory of what they expected to match what happened, and nothing is learned. With one, a gap between expected and actual effect is visible and can be traced.

stories.text: Fable 12.1, "The Expectations That Drowned": executive teams that wrote down their expected results before getting feedback learned faster than teams that did not.
A marketing department tracked the deviations between forecast and actual results every month across 200 areas. Over time its forecast errors fell from about 4% to a fraction of 1%.

steps: Record the decision, the assumptions, the expected effects and their timing.
Check the assumptions and the actual outcomes against the record at regular intervals.
Flag the deviations.
Diagnose each deviation as one of four causes: faulty information, a faulty decision process, instructions that were not carried out, or an unforeseen change in the environment.
Fix the part that matches the cause.

limits: Collecting too much data can swamp the signal.

quotes.text: Memory erases mistakes and thus prevents our learning from them.
quotes.source: Russell L. Ackoff, The Art of Problem Solving

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When you hand an agent a task, write down what you expect it to produce and how long it should take. Afterward, when the result differs, sort the gap into Ackoff's four causes: wrong context given, a weak plan, an instruction the agent ignored, or something that changed in the codebase. Each cause points to a different fix.

concepts.concept: Certainty is a feeling, not evidence
concepts.name: The feeling of knowing

card.title: The feeling of knowing
idea: Burton argues that certainty is a sensation. It arises below conscious reasoning, involuntarily, and it can attach to a thought whether or not the thought is correct. He calls these "mental sensations that feel like knowledge but occur in the absence of any specific knowledge."
It follows that you cannot test a belief by asking how sure you feel. Only evidence outside your own head can test it.
why: People treat strong conviction as a sign of a sound conclusion. If conviction is produced by a separate mechanism, then a person can be fully certain and wrong, and the feeling gives no warning.

stories.text: Mr. C insisted that his desk was a fake because it did not feel familiar to him: "I know real when I see real."
Electrical stimulation of limbic structures, including the hippocampus and the amygdala, can produce feelings of déjà vu, familiarity or truth when there is nothing to be familiar with.

limits: The source offers no method. It describes the problem and says introspection cannot fix it.

quotes.text: mental sensations that feel like knowledge but occur in the absence of any specific knowledge
quotes.source: Robert Alan Burton, On Being Certain

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Treat an agent's confident tone, and your own sense that the answer is right, as no evidence. Ask what check would show it to be wrong, and run that check. Verification replaces the feeling of certainty with something observable.

concepts.concept: Confidence follows the story, not accuracy
concepts.name: The illusion of validity

card.title: The illusion of validity

sources.book: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

idea: Kahneman says that confidence in a judgment depends mostly on the quality of the story you can tell about the evidence, not on how good the evidence is. A coherent story feels reliable even when it rests on very little. He calls the resulting gap between confidence and accuracy the illusion of validity.
why: A person who judges from a good story feels sure and may be no better than chance. Confidence therefore cannot be used to decide whose prediction to trust.

stories.text: As a young psychologist in the Israeli army, Kahneman helped assess officer candidates. The candidates faced an obstacle field, and they had to get a log over a wall. In a few minutes the assessors felt they saw each man's true nature. When the army later compared the assessments with how the men did in officer training, the predictions were little better than random guesses. The next batch of candidates arrived the following day. The assessors did the same exercise, and the dismal result had no effect on how they evaluated the new men and very little effect on their confidence. Kahneman compared it to the Müller-Lyer illusion, where you know the lines are equal and still see them as different. He coined the term illusion of validity for the experience.

method.intro: Kahneman and Sibony give a way to decide when to trust an intuition. Valid intuition needs a regular environment and long practice with fast, clear feedback.
steps: Ask whether the environment is regular enough to be predictable.

Ask whether the person has had long practice with fast, clear feedback. Kahneman contrasts anesthesiologists, who see results immediately, with radiologists reading mammograms, who rarely learn the outcome.
If either answer is no, set the confidence aside and use base rates, formulas or reference classes.

limits: Kahneman writes that subjective confidence follows the coherence of the story, so training rarely changes it. He is not optimistic that it can be overcome.

quotes.text: The confidence that individuals have in their beliefs depends mostly on the quality of the story they can tell about what they see, even if they see little.
quotes.source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

quotes.text: Valid intuitions develop when experts have learned to recognize familiar elements in a new situation and to act in a manner that is appropriate to it.
quotes.source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: A fluent, well-organized agent answer is the story Kahneman describes. Do not use how convincing it sounds as a signal. Ask for the evidence, such as test output, a log or a source line, and judge that. For judgments that have no feedback, such as architecture taste, treat both the agent's confidence and your own as weak.

concepts.concept: Probabilities, equivalent bet test, Brier scores; superforecasters
concepts.name: Calibration

card.title: Calibration
idea: Galef defines calibration as the match between your stated confidence and how often you turn out right. If you are perfectly calibrated, your "70% sure" claims come true 70% of the time, your "60% sure" claims 60% of the time, and so on. She calls perfect calibration an abstract ideal, but a useful benchmark.
Vague words hide how unsure you are. Putting a number on a belief, and tracking the results, makes the doubt visible.
why: Galef points to Philip Tetlock's superforecasters. In a forecasting tournament sponsored by IARPA, a branch of the US intelligence community, they beat teams of professors by margins of up to 70 percent, and IARPA dropped the other teams after two years. They were mostly amateurs and outperformed the CIA's professional analysts, who had classified information. Galef says they were not smarter than everyone else and did not have more knowledge or experience.

stories.text: Galef sometimes hears a forecast such as "Self-driving cars will be on the market within the year!" and scoffs. To find out how sure she is that it is wrong, she uses an equivalent bet test, adapted from the decision-making expert Douglas Hubbard. She compares betting $10,000 on self-driving cars with a ball bet: a box holds four balls, one gray, and she wins if she draws the gray one. She prefers the ball bet (1 in 4), so she is below 25 percent confident. With sixteen balls she prefers the cars (1 in 16, about 6 percent), so she is above that. With nine balls (about 11 percent) the bets feel equivalent. Her honest estimate is therefore roughly 11 percent. She still thinks the forecast is unlikely to come true but has moved from a glib "That's crazy" to a number.

To show how calibration is measured, Galef went through all of Spock's appearances in Star Trek and collected 23 probability claims. Spock does poorly: apart from "likely" claims, his predictions run the wrong way, and things he calls 99.5 percent likely happen 17 percent of the time. She also offers a 40-question trivia exercise to test your own calibration, and says calibration is a skill with a quick learning curve.

steps: State your confidence as a percentage.
Use the equivalent bet test to find the number you really believe: offer yourself a ball bet with known odds and adjust the odds until you cannot choose between the two bets.
Record your forecasts and check later how often each confidence level came true.
Score the results. In the tournament, the measure was the Brier score, which sums squared deviations between forecasts and what happened (0 is best).

limits: Calibration measures whether your confidence fits your record. It cannot create accuracy in a domain that cannot be predicted.

quotes.text: Contemplating a bet can also be used to pin down how sure you are quantitatively, helping you put a number on your degree of confidence.
quotes.source: Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When an agent reports that a change is safe, ask for a probability that it is correct, and keep a short log of those numbers against what the tests later showed. After a few weeks you will see whether its "95% sure" means anything. Give yourself the same exercise on your own estimates.

concepts.concept: Challenge, complexity, connection; deskilling when experts only inspect
concepts.name: The skill code

card.title: The skill code
idea: Beane says that expertise grows in a relationship between an expert and a novice that combines three things: challenge, complexity and connection. The novice works near the edge of their ability, sees the whole system and not just a piece, and has a bond with an expert who is close enough to teach. He calls this "the skill code".

New technology often breaks it. When tools let an expert work alone and have novices only inspect the output, the novices lose the practice. Beane's claim is that this happens in millions of workplaces.
why: The people who will need judgment in future are the ones now being kept away from the work. An organization that uses the tool to speed up experts can lose its next generation of experts without noticing.

stories.text: Robotic surgery. In open surgery, residents assisted at the table and learned by doing. With a surgical robot, the senior surgeon sits alone at a console and residents get little hands-on practice.
Investment banking. New tools let senior bankers build analyses themselves, without junior analysts doing the work alongside them.
Joseph Lister. Beane describes how in 1872 a large share of patients with compound fractures died of infection, and juniors learned his antiseptic methods by working at his side.

steps: When designing work, protect challenge, complexity and connection for novices.
Avoid deployments that turn seniors into solo operators and juniors into passive inspectors.
Where the bond has already been broken, use shadow learning: novices find ways around the system, such as practice partners, off-hours simulation and video study.

limits: Shadow learning is fragile and does not scale without support.

quotes.text: In millions of workplaces, we're blocking the ability to master new skills because we are separating junior workers from senior workers, novices from experts, by inserting technology between them.
quotes.source: Matt Beane, The Skill Code

quotes.text: The working relationship between experts and novices is a bundle of three Cs that humans need to develop mastery: challenge, complexity, and connection.
quotes.source: Matt Beane, The Skill Code

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: If an agent does the routine work that juniors used to do, decide where they will still get real problems with an expert beside them. For yourself, review agent output by working through part of the task yourself from time to time. Reading finished output alone does not keep a skill alive.

concepts.concept: Control raises plan execution and kills the ability to diverge; ToMo
concepts.name: Tactical vs adaptive performance

card.title: Control against context: tactical and adaptive performance
idea: Tactical performance is executing a plan. Adaptive performance is diverging from the plan when the situation requires it. Doshi and McGregor say that most organizations manage only the first. Heavy control and approval raise tactical performance and reduce adaptive performance.
why: Motivation has six motives. Three are direct: play, purpose and potential. They raise total motivation (ToMo) and adaptive performance. Three are indirect: emotional pressure, economic pressure and inertia. They enforce compliance, lower ToMo and produce maladaptive performance, such as gaming metrics and undermining colleagues.
A single-minded focus on tactical performance can cripple adaptive performance. In a volatile world, the authors say, that mistake can be fatal.

stories.text: Travelers Insurance redesigned the jobs of 90 keypunchers. The new jobs had direct customer contact, self-scheduling and direct error reports. Errors fell 35 percent, absenteeism fell 24 percent and productivity rose 40 percent.
Microsoft's stack ranking (2003 to 2012) led to politics and sabotage among employees.

The USS Benfold was one of the worst-performing warships in the US Navy. Michael Abrashoff, in his first sea command, turned it into one of the highest-performing ships in under twenty months. He did not fire or demote anyone, change the hierarchy or change the technology. At a Sunday cookout he saw officers cutting to the head of the lunch line, went to the end of the line himself, and sat down with the sailors. The next weekend everyone waited in line and ate together. No command was ever issued. Parrish uses the case to show that you cannot simply order people to be better.

In World War II, pilots in the Pacific were refusing to fly. Reports suggested something was wrong with the planes. Marshall had a plane stripped of its armor to make it lighter, but the pilots did not want that. Talking to the commander gave him no insight, so he sent someone to look around and see things that were not being reported. The ground crews had no protection from mosquitoes, were sick with malaria or its medication, and the pilots did not trust their work. Marshall diverted part of the combat tonnage to mosquito netting.

steps: Measure ToMo: score play, purpose and potential, and subtract emotional pressure, economic pressure and inertia.
Raise play: let people experiment and follow curiosity.
Raise purpose: connect the work to its real impact.
Raise potential: show how the work builds future ability.
Cut indirect motives: remove high-pressure contests, rank-and-yank and micromanaged approvals.

limits: Adaptive management without tactical controls can drift in routine, high-repetition work.
card.tension: Control and context each suit a different kind of work. Compliance zones (non-negotiable protocols, a plan to execute) call for tactical control. Volatile or ambiguous work, where the plan may be wrong, calls for context and room to diverge.

quotes.text: Most organizations manage tactical performance—the ability to execute against a plan. But adaptive performance—the ability to diverge from a plan—is just as important.
quotes.source: Neel Doshi and Lindsay McGregor, Primed to Perform

quotes.text: Instead of redesigning the hiring process, Travelers had redesigned the jobs. They didn’t change the player. They changed the game.
quotes.source: Neel Doshi and Lindsay McGregor, Primed to Perform

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: one of the biggest things that managers would talk about was this idea of context not control

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Give the agent the situation: who the work is for, what has already been tried, what a good result looks like, and what to do when the plan does not fit. Keep step-by-step control for the parts that need exact compliance. If you find yourself approving every small step, add the context the agent was missing.

concepts.concept: Perception, response and delivery delays make systems oscillate
concepts.name: Delays make systems swing

card.title: Delays make systems oscillate
idea: A decision made on delayed information makes a balancing loop overshoot, oscillate or collapse. Meadows says every balancing loop has three delays: perception (noticing a change), response (deciding and acting) and delivery (the action taking effect).
why: Acting on old information means acting on conditions that no longer exist. People overcorrect, then correct the overcorrection.

stories.text: A car dealership model: demand rises 10 percent on day 25. The dealer averages sales over five days (the perception delay) and adjusts orders partly over three days (the response delay). The factory takes five days to deliver (the delivery delay). Inventory falls, then overshoots, and keeps oscillating around the target.
Meadows suggests taking a shower with a very long pipe between the hot- and cold-water mixer and the showerhead. Because of the long response delay you get hot and cold oscillations.
Power plants take years to build and last for decades, so capacity cannot follow demand in real time.

steps: Identify the perception, response and delivery delays in the loop.
Shorten information delays where possible.
Slow the rate of change so that unavoidable delays do not cause swings.
"Thou shalt not distort, delay, or withhold information."

limits: Speeding up information without changing the physical delays can make a system more unstable, as in fast financial markets.
Long delays near irreversible thresholds lead to overshoot and collapse.

quotes.text: A delay in a balancing feedback loop makes a system likely to oscillate.
quotes.source: Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems

quotes.text: Thou shalt not distort, delay, or withhold information.
quotes.source: Donella Meadows, Thinking in Systems

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: the snapshot can go stale

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: A long agent run works from a snapshot of your instructions and of the world. Before it takes an irreversible step, have it re-read the current state (the latest messages, the file on disk, the ticket) and compare it with the snapshot. For quick feedback, shorten the loop and check progress at set points.

concepts.concept: Weekly scorecard, 90-minute meeting, Identify-Discuss-Solve
concepts.name: Weekly scorecard

card.title: Weekly scorecard and the Level 10 meeting
idea: Regular, structured reporting brings problems up before stale assumptions cause damage. Wickman's tools are a weekly Scorecard, 90-day Rocks, and a weekly 90-minute Level 10 Meeting in which issues are solved by IDS: Identify, Discuss, Solve.
why: Wickman says that because you review the numbers regularly, you can spot and solve problems as they come up, and not react to bad numbers in a financial statement long after the fact.

stories.text: In his first business Wickman managed the entire company using 14 numbers. He says how many numbers you need depends on the business, and that with over 400 EOS clients there are over 400 different Scorecards.

steps: Keep a Scorecard: a weekly report with five to 15 high-level numbers for the organization. Everyone in the organization has at least one number they are accountable for each week.
Set Rocks: clear 90-day priorities for each person.

Hold the Level 10 Meeting every week with the leadership team, for 90 minutes. The agenda is Segue (5 minutes), Scorecard (5), Rock review (5), customer and employee headlines (5), To-Do list (5), IDS (60) and Conclude (5).
Solve each issue with IDS. In Identify, the issue owner says what type of issue it is and what is needed. In Discuss, the team talks it through. In Solve, the team agrees on the action.

limits: Reporting goes underground if surfaced problems are punished.

quotes.text: A Scorecard is a weekly report containing five to 15 high-level numbers for the organization.
quotes.source: Gino Wickman, Traction

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: I tell it to append it to a document. And then every couple of days I look at it and I see actually these are all the same thing

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Keep a short running log of what the agent got wrong or took for granted, and review it on a fixed day each week. Group items into patterns, and fix the cause once in the instructions, checks or environment. A recurring list of numbers (failed checks, reverts, corrections you made) shows whether it is getting better.

concepts.concept: Keep asking why past the person to the system
concepts.name: The five whys

card.title: The five whys
idea: When something goes wrong, ask why it happened. Then ask why about that answer, and repeat about five times. The method comes from Sakichi Toyoda at Toyota, and Berger describes how Eric Ries uses it in his Lean Startup work. The aim is to get past the first, most obvious explanation, which usually names a person, and reach the system behind it.
why: Ries explains the method as "really designed to overcome the limits of human psychology". People look for the easiest, most obvious explanation, and "we tend to personalize things that are really systemic." It is easier to blame the assembly-line worker than to consider the interrelated factors behind the problem.

stories.text: Ries's example. A faulty part comes off the line. Why? A worker made a mistake. Why? The worker had not had enough training. Why? The training program was underfunded. Why? Corporate spending priorities. The cause sits at the end of the chain, not with the worker.

IDEO uses the same chain for personal habits. Why do you exercise? Because it is healthy. Why is it healthy? Because it raises my heart rate. The chain continues until it ends in a reason about social pressure to look fit.

DuckDuckGo requires a postmortem after every project and uses repeated whys to reach root causes. On the Challenger shuttle, the proximate cause was hot gas leaking past an O-ring in cold weather. Feynman and the Rogers Commission found the root cause in NASA's organization and communication.

steps: When an error occurs, ask why it happened.
Ask why four more times, each time about the previous answer.
Keep going past individual error to systemic causes.
Fix the root cause.

limits: Five is a rough number. It may take three or six, and the method can fail.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: you think about all the inefficiencies, the bad patterns that the agents are doing and then you think about how to course correct the environment, right? Not not that single agent.

quotes.text: we tend to personalize things that are really systemic
quotes.source: Eric Ries, quoted in Warren Berger, A More Beautiful Question

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When an agent makes a mistake, ask why until the answer is something you can change in the setup: missing context, an unclear instruction, a check that did not exist, a rule that was never written. Fix that, not just the output. If you stop at "the agent made an error", it will make the same error again.

concepts.concept: Redesign the system so the problem stops occurring; enlarge the system
concepts.name: Dissolving problems

card.title: Dissolving problems
idea: Ackoff separates four ways to deal with a problem. You can resolve it (find an answer that is good enough), solve it (find the optimal answer), or dissolve it by redesigning the system so the problem no longer occurs. Dissolving often means enlarging the system you consider changing, so that the cause sits inside it.

His method is idealized redesign. Describe the system you would have right now if you could have anything, limited only by technological feasibility and operational viability. Then work back toward it.
why: A problem that resists every solution may be a product of how the system is set up. Better solutions inside the same boundaries only repeat the cycle.

stories.text: A paper company struggled with production scheduling that tried to minimize machine setups. The problem went away when the company dropped its unprofitable lines, which had caused most of the setups.
A machine-tool company (Fable 4.3, "One for the Road") suffered demand swings that followed the economic cycle.
Salesmen paid on sales volume pushed production into scheduling crises. Changing their pay to profit dissolved the scheduling problem.

steps: Do an idealized redesign: describe what you would have now if you could have anything, limited only by technological feasibility and operational viability.
Widen the boundary of the system you are willing to change: incentives, product lines, environment.
Change the rules and incentives so the problem stops occurring.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: that's a sign that you should go off and think about how to uh amend your kitchen or your factory, right? Like thinking about your skills, your constraints, your lints, your type systems um and setting or adjusting it so that that problem doesn't happen again.

quotes.text: Problems that resist solution can often have their backs broken by enlarging the system we consider changing.
quotes.source: Russell L. Ackoff, The Art of Problem Solving

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: If you keep correcting the same agent behavior in prompts, widen the frame. Change the environment so the behavior cannot occur: a lint rule, a type, a tool that does the step deterministically, or a different task split. This removes the problem and spares you from catching it each time.

concepts.concept: A root cause is a reason, not an action; person or design?
concepts.name: A root cause is a reason

card.title: A root cause is a reason
idea: Dalio treats an organization as a machine made of design and people. After a bad outcome he asks whether the responsible person is not capable of the job or whether the design of the work is flawed. He says a root cause is a reason, not an action. "The person made a mistake" describes what happened. A reason says why it happened.
At Bridgewater, each problem goes into an Issue Log and is drilled down to the violated principles and design flaws.
why: If you fix only the action, the same design produces the same action again. Dalio's line is that if you have the same people doing the same things, you should expect the same results.

stories.text: In the early 1990s Bridgewater's head of trading, Ross, forgot to place a client trade, which cost several hundred thousand dollars. Dalio did not fire him, because that would have taught everyone to hide errors. Together they built the Error Log, which later became the Issue Log.

steps: Diagnose: was the outcome bad, who was responsible, and is the cause the person or the design?
Find root causes as reasons, not actions.
Drill down to get an 80/20 understanding of a troubled area.
Redesign: change principles, re-script the workflow, reassign roles.

limits: Dalio's list also tells managers to separate a capacity issue from a capability issue, and says the process breaks down if incapable people who will not reflect are kept in the role.
card.tension: Berger's five whys (A More Beautiful Question) points away from the individual and toward the system. Dalio asks you to decide first whether it is the person or the design, and he does not rule out the person. Use the five whys when one failure looks like bad luck or carelessness. Use Dalio's split when the same result keeps appearing and you need to know whether to change the role, the process or the person in it.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: But if you actually notice that multiple agents are are having the same issue, right? They're taking the same shortcut. they're they're propagating the same workaround everywhere.

quotes.text: Remember that a root cause is not an action but a reason.
quotes.source: Ray Dalio, Principles

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: After a failed agent run, write the cause as a reason ("the task did not say which test suite counts") rather than an action ("the agent skipped the tests"). If several agents fail the same way, the design is at fault, and you fix the setup. If one run fails in a way no other does, a one-off is more likely.

concepts.concept: Auditors outside the department, methods unannounced
concepts.name: Independent audits

card.title: Independent audits
idea: Dalio says that where there are rules, you need auditors to check them. The auditors must be independent of the people they audit. They should report to people outside the audited department, and the audit procedures should not be made known to those being audited. Dalio calls this one of Bridgewater's few exceptions to radical transparency.
why: People who are never checked give themselves slack, and some cheat. If the checker works for the person being checked, or is known in advance, the check turns into a formality. Dalio also warns against rubber-stamping where a person's role is to review a high volume of transactions.

steps: Decide which actions need approval beforehand and which can be audited afterward.

For mission-critical work such as finance, where large amounts of money are at risk, use a "double-do" instead of a double-check: two different people do the same task and produce independent answers. Dalio says double-checking has a much higher error rate.
Have auditors report to someone outside the audited department.
Keep the audit procedures unknown to those audited.
Watch for rubber-stamping where reviewers handle a high volume.
Make sure the auditors are able to do the work themselves.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: verification loop where it will spawn a bunch of verifier agents for every pull request and it will fuzz

quotes.text: Remember that there is no sense in having laws unless you have policemen (auditors).
quotes.source: Ray Dalio, Principles

quotes.text: The people doing the auditing should report to people outside the department being audited, and auditing procedures should not be made known to those being audited.
quotes.source: Ray Dalio, Principles

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Use a separate verifier agent, with its own context and without the author's explanation, to check an agent's work. Do not give it the author's reasoning or let the same prompt grade itself. Vary what it checks from run to run, so the author cannot optimize for a known test.

concepts.concept: Daily spot checks on top of a written system
concepts.name: Spot checks

card.title: Spot checks
idea: A written system sets the standard, and spot checks confirm that the standard is being met. Supervisors do not inspect everything. They sample outputs regularly and look at a few closely, and the checking is not tied to any incident.
why: Inspecting all output does not scale. A written standard makes a sample informative: it shows whether the system works, and a failure points to a specific part of it.

stories.text: Gerber stops for the night at the Venetia, a hotel in a redwood grove above the Pacific, and finds that every detail has been designed. The manager, who a few months earlier was a short-order cook with no hotel experience, shows him the hotel's Operations Manual. It is a set of color-coded checklists. Each Room Support Person (RSP) gets a package of checklists for each of eight rooms. The back of each checklist has a drawing of the room that shows each task and its order, and the person ticks off each task and signs the checklist. Signing without doing the work is grounds for instant dismissal. With the drawing, the manager says, new people can be trained almost instantly and produce the same result as someone who has been there a long time. Then: "As added insurance, my RSP Supervisors run spot checks every day to make certain that any errors are caught in time." He adds that there are rarely any errors: "The system works like a charm."

Chef Andre strides through his kitchen during the day and spot-checks the work. At the soup station he calls out, "One forty-nine, chef!?" and the cook answers after dunking a thermometer. He asks a prep cook, Kate, whether the diced onions are fine enough. She says no and takes a second look. Beane says the tight supervision may not be fun for the staff, but they trust Andre's standards.

steps: Write standards and manuals for the routine work.
Spot-check outputs every day.
Use open questions in the check to find out how the worker understands the task.

limits: Without a written standard to check against, spot checks turn into firefighting.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: also, you know, for scale, you cannot be tasting every single dish that comes out of your kitchen, especially if you have multiple restaurants. So it becomes more about sampling

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: as a quality supervisor on a factory you you can't look at every single item you sample right you take you you you go in there every day and you look at the quality of the pull requests

quotes.text: As added insurance, my RSP Supervisors run spot checks every day to make certain that any errors are caught in time.
quotes.source: Michael E. Gerber, The E-Myth Revisited

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Do not read every agent diff. Pick a few each day at random, read them closely against a written standard (your rules file or review checklist), and when you find a pattern, change the setup. If you have no written standard, write it first.

concepts.concept: Check inputs, sampling and provenance at scale
concepts.name: Garbage in, garbage out

card.title: Garbage in, garbage out
idea: At scale, you cannot check every item, so you check the inputs, the sampling and the provenance. Bergstrom and West give a short list of questions for judging a number or a claim from data.

The first is garbage in, garbage out (GIGO). The authors write about training data and labels fed to an algorithm: begin with bad data and labels, and you get a bad program that makes bad predictions.
why: The authors say the problem is easy to spot if you look at the data going in. Checking the source is cheaper than checking each result.

steps: Check the data going in (garbage in, garbage out).
Look for sampling and selection bias: who or what ended up in the data, and who or what did not.
Sanity-check the outputs and track units.
Check provenance: who collected the data, how, and why.

limits: A biased sample defeats the method, since a sample that looks fine on its own terms can still misrepresent the whole.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When an agent summarizes or analyzes a large set of files, tickets or logs, ask what it actually read and how it chose. Check the sample it saw before you trust the totals.

concepts.concept: Interruptions cost switching; thrashing; interrupt coalescing
concepts.name: Context switching

card.title: Context switching
idea: Every interruption forces a context switch: you save your place, clear working memory and load something else. The switch has a cost that does no useful work. If the interruptions come often enough, the system reaches thrashing, in which it runs at full speed and accomplishes nothing at all.

Christian and Griffiths take two remedies from computer science. First, stay on one task as long as possible without dropping your responsiveness below the minimum acceptable level: decide how responsive you need to be, then be no more responsive than that. Second, interrupt coalescing: gather the interruptions and handle them together.
why: The authors apply a computing idea to people: the more you switch, the more of your effort goes into the switching.

stories.text: In computing, the Linux scheduler developer Peter Zijlstra describes the problem with caches: they are warm for the current workload, and a context switch invalidates them. The authors use this to introduce thrashing, where tasks keep evicting each other's working data.

For credit card bills, do not pay each one when it arrives. If bills are never due less than 31 days after arrival, set one day a month, say the first, and process everything on your desk. The authors apply the same idea to email: if none of your correspondents needs a reply right away, you can answer in batches. They note that academic office hours coalesce student interruptions. Regular weekly meetings serve as a defense against spontaneous interruptions.

Donald Knuth is their model of a minimal-switching life. "I do one thing at a time," he says. "This is what computer scientists call batch processing." On January 1, 2014, he started "The TeX Tuneup of 2014" and fixed all the bugs reported in his typesetting software over six years in one run.

steps: Decide how responsive you need to be and be no more responsive than that.
Batch interruptions into scheduled blocks, such as one day for bills or set office hours.
Use regular meetings to absorb ad hoc interruptions.
Process mail in batches, as Knuth does.

limits: Batching trades responsiveness for throughput, so urgent items wait.

quotes.text: Interruptions mean certain bugs. You must not get off the train.
quotes.source: Ellen Ullman, quoted in Christian and Griffiths, Algorithms to Live By

quotes.text: I do one thing at a time
quotes.source: Donald Knuth, quoted in Christian and Griffiths, Algorithms to Live By

quotes.text: The caches are warm for the current workload, and when you context switch you pretty much invalidate all caches. And that hurts.
quotes.source: Peter Zijlstra, quoted in Christian and Griffiths, Algorithms to Live By

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Do not interrupt a long agent run to ask small questions. Keep them in a list and send them at the next natural stopping point. When you switch to a different task in the same session, start a clean one rather than carrying the old context along. Both choices reduce the cost of switching on your side and the agent's.

concepts.concept: Barriers of space and time; prime time
concepts.name: Barriers of space and time

card.title: Barriers of space and time
idea: Berger quotes John Cleese on the conditions for creative work. Cleese says a creative person needs a shell that limits interruptions and, to be productive, must create "barriers of space and time": a place and a block of time that others cannot break into. How long a block takes depends on the person. Berger works in blocks of no less than three and a half hours, because he needs three hours of uninterrupted work and half an hour to get started.

To find the best time of day, Berger cites Daniel Pink, who suggests a "flow test": keep track of your most creative periods each day, look for a pattern, then restructure the day to use those peak periods.
why: Interruptions fragment attention, and deep work needs long unbroken blocks.

steps: Add friction to interruptions, for example by turning off notifications and batching email.
Run a flow test to find your daily prime time.
Protect those hours for deep work.

quotes.text: barriers of space and time
quotes.source: John Cleese, quoted in Warren Berger, The Book of Beautiful Questions

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Do your own thinking, such as specs, design decisions and reviews of what agents wrote, in your protected blocks. Let agents run in the other hours and read their results in a batch afterwards.

concepts.concept: Stocks absorb swings; too big makes systems slow
concepts.name: Buffers

card.title: Buffers
idea: In Meadows's terms, a stock is an accumulated quantity, such as the inventory on a car lot. Stocks usually change slowly. Because they change slowly, they absorb swings between what flows in and what flows out, and the rest of the system is not forced to react to every change.
A buffer also costs something. If it is too large, the system becomes slow and expensive to run.
why: A system without buffers has to respond to every fluctuation as it happens, which means constant firefighting. A buffer evens out short-term variation.

stories.text: A car dealer keeps a lot of inventory. The inventory absorbs daily swings in customer demand, so the dealer does not have to reorder with every sale.

limits: Too big a buffer makes the system slow and costly.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: that gives me, you know, you almost want like a buffer, a queue. Sometimes that's actually more effective than just spawning off a couple of like a lot of sub agents to fix every single thing

quotes.text: Stocks usually change slowly. They can act as delays, lags, buffers, ballast, and sources of momentum in a system.
quotes.source: Donella H. Meadows, Thinking in Systems

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Put a queue between detecting problems and fixing them. Let agents log issues to a file, and have them or you review the file on a schedule. Keep the queue short enough that items do not go stale.

concepts.concept: Park non-urgent issues, solve them in a batch
concepts.name: The issues list

card.title: The issues list
idea: Both books give the same answer to non-urgent problems: write them down and handle them together later, so they do not interrupt the work or get lost.

Wickman's Issues List collects issues during the week. They are solved in the weekly 90-minute Level 10 Meeting using IDS: Identify, Discuss, Solve. Webb's version is a parking lot: dump your thoughts on paper, put off-topic items in a parking lot, and chunk the rest under three or four headings.
why: Handling each issue as it appears breaks concentration and gives each one the same weight. A list lets you pick the important ones and see which come up repeatedly.

steps: Wickman: log issues on the Issues List during the week.
Wickman: solve them in the weekly 90-minute Level 10 Meeting using IDS (Identify, Discuss, Solve).
Webb: dump thoughts on paper and put off-topic items in a parking lot.
Webb: chunk the remaining items under three or four headings.
