conversation.text: I don't actually tell it to fix the issue first. I tell it to append it to a document. And then every couple of days I look at it and I see actually these are all the same thing, you know,

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Have agents add problems they notice to a shared file instead of fixing everything at once. Review the file every few days, group the repeats, and fix each group once at its cause.

concepts.concept: One-way vs two-way doors and the cost of heavy process everywhere (Bezos)
concepts.name: One-way and two-way doors

card.title: One-way and two-way doors
idea: Sort decisions into reversible and irreversible, and use a different process for each. One-way doors need a slow, methodical process with consultation. Two-way doors should be decided fast: if the choice turns out wrong, you go back through the door.

The idea comes from Jeff Bezos, who also names the opposite failure. Large organisations tend to use the heavy process for most decisions, reversible ones included. The result is slowness, risk aversion and too little experimenting.
Parrish uses the same sorting in Clear Thinking: place a decision on two axes, how consequential it is and how reversible it is.
why: Most decisions can be undone cheaply. Treating them as irreversible slows everything. Treating a real one-way door as casual removes the chance to correct it.

method.intro: Four questions from the books for telling the doors apart.
steps: Cost to quit: what would it cost, in money, contract terms or effort, to abandon this path and return to where you started? If the exit cost is small, replace slow analysis with fast experiments. If unwinding is practically or legally impossible, the door is one-way.

Options lost: does this choice keep options open or close them? Reversible decisions preserve alternatives or produce information that creates new ones. Irreversible ones remove paths for good. Past a certain point, waiting also closes options: deadlines expire and partners walk away.

Size of the downside: is the worst case bounded? Reversible decisions have a limited downside. Irreversible ones carry tail risk such as insolvency, loss of life or liability that cannot be hedged. The books use the Challenger disaster as the example.

When feedback arrives: for reversible decisions, acting produces faster, cheaper and richer information than research, so act and learn. For irreversible ones, feedback arrives after the damage is done, so the analysis has to happen before.

limits: Duke's How to Decide does not use the terms one-way and two-way doors; they are Bezos's, quoted in Super Thinking and Clear Thinking.

conversation.speaker: Matt Pocock
conversation.text: some PRs are kind of like two-way doors which is you can merge it and then revert it

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: the oneway doors become two-way doors in a sense

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Mark each task before you hand it over. Two-way doors go to the agent with full autonomy. One-way doors (sending, deleting, publishing, paying, filing) stay behind your approval. Run the four questions on the last thing your agent did without asking you; if any answer points to one-way, move that action behind a gate.

quotes.text: If you walk through and don't like what you see on the other side, you can't get back to where you were before.
quotes.source: Jeff Bezos, quoted in Super Thinking

concepts.concept: Consequence × reversibility; decide irreversible things as late as possible
concepts.name: As late as possible

card.title: As late as possible
idea: Place a decision on two axes: how consequential it is and how reversible. Consequential, irreversible decisions are what Parrish calls lead dominoes. Make them as late as possible (ALAP), so you can gather information and keep your options open.
Small, reversible decisions go the other way: decide fast and learn by doing.
why: Waiting has a cost, but it buys information. When the cost to undo a decision is high, that information is worth more than the speed.

stories.source: Clear Thinking (from Michael Lewis, The Undoing Project)
stories.text: At Sunnybrook Hospital, next to Canada's busiest highway, trauma doctors were missing injuries during hectic evaluations. Dr. Don Redelmeier got them to pause briefly before finishing an evaluation.

steps: Plot the decision by consequence and reversibility.
If it is small and reversible, decide fast and learn by doing.
If it is consequential and irreversible, decide as late as possible, counting the cost of the extra analysis.
Act when Stop, FLOP or Know applies.

limits: Delay has its own price. Parrish asks you to count the cost of analysis, so ALAP is not a licence to postpone indefinitely.
card.tension: Parrish says to delay an irreversible decision. Flyvbjerg and Gardner (see Think slow, act fast) say to plan thoroughly while changes are cheap, freeze the plan, then deliver fast to shorten exposure. Waiting fits when new information is still arriving. Once the plan is tested and frozen, extra waiting mostly lengthens the risky phase.

conversation.speaker: Matt Pocock
conversation.text: do something that can't be easily walked back

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When a task will end in something you cannot take back, ask the agent to prepare everything but stop before the final step. Keep the final action for later, after more information has come in. Let it finish reversible steps right away.

quotes.text: If the cost to undo a decision is high, make it as late as possible.
quotes.source: Shane Parrish, Clear Thinking

concepts.concept: Small easy-to-quit decisions before a big one
concepts.name: Decision stacking

card.title: Decision stacking
idea: Judge a decision by what it costs to quit. Before a high-impact, hard-to-quit decision, make low-impact, easy-to-quit decisions that gather information first.
why: Many choices feel like permanent commitments but are not. Cheap steps in front of the big one show you what you would otherwise learn only after committing.

stories.text: People agonize over choosing a college as if it were a four-year commitment, but 37% of college students transfer, and nearly half of those transfer more than once.
Dating before committing to a relationship, and renting in a neighborhood before buying a house there, are examples of easy-to-quit decisions placed in front of a hard-to-quit one.

steps: Judge the cost of quitting or changing your mind.
If the cost is low, use the Menu Strategy: sort good options from bad, then pick quickly. If several options pass the Only-Option Test, flip a coin.
If the cost is high, find cheaper, easy-to-quit decisions to stack in front of it.
Apply the additional-information test: is there information at reasonable cost that would make one option clearly better or change your preference? If not, decide.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Before asking an agent for a large, hard-to-undo change, give it a small version first: one file, one record, one client, one week of data. Look at what happens, then decide on the full run.

quotes.text: Finding ways to make low-impact, easy-to-quit decisions in advance of a high-impact, harder-to-quit decision.
quotes.source: Annie Duke, How to Decide

concepts.concept: A setting where mistakes are cheap and reversible
concepts.name: The sandbox

card.title: The sandbox
idea: A sandbox is a setting where mistakes are inconsequential and easily reversed. You practise there and learn from mistakes while their cost is contained, which raises the odds of success when the stakes rise.
Parrish's example: new managers usually start with one person or a small team, so their failures stay small. Running a whole organisation comes later, when mistakes cost more.
why: Verification can turn some one-way doors into two-way doors. Where it cannot, a sandbox gives you the same freedom to try things without paying for failure.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: the oneway doors become two-way doors in a sense

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Give the agent a copy to work on: a draft folder, a test account, a branch, a duplicate document. Let it act freely there. Make the step that touches the real thing the only one that needs your approval.

quotes.text: A sandbox allows you to make and learn from mistakes while containing their cost.
quotes.source: Shane Parrish, Clear Thinking

concepts.concept: Plan and iterate slowly, deliver fast; point of no return
concepts.name: Think slow, act fast

card.title: Think slow, act fast
idea: Successful big projects spend a long time planning, testing and iterating while mistakes are cheap, then deliver quickly. Risk lives in delivery: the longer it runs, the more can go wrong.

The point of no return is where plans on paper or screen turn into physical commitment. Before it, changes are nearly free. After it, they are expensive, and the project sits in what the authors call the window of doom.
why: Planning is where iteration costs little. Delivery is where mistakes are paid for, so the aim is to move as much learning as possible into planning and then shorten delivery.

stories.text: Pixar lets directors spend years in development, trying and reworking ideas, because changes are cheap there. Flyvbjerg calls this Pixar planning: try, learn, do it again before committing.
For the Copenhagen Opera House, Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller cut architect Henning Larsen's planning time from five years to four ("You'll get four!"). Bitter clashes and defects followed.
Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao and 8 Spruce Street in New York were iterated digitally before construction, and the tower had no change orders.

steps: Think slow: experiment and simulate while still reversible.
Freeze the design before the point of no return.
Act fast after it, to shorten exposure.

limits: Slow planning has to be active testing, not dithering.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: it does take time to get to that point

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: For a high-stakes task, split the session in two. First let the agent plan, simulate and critique the approach as often as needed. Start execution only when the plan stops changing, and keep execution short.

quotes.text: Planning is a safe harbor. Delivery is venturing across the storm-tossed seas.
quotes.source: Flyvbjerg and Gardner, How Big Things Get Done

quotes.text: Getting to that point of no return is the real goal of strategic misrepresentation.
quotes.source: Flyvbjerg and Gardner, How Big Things Get Done

concepts.concept: Simulate before building: storyboards, CATIA
concepts.name: Pixels before bricks

card.title: Pixels before bricks
idea: Experimentation in planning needs a simulation of the project to come: storyboards, 3D models, mock-ups, digital twins. You change the simulation and see what happens, which is cheaper than changing the building.
why: Changes made in a simulation cost almost nothing. The same changes made after construction starts are the expensive ones.

stories.text: At Pixar, storyboards each cover about two seconds, so a ninety-minute film needs about 2,700 drawings. Strung together with dialogue read by employees, the whole film exists in crude form in three or four months (told by Pete Docter).
Frank Gehry used Dassault's CATIA aerospace software to simulate his 76-story tower at 8 Spruce Street in New York. He got a custom curtain wall instead of a flat one, with no change orders.

steps: Build a simulation: storyboards, 3D models, mock-ups, digital twins.
Iterate many times.
Keep what works and drop what does not.
Freeze the plan when it is complete and detailed.
Deliver fast.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Ask the agent to produce a rough version of the result before the real one: an outline, a mock layout, a sample of five records. Change the rough version until it is right, then ask for the full run.

quotes.text: Experimentation in planning requires a simulation of the project to come. With that, you can make changes in the simulation and see what happens.
quotes.source: Flyvbjerg and Gardner, How Big Things Get Done

concepts.concept: Simulators and digital twins as risk-free playgrounds
concepts.name: Digital twins

card.title: Digital twins

sources.authors: Ajay Agrawal, Joshua Gans, Avi Goldfarb

idea: A digital twin is a virtual copy of a real system, such as a simulator or a detailed model. Zero-tolerance fields build environments where hard constraints can be rehearsed without risk.
why: In fields where a real mistake is unacceptable, practice has to happen somewhere else. The copy gives that place.

stories.text: Astronauts spend 70% of their training in high-fidelity simulators, working through failures across several systems at once.
Nuclear recovery teams have built physical models the size of a tennis court to practise high-radiation work down to the second.
Sailing teams use AI-driven digital twins to test thousands of boat designs before touching any material.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: It's going to click around and try to use it like a real human.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Ask what a cheap stand-in for the real thing would look like: a test inbox, sample data, a role-played client or counterparty. Have the agent run against the stand-in first and report what broke.

quotes.text: a risk-free playground for innovation
quotes.source: Accenture, quoted in Power and Prediction

concepts.concept: Separate zones for experimenting and for executing
concepts.name: Playground and compliance zones

card.title: Playground and compliance zones
idea: Organisations divide work into two kinds of zone. In compliance zones, non-negotiable protocols apply and the job is to execute the plan. In the playground, where conditions are volatile and ambiguous, people may experiment, fail and adapt without asking permission.
Doshi and McGregor call these tactical and adaptive performance and treat them as opposites: one is the ability to execute the plan, the other the ability to diverge from it.
why: An organisation that optimises only for executing the plan freezes. Keeping the two zones separate lets experiments fail without touching the work that has to be exact.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: the codebase is designed in a way that there's really only one way to do something

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: exploring rewriting it in a different language just for fun

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Write down which parts of your agent setup are compliance zones (one allowed way, enforced by rules) and which are playgrounds (free to explore). Keep them in separate folders, branches or projects so the agent always knows which one it is in.

concepts.concept: A test can fail; a pilot is built to persuade
books: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
concepts.name: Test vs pilot

card.title: Test vs pilot

sources.book: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

idea: A pilot is a demonstration meant to build consensus for a rollout that has already been decided. A test is an experiment designed to produce disconfirming data, and it allows the plan to be dropped completely if the hypothesis fails.
why: A trial that cannot fail tells you nothing about the real rollout.

stories.source: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
stories.text: Sibony's pilot stores get extra funds and full management attention, so their results say little about how the real rollout will go.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: It's just a toy.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When you trial an agent on a new kind of work, pick ordinary and hard cases, including ones you expect it to get wrong. Decide in advance which result would make you drop the approach.

quotes.text: A test serves to refine a plan and help you decide whether to launch it or not.
quotes.source: Olivier Sibony, You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

concepts.concept: Cheap prototypes before rollout; J.C. Penney without a pilot
concepts.name: Prototype before rollout

card.title: Prototype before rollout

sources.authors: Bernard Garrette, Corey Phelps, Olivier Sibony

idea: Build cheap, rough versions of a product, service or process and test them with real users before committing money. Tim Brown of IDEO puts it this way: prototypes slow us down to speed us up.
why: A rollout without a pilot puts the full cost behind an untested idea.

stories.text: The McDonald brothers drew kitchen layouts in chalk on a tennis court and had employees act out the Speedee Service System.
Disney built full-scale mock-ups to test guest experiences.

Ron Johnson became CEO of J.C. Penney in 2011 and rolled out his new approach nationwide without pilot tests, spending about $120 million on boutiques. Revenue fell sharply and he was out after 18 months.

steps: Generate several solution concepts and pick the promising ones.
State what hypothesis the prototype tests.
Build low-fidelity prototypes: chalk, paper, cardboard.
Test with real users in their real setting before committing money.

limits: Tests in unrepresentative settings or with fans produce false positives.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Before asking an agent to process a whole batch or rewrite a whole system, write down what the first small version should prove. Run it on a few real cases, in the same setting the full run will use, and read the results yourself.

quotes.text: prototypes slow us down to speed us up
quotes.source: Tim Brown of IDEO, quoted in Cracked It!

concepts.concept: Small calibrated experiments before committing everything
concepts.name: Bullets, then cannonballs

card.title: Bullets, then cannonballs
idea: Bullets before cannonballs is Jim Collins's idea, retold by Parrish. Fire small, cheap experiments first. Commit full resources only after one of them hits.
why: A cannonball fired at the wrong target is expensive. Bullets show where the target is.

steps: Fire a bullet: a small, cheap experiment testing the hypothesis.
Check whether it hit.
If not, adjust and fire again.
When a bullet hits, fire the cannonball: put full resources behind the validated path.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Treat the first agent run on a new type of task as a bullet: small scope, easy to discard. Scale up the scope only after the result matches what you checked by hand.

concepts.concept: Deal-breakers written weeks before sign-off
books: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
concepts.name: The memo in the drawer

card.title: The memo in the drawer

sources.book: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

idea: Weeks before an irreversible milestone, such as a major acquisition, the team writes a confidential memo listing the deal-breakers that must be resolved. The CEO locks it away.
On the day of sign-off, the CEO reads the memo and checks the decision against it. This is a dialogue with an earlier self who was less caught up in the emotions and biases of the moment.
why: By the time of sign-off, momentum and sunk effort push toward yes. A list written earlier is not affected by that pressure.

method.source: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
steps: Weeks before the milestone, write down the deal-breakers that must be resolved.
Keep the memo confidential and locked away.
On the day of sign-off, read the memo and check the decision against it.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: I review the pull request after it's landed

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Before a long agent run, write down three to five conditions under which you would reject the result. Save them outside the chat. Read them before you look at the output, then check the output against them.

quotes.text: someone who has all the required expertise and her complete trust: herself.
quotes.source: Olivier Sibony, You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

concepts.concept: Bind yourself in advance against later impulses
concepts.name: The Ulysses contract

card.title: The Ulysses contract
idea: A Ulysses contract is a decision made while calm that stops you acting on impulse later. Ulysses had his crew plug their ears with beeswax and tie him to the mast, so he could hear the Sirens without steering onto the rocks.
Add trip wires: precommitments to turn back or change course at a set time, amount or circumstance.
why: Precommitment protects against tilt, sunk-cost thinking and escalation when pressure rises.

method.intro: Parrish's execution fail-safes.
steps: Set trip wires: precommit to action at a set time, amount or circumstance.
Empower others with commander's intent.
Tie your hands with physical, financial or legal barriers.

limits: Rigid or frustrating guardrails invite workarounds.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: How do I make it so that the code base makes this impossible?

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Turn the actions you never want taken without you into hard blocks or required confirmations in your tool settings. Then set trip wires, for example: stop and ask if the change touches client data or more than ten files.

quotes.text: past-us preventing present-us from doing something stupid
quotes.source: Annie Duke, Thinking in Bets

concepts.concept: Log every mistake; Ross's missed trade; Pain + Reflection = Progress
concepts.section: 9. Codifying process and learning from mistakes
concepts.name: The issue log

card.title: The issue log
idea: Pain plus reflection equals progress. Log every mistake, diagnose the root cause, and redesign the process so it does not repeat. Dalio also writes down his decision criteria each time he decides; over time they become what he calls recipes for decision making.
why: A mistake handled as blame teaches everyone to hide errors. A mistake logged with its cause becomes input for the next version of the process.

stories.text: In the early 1990s, Bridgewater's head of trading, Ross, forgot to place a client trade, which cost several hundred thousand dollars. Dalio did not fire him, because that would have taught everyone to hide errors. Together they built the Error Log, which later became the Issue Log.

In 2011 the Client Service department sent out memos with errors. New managers lacked synthesis skills, and people had become rubber stampers, while the top people who were supposed to taste the soup, meaning check that the work was excellent, were focused on other things.

method.intro: Dalio's five steps.
steps: Have clear goals.
Identify problems and do not tolerate them: log each in the Issue Log with severity and owner.
Diagnose to root causes: keep asking why, and separate proximate causes from root causes.
Design a plan around the problem: script who does what over time, like a movie.
Push through to results.

limits: Distinguish acceptable from unacceptable mistakes. The process fails if incapable people who will not reflect are kept. Written learning does not replace experience, and manuals fail when managers rubber-stamp instead of tasting the soup.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: interesting thing about that one is that I don't actually tell it to fix the issue first. I tell it to append it to a document. And then every couple of days I look at it and I see actually these are all the same thing, you know, and so

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Keep a plain file where every agent mistake gets one line: what happened, the root cause, and the fix (a rule, a check or a prompt change). Review it every few days and fix patterns, not single cases.

quotes.text: With time, my collection of principles became like a collection of recipes for decision making.
quotes.source: Ray Dalio, Principles

quotes.text: Pain + Reflection = Progress
quotes.source: Ray Dalio, Principles

concepts.concept: Ask experts for variables, what they see, and their process
concepts.section: 9. Codifying process and learning from mistakes
concepts.name: Asking an expert the right way

card.title: Asking an expert the right way
idea: Ask experts for the variables and the process behind their judgment, not for a single recommendation. A recommendation fits their situation. Their variables and process can be reused in yours.
why: Parrish writes that the goal is to gather information relevant to the decision, which requires understanding the why and how behind the data points.

stories.text: Person A asks a developer friend, "Whom should I hire?" Person B asks which skills matter, which can be learned, where to find people and how to test them. Person B is far more likely to hire well.
Parrish was stuck for weeks on a coding problem at an intelligence agency where he could not search the web. He learned to ask the experts around him.

method.intro: Three questions to put to an expert.
steps: What variables would you use to make this decision in my shoes, and how do they relate?
What do you know about this problem that I (or other people) do not? What can you see from experience that someone without it cannot? What do most people miss?
What would your process be for deciding in my shoes?

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When you want an agent to follow a practice you do not know well, interview the person who does. Use the three questions, put the answers into a skill or instruction file, and ask the expert to read the file back.

quotes.text: Our goal in decision-making is not just to gather information, but to gather information relevant to our decision.
quotes.source: Shane Parrish, Clear Thinking

quotes.text: That requires more than building an inventory of data points; it requires understanding the why and how behind those data points—the principles that good decision-makers use in this area.
quotes.source: Shane Parrish, Clear Thinking

concepts.concept: "We know more than we can tell": what manuals can't hold
concepts.section: 9. Codifying process and learning from mistakes
concepts.name: We know more than we can tell

card.title: We know more than we can tell
idea: Explicit knowledge can be written down. Tacit knowledge is felt and never fully captured in words. It builds through experience; the authors note that the word comes from experiri, to try.
why: Manuals, rules and skill files hold the explicit part. Some of the most valuable knowledge is the other part.

stories.text: When an adult gives a child what she thinks are complete instructions on how to ride a bike (put your foot on the pedal, push off, press down on the other pedal), the child typically falls on her first tries.
Art experts instantly felt, correctly, that a supposedly ancient Greek statue was a fraud, even though it had passed various scientific tests and even if they could not say why they felt that way.

limits: The source gives no method for capturing tacit knowledge. It names Gehry and Pixar's Pete Docter as people whose judgment comes from experience.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Expect instruction files to miss something. Where an expert's judgment matters, keep that person in the review step and let the agent's output be checked against examples they accept or reject.

quotes.text: much of the most valuable knowledge we can possess and use isn't like that; it is "tacit knowledge." We feel tacit knowledge. And when we try to put it into words, the words never fully capture it.
quotes.source: Flyvbjerg and Gardner, How Big Things Get Done

quotes.text: We can know more than we can tell.
quotes.source: Michael Polanyi, quoted in How Big Things Get Done

concepts.concept: "This is how we do it here": prototype, quantify, orchestrate
concepts.section: 9. Codifying process and learning from mistakes
concepts.name: The operations manual

card.title: The operations manual
idea: Turn one expert's way of working into a documented prototype and operations manual, so ordinary people get predictable results. Documentation says: this is how we do it here.
Gerber also argues for working on the business, not in it. Ray Kroc built a business that could work without him.
why: A business that depends on its owner doing the work cannot run without them. If the manuals run the work and people run the manuals, the business can.

stories.text: At E-Myth Worldwide, whoever ran a seminar had to clean the whiteboards afterwards. In their haste, people let the eraser fly over the edge, and blue ink streaked the white walls. Memos, Blue Ink On the Walls meetings, cleaning policies, cleaning teams, wall tours, spot checks and warning signs did not stop it. A clear Lucite collar, extending four inches out from each edge of every board, did. Gerber calls it the Prevent-a-Smudge System.
Sarah of All About Pies worked sixteen-hour days as a technician. She said: "But I can't even imagine what my business would be like without me doing the work."

steps: Innovate: find the best way to do the task.
Quantify the results and interactions.
Orchestrate: document each step in the operations manual.
State the purpose, the steps and the standards for process and result.
Write a manual for each position; technicians follow procedures while managers run the system.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: agree with you that they're like a skill is really much just process. I mean it's just at the end of the day a skill is just English or or language.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Treat a skill or instruction file as the operations manual for one job: purpose, steps, and what a good result looks like. Write it once from the best run you have, then have the agent follow it and update it when you correct a step.

quotes.text: Documentation says, "This is how we do it here."
quotes.source: Michael E. Gerber, The E-Myth Revisited

concepts.concept: Minimal prompts that point at the right cues, no interpreting
concepts.section: 9. Codifying process and learning from mistakes
concepts.name: Point attention, don't explain

card.title: Point attention, don't explain
idea: Give a learner a brief orientation, put them into the real work, and use minimal prompts that direct attention to information-rich cues without interpreting them.
why: Telling a beginner how everything works takes the work out of their hands. A prompt about where to look leaves the learning to them.

stories.text: Philip, a supervisor, did not tell Sita how everything worked or how to do her new tasks as she rotated through new areas. He did not ask her to analyze what she was experiencing. He suggested she focus somewhere new. He noticed she looked at what other people were doing, so in the boxing area he nudged her to look at technology. He noticed she treated defects as normal, so he encouraged her to watch the product as it came into the presort area. Once her attention was directed, she learned implicitly, and she had a wealth of skill to draw on when he later asked for process improvements.

Richard Magill, a kinesiologist at New York University, says not to ask a trainee how the ball was released. Ask: "Where were you looking to see what type of pitch it was?" The first question has the novice pick the action apart. The second only asks where they were looking.

steps: Give basic facts just before the work.
Put the learner in the real environment.
Limit explicit guidance to prompts that direct attention.
Leave time away from action for reflection.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When you teach an agent a task by example or review, point at the part to look at ("check the date format in column D") instead of rewriting the whole procedure. Keep standing instructions short and name what to attend to.

quotes.text: explicit instruction should only serve to direct the novice's attention to "information-rich" (that is, complex) aspects of context without interpreting them
quotes.source: Matt Beane, The Skill Code

concepts.concept: Map the engagement, collect experts' tips for each step
concepts.section: 9. Codifying process and learning from mistakes
concepts.name: Moments of truth

card.title: Moments of truth
idea: Knowledge can be codified; skills need practice. Map the client engagement, find the moments of truth, and collect experts' tips for each one.
why: Writing down what experienced people do at the points that matter lets less experienced staff start from their practice.

stories.text: One consulting firm held mandatory Monday-morning case presentations and kept videotapes of senior staff explaining interviewing and analysis.

steps: Flowchart the client assignment.
Mark each moment of truth.
Interview experienced people for tips on each stage.
Review client feedback and discuss it in departments.
Write the practices into operating methodologies.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Map your agent workflow step by step. At the two or three steps where a mistake costs most, ask the best person you know for their tips and add them to the instructions for that step.

quotes.text: While professional knowledge can be codified and easily shared, professional skills can only be developed through practice.
quotes.source: David H. Maister, Managing the Professional Service Firm

concepts.concept: Four levels: yourself, team, client, peers
concepts.section: 9. Codifying process and learning from mistakes
concepts.name: Four levels of debriefing

card.title: Four levels of debriefing
idea: A structured review after a piece of work, done at four levels: yourself, your team, your client and your peers.
why: Without a review, the lessons from a piece of work stay with whoever did it and are often lost.

steps: Debrief yourself: what went well and why, what did not and why. Keep a journal.
Debrief with the team, including juniors.
Debrief with the client: what could both sides have done better?
Debrief with peers in practice groups.

limits: Debriefing is unbillable, so unless it is mandatory it is postponed forever.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: chats I I often say is like a a treasure trove of context because that, you know, it's it's like the process materialized,

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: After a long agent session, ask the agent to list where you corrected it and what in the setup would have prevented each correction. Add the useful ones to your instruction file, and ask a colleague what they saw in the same work.

concepts.concept: Five steps after a mistake; Tales from the Crypt
concepts.section: 9. Codifying process and learning from mistakes
concepts.name: Discovery mode after a mistake

card.title: Discovery mode after a mistake
idea: After a mistake, people drop into defensive mode, with its threat response and narrow thinking. Webb's aim is to move them to discovery mode: curiosity and problem-solving.
why: Extracting the lessons makes it more likely that the same thing does not happen again, and it is good for colleagues' resilience and motivation.

stories.text: Astro Teller's team at X runs Bad Idea Brainstorms, premortems and Tales from the Crypt. Every time a project is shut down, the team writes up what they tried, what they learned and where the insights might be reused. Every year around Halloween, X hosts an event where people read these write-ups, in costume.
Mariah's company ran a retrospective after a spreadsheet error in a T-shirt forecast.

steps: Orient yourself: get into discovery mode.
Rally the crew without drama.
Map the terrain: what is going well amid this?
Chart a course: fix the immediate problem.
Land the learning: Why did this happen? What have we learned? What will we do differently?

limits: Discovery mode does not excuse repeated individual errors. Check system versus individual, and one-off versus pattern.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When an agent gets something wrong, start with 'what in the setup made this likely?' rather than with 'why did you do that?'. Then fix the immediate problem and ask for the lesson to be added to your instructions.

quotes.text: When something has gone wrong, it's vital to extract the lessons from the experience.
quotes.source: Caroline Webb, Leadership Intelligence

concepts.concept: Accept, learn, commit, repair; cover-ups cost more
concepts.section: 9. Codifying process and learning from mistakes
concepts.name: Owning a mistake

card.title: Owning a mistake
idea: Four steps for handling your own mistakes: accept responsibility, learn from it, commit to doing better, and repair the damage. Covering up a mistake costs more than the mistake.
why: Parrish's line is that the first mistake is expensive and the second one costs a fortune.

stories.text: Parrish's children broke a vase and hid the pieces in the trash. They were punished for hiding it, not for breaking it.
A sports general manager's mentor made an impulsive bad trade and then let it paralyze him.

steps: Accept responsibility.
Learn from it: reflect on thoughts, feelings and actions, and find root causes.
Commit to doing better with a plan or a safeguard.
Repair the damage.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: If you notice an agent run went wrong, say so in the session straight away and have the agent list what it changed. Reverse or repair first, then record a safeguard so the same slip cannot recur.

quotes.text: The first mistake is expensive; the second one costs a fortune.
quotes.source: Shane Parrish, Clear Thinking

concepts.concept: Mandatory postmortems; the Challenger's root cause
concepts.section: 9. Codifying process and learning from mistakes
concepts.name: Postmortems

card.title: Postmortems
idea: A postmortem is a mandatory review of a failure or project that asks why repeatedly until the root cause is found, and then fixes the root cause.
why: The proximate cause is usually not the one that matters. Fixing it leaves the real problem in place.

stories.text: DuckDuckGo requires a postmortem after every project.

In the Challenger disaster, the proximate cause was hot gas leaking past an O-ring in cold weather. Richard Feynman and the Rogers Commission found the root cause in NASA's organization and communication.

steps: Hold a postmortem, and make it mandatory.
Ask why repeatedly until you reach the root cause (the Five Whys).
Fix the root cause.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: and then you think about how to course correct the environment, right? Not not that single

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: For an agent failure that happens twice, ask 'why' five times down to a setup cause such as a missing rule, a vague instruction or no check, and fix that. For a one-off failure, a note is enough.

concepts.concept: Document the 20% that produces 80%; kill stupid rules
concepts.section: 9. Codifying process and learning from mistakes
concepts.name: Document the 20 percent

card.title: Document the 20 percent
idea: Document the 20 percent of processes that produce 80 percent of results, at a high level. Do not write a 500-page manual. Remove rules that exist only because of tradition.
why: Long manuals go unread and keep obsolete steps alive.

stories.text: A man watched his wife cut the back off a ham before putting it in the oven. She said, "It's tradition." Her mother said the same. Her grandmother said that once the pan was too small, and cutting the ham was the only way to make it fit.

A client had written 100 procedures. After the team agreed on seven core processes, each procedure became part of one of them, was better organized and could be transferred to all 120 employees. Wickman notes it would have saved time to identify the core processes first.
Lisa Bodell asks groups: "What stupid rule would you most like to kill?"

steps: Identify the core processes (usually a handful).
Document the 20% that produces 80% of results, at a high level.
Simplify: remove redundant steps and rules that exist only for tradition, and turn routine steps into checklists.
Put them in one manual and train everyone.
Review regularly.

limits: High-risk work such as surgery or flying needs full detail.

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: commands you know you should use right I think with the latest models you can

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Keep instruction files short. Once a model gets better, delete the steps it no longer needs, and review the file on a schedule. Ask periodically which rule in it you would most like to remove.

quotes.text: What stupid rule would you most like to kill?
quotes.source: Lisa Bodell, quoted in The Book of Beautiful Questions

quotes.text: Document the 20 percent that produces 80 percent of the results. In other words, document at a very high level. You should not be creating a 500-page document.
quotes.source: Gino Wickman, Traction

concepts.concept: Models and people validate the asker; certainty without truth
concepts.name: Sycophancy

card.title: Sycophancy

sources.book: Sycophantic AI (A Rational Analysis of the Effects of Sycophantic AI)

idea: Sycophancy is the tendency of AI models, and of people, to validate the beliefs of the person asking at the expense of the truth. Batista's source is a research paper, not a trade book.

His finding is that confirming feedback makes people more certain without bringing them closer to the truth. The feedback is drawn from the asker's own hypothesis, so each round of belief updating feeds back into itself.
why: Models trained on human ratings learn that agreement is rewarded. Subordinates learn the same thing from their bosses. In both cases the answer you get reflects what you already said.

stories.text: Batista asked Gemini-3-Pro: "I'd like to write a paper about sycophantic AI... What do you think?" It replied: "This is a strong, timely, and high-impact research topic."

Sharma et al. found that models change their answers when users push back. Wang et al. found that simple opinion statements from the user induced agreement with incorrect beliefs 63.7% of the time on average across seven model families, and up to 95.1%.

In Batista's experiment, 557 participants did the Wason 2-4-6 rule-discovery task, where you test number triples to find a hidden rule. Sycophantic AI suppressed discovery. Unbiased feedback produced about five times more discovery.

steps: Spot loops where the feedback mirrors the asker.
Replace confirming feedback with unbiased sampling.
Test hypotheses against disconfirming data.
Compare your belief updating with rational standards.

limits: Unbiased feedback frustrates people who prefer validation.

quotes.text: sycophancy distorts reality by returning responses that are biased to reinforce existing beliefs
quotes.source: Rafael M. Batista, Sycophantic AI

quotes.text: manufacturing certainty where there should be doubt
quotes.source: Rafael M. Batista, Sycophantic AI

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Do not ask the agent whether your plan is good. Ask it to list the ways the plan fails, or to argue the opposite case, and ask a second agent that has not seen your preferred answer. Treat any reply that praises the idea without a concrete objection as a sign that the question steered the answer.

concepts.concept: Two columns and counterexamples until the definition breaks
concepts.name: The Socratic method

card.title: The Socratic method
idea: Test a general rule against counterexamples until its hidden assumptions show and the definition has to be refined. Robertson presents this as a method anyone can run on a concept such as justice, honesty or quality.
The method ends in aporia: productive confusion in which shallow assumptions are replaced by real inquiry.
why: Sayings and rules are generalizations, and generalizations do not always hold. A person who memorized them can state them confidently and still fail to see where they break.

stories.text: Socrates meets Euthydemus near a saddlery by the Athenian Agora. Euthydemus is proud of his library of wise sayings. Socrates draws two columns on a wax tablet, Justice and Injustice. Lying, stealing and plundering go under Injustice. Then Socrates asks about doing these things to enemies in war. He asks about a general who lies to demoralized troops, about hiding a depressed friend's sword, and about tricking a sick child into taking medicine. Each case pulls an act across to the Justice column, and the first definition has to be revised.

steps: Draw two columns for a concept and its opposite.
Have the other person list obvious examples of the negative.
Present scenarios where those acts turn out to be good.
Move them across and revise the definition.
Test the revised definition with new scenarios.
Reach aporia: productive confusion that replaces shallow assumptions with real inquiry.

quotes.text: Euthydemus believed that he was acquiring wisdom and becoming a better person, by memorizing sayings about morality from the books of famous wise men.
quotes.source: Donald J. Robertson, How to Think Like Socrates

quotes.text: By their very nature, though, these were generalizations, which don't always hold true.
quotes.source: Donald J. Robertson, How to Think Like Socrates

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: It it draws those words out of you, right? or or at least it helps the agent understand your thinking so that they can propose those words to you and you can pick up and say yes exactly that.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When you give an agent a vague rule such as 'keep functions small', ask it for the cases where the rule would give a bad result, then rewrite the rule with those cases in it. The same loop works in the other direction: have the agent question your definition until the gaps in it show.

concepts.concept: Four minutes of questions only; reframes 80% of the time
concepts.name: The question burst

card.title: The question burst
idea: A Question Burst is a timed session in which people generate only questions about a challenge. There are no answers and no preambles.
why: Questions-only input loosens the existing frame and changes the feeling of being stuck. It also brings in other people's knowledge without loading them with the owner's assumptions.

stories.text: An executive running four business units held a Question Burst about toxic behavior in his division. He realized he had assumed the founders wanted a separate culture there. When he asked them, they were dismayed that it existed.
Intuit CEO Brad Smith describes a problem worth questioning as one that "makes your heart beat fast."

steps: Set the stage. Pick a challenge you care about. Invite two or three people with very different views. Describe the challenge in two minutes at a high level. The rules are questions only and no preambles. Note your emotional state (10 seconds).
Generate. Spend four minutes producing at least 15 to 20 questions, written verbatim, with no pushback. Add your own. Check your emotions again.
Unpack alone. Pick the questions that surprise you, are honest, and feel right. Expand them with the Five Whys. Plan actions for the next three weeks.

quotes.text: About 80 percent of the time, this exercise produces at least one question that usefully reframes the problem and provides a new angle for solving it.
quotes.source: Hal Gregersen, Questions Are the Answer

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Before you write the task for an agent, ask it for 15 to 20 questions about the problem and tell it not to propose solutions. Read the list yourself first and pick the three that surprise you. Answer those in the prompt before you ask for any work.

concepts.concept: Step back, imagine, then build
concepts.name: Why, what if, how

card.title: Why, what if, how
idea: Berger describes questioning as a sequence of three kinds of question. Why steps back and questions the situation. What if explores possibilities without worrying about implementation. How prototypes and tests.
why: The sequence puts some order on a process Berger calls chaotic and unpredictable. Each stage asks a different kind of question, so the person does not jump to building before the situation has been examined.

stories.text: In 1943, on vacation in Santa Fe, Edwin Land took photographs of his three-year-old daughter Jennifer. She asked why they could not see the picture he had just taken without having to wait. Land asked what if there were a darkroom inside the camera. That question led to the Polaroid instant camera.

steps: Why: step back and question the situation.
What if: explore possibilities without worrying about implementation.
How: prototype and test.

quotes.text: The Why/What If/How progression offers a simplified way to approach questioning; it's an attempt to bring at least some semblance of order to a questioning process that is, by its nature, chaotic and unpredictable.
quotes.source: Warren Berger, A More Beautiful Question

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Split an agent task into three prompts. First ask why the current behavior exists. Then ask for several alternative designs with no code. Only then ask for an implementation of one of them with a test.

concepts.concept: Value and descriptive assumptions behind arguments
concepts.name: Hidden assumptions

card.title: Hidden assumptions
idea: Reasons support a conclusion only through unstated assumptions. The book separates two kinds. Value assumptions are about how the world should be. Descriptive assumptions are about how the world was, is or will be.
why: The assumptions are invisible, yet the visible argument only makes sense because of them. Finding them is the way to judge whether an argument holds.

stories.text: An argument that police should crack down on public intoxication rests on a value assumption that favors collective responsibility over individual responsibility.
"Buy this model because it worked well before" assumes that quality stays the same across model years. That is a descriptive assumption about consistency over time.

steps: Find the conclusion and the reasons.
Ask what idea is needed to connect each reason to the conclusion.
Look for value assumptions by spotting value conflicts.
Look for descriptive assumptions about the world, behavior and consistency over time.
Judge whether the assumptions hold.

quotes.text: Hidden or unstated beliefs provide an invisible structure that permits the visible structure to make sense.
quotes.source: M. Neil Browne et al., Asking the Right Questions

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When an agent gives a recommendation, ask it to write down the conclusion, each reason, and the assumption that links them, labelled as value or descriptive. Check the descriptive ones against the repository or the logs before you accept the recommendation.

concepts.concept: Loaded wording; split-ballot tests
concepts.name: Loaded questions

card.title: Loaded questions
idea: Small changes in wording shift the answers people give. Payne's way to find out how much is to give different wordings to split samples and compare.
why: Every question frames to some degree. A question that states one side, names a prestigious person or begs for agreement will pull answers toward that side.

stories.text: "Isn't that loaded?" begs for agreement. "Is that loaded or not?" does not.
The 1948 Gallup poll overstated Dewey by 4.4 points. The 1936 Literary Digest poll overstated Landon by about 19 points.

steps: Clarify the issue: who, what, why, when, where, how.
Pick the structure: free answer, two-way (both sides stated) or multiple choice.
Remove loaded words, prestige names and one-sided statements.
Split-ballot test alternative wordings.
Run the wording checklist.

limits: Every question frames to some degree. Surveys report what people say when asked, which is not necessarily what they thought before.

quotes.text: When we speak of a question's being "loaded" or "leading," we imply that it may lead some respondents to give different answers than they would give to another wording of what was intended to be the same issue.
quotes.source: Stanley Le Baron Payne, The Art of Asking Questions

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Run the same question through an agent in two or three wordings in separate sessions, including one that states the opposite of what you hope for. If the answers differ, the wording is doing part of the work, and you should use the neutral version.

concepts.concept: Open questions with clients; check what they understood
concepts.name: Diagnostic questions

card.title: Diagnostic questions
idea: Open, non-judgmental questions let clients tell what actually happened. Leading questions shape the client's memory and answers. Aaron wants the lawyer to find out what the client already understands before explaining anything.
why: A client can nod along to an explanation and understand little of it. Without a question that checks, the lawyer does not find out.

stories.text: Corporate counsel tells a marketing VP that the spin-off agreement "may give rise to a non-frivolous preliminary injunction motion." The VP nods but understands little.

steps: Find out what the client already understands.
Ask open questions ("What happened next?") instead of leading ones ("You didn't agree to that, right?").
Translate legalese without dropping the risks.
Leave room for confusion or disagreement.
Confirm understanding without pushing for agreement.

quotes.text: there's no harm in the lawyer asking what the client has already gleaned.
quotes.source: Marjorie Corman Aaron, Client Science

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: After an agent explains a change or a plan, ask it to state in its own words what you asked for, and ask yourself the same about its summary. Ask the agent open questions such as 'what happened next?' when you debug, so it does not just confirm your guess.

concepts.concept: Avoid leading and critical questions
concepts.name: Humble inquiry

card.title: Humble inquiry
idea: Berger cites Edgar Schein: leaders should avoid questions that carry a judgment or a built-in answer. The questions you ask also set the direction of the group that hears them.
why: David Cooperrider's observation, as Berger reports it, is that organizations move toward the questions they ask.

stories.text: "Wasn't that movie awful?" is a leading question. "Do you think that movie lived up to the hype?" is milder. "What did you think of that movie?" is open.

steps: Before asking, check your motive: information, or steering?
Strip judgment and built-in answers.
Prefer what and how over accusing why or who.
Ask about strengths and possibilities (appreciative inquiry).

quotes.text: Schein urges leaders to avoid "leading questions, rhetorical questions, embarrassing questions, or statements in the form of questions." In particular, avoid critical questions
quotes.source: Warren Berger, The Book of Beautiful Questions

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Check your prompt for built-in answers, such as 'why is this code wrong?' or 'wasn't this a regression?'. Rewrite it as 'what does this code do in this case?'. The agent will often accept the premise in your wording.

concepts.concept: "What's on your mind? And what else? What's the real challenge?"
concepts.name: Taming the advice monster

card.title: Taming the advice monster
idea: The Advice Monster is the urge to give advice before you know the real problem. Bungay Stanier's remedy is to ask a few short questions and let the other person talk.
why: Advice given early is usually aimed at the first problem mentioned, which is often not the real one.

stories.text: Howard Beckman and Richard Frankel's 1984 study found that doctors interrupted patients after eighteen seconds on average.

steps: Notice the urge to give advice.
Ask: "What's on your mind?"
Ask: "And what else?"
Ask: "What's the real challenge here for you?"
Replace "Why did you do that?" with a what question.

quotes.text: Tell less and ask more. Your advice is not as good as you think it is.
quotes.source: Michael Bungay Stanier, The Coaching Habit

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Use the three questions on yourself before you prompt: what is on my mind, what else, what is the real challenge. Use them on the agent too when it jumps to a fix, by asking what else could cause the symptom and what the real problem is.

concepts.concept: "How do I know I'm right?"; believability weighting
concepts.name: Idea meritocracy

card.title: Idea meritocracy
idea: Dalio replaces deference to rank with an idea meritocracy: radical transparency and opinions weighted by believability.
why: His starting point is a change of question, from "I know I'm right" to "How do I know I'm right?". The aim is to get the right answer, whoever supplies it.

stories.text: At Bridgewater the Dot Collector let people rate everyone's contributions in meetings in real time, Dalio's included.

steps: Practice radical open-mindedness: move from "I know I'm right" to "How do I know I'm right?"
Seek out the most believable people who disagree and understand their reasoning.
Weight opinions by track record and by the quality of the reasoning.
Log errors and capture meeting feedback.
Run algorithms alongside human judgment.

quotes.text: I just want to be right—I don't care if the right answer comes from me.
quotes.source: Ray Dalio, Principles

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: When an agent and you disagree, ask the agent how it knows, and ask yourself the same. Settle the question with a test or a measurement and keep the result, so the next disagreement has a track record to point to.

concepts.concept: Schlesinger's timid objections; collect views before discussion
books: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
concepts.name: Groupthink

card.title: Groupthink

sources.book: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

idea: Groups suppress doubts, especially when a leader has already shown which way they lean. Sibony's answers are structural: change how a decision is made so that dissent is gathered before the group discusses.
why: Individuals who privately doubt a plan often stay silent when the group and its leader favor it.

stories.source: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
stories.text: At the Bay of Pigs in 1961, Arthur Schlesinger Jr. thought the plan was a mistake, yet he raised only a few timid objections.

stories.source: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
stories.text: Asch's conformity experiments show the same pressure in a laboratory setting.

stories.source: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
stories.text: Buffett's advisor is paid only if the deal does not happen, which makes the advisor's incentive point toward objection.

method.source: You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!
steps: Use red teams or war games against high-stakes proposals.
Run premortems with written individual reasons.
Collect individual views or votes before group discussion.
Allocate resources through portfolio reviews rather than champions.

quotes.text: Yet this renowned intellectual could not find it in himself to "do more than raise a few timid objections." He silenced his doubts and sided with the prevailing opinion of the group and its leader.
quotes.source: Olivier Sibony, You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake!

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Collect independent answers before you show one model's view to another. Ask several agents the same question in separate sessions, compare, and only then discuss. Tell the reviewing agent to find reasons the change should not merge, and do not tell it which way you lean.

concepts.concept: Truth-seeking norms for a group
concepts.name: Truth-seeking norms

card.title: Truth-seeking norms (CUDOS)
idea: Duke borrows the CUDOS norms of science, described by Robert K. Merton, as a charter for a group that wants to find out what is true.
why: A group with agreed rules about sharing data, judging claims and allowing dissent can discuss bad outcomes without blame.

stories.text: Robert K. Merton was born Meyer R. Schkolnick and, as a teenage magician, performed as "Robert Merlin." He went on to describe the norms of science. Duke mentions Heterodox Academy as a modern attempt to protect dissent, and her own poker group banned complaining about bad luck.

method.intro: CUDOS:
steps: Communism: share data with the group.
Universalism: judge claims by the same standards whoever makes them.
Disinterestedness: watch for conflicts of interest.
Organized skepticism: make dissent a normal part of meetings.

limits: Groups must opt in. Imposing the norms on people who have not agreed to them damages cohesion.

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Put the rules in the instruction file that the agent reads: report the data behind a claim, judge a claim the same way whichever tool produced it, say when the answer would benefit the agent's own earlier choice, and list objections as a normal part of every review.

concepts.concept: Choosing the worse option because it protects you
concepts.name: Defensive decisions

card.title: Defensive decisions
idea: In defensive decision making a person or group ranks option A as best, yet chooses an inferior option B to protect itself if something goes wrong. A negative error culture breeds it.
why: When blame falls on the person who made a mistake and not on the person who followed the safe procedure, people choose the procedure.

stories.text: A medical charity chose a big international accounting firm over a better local one, so that it would be safe from donor criticism.
After the 2010 volcanic ash cloud, flights were banned, a decision Gigerenzer discusses as an example of this pattern.

steps: Diagnose whether errors are used for learning or for punishment.
Shift from avoiding errors to managing uncertainty.
Remove incentives that reward safe, inferior choices.
Make admitting mistakes safe.

quotes.text: Defensive decision making: A person or group ranks option A as the best for the situation, but chooses an inferior option B to protect itself in case something goes wrong.
quotes.source: Gerd Gigerenzer, Risk Savvy

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: If an agent adds extra confirmation steps, hedges every answer or picks the most conventional design, ask it which option it thinks is best before it chooses. In your own review, check whether you accepted a change because it was safe to defend and not because it was best.

concepts.concept: Wanting an accurate map; outsider and selective-skeptic tests
concepts.name: Scout mindset

card.title: Scout mindset
idea: Galef contrasts two stances. In soldier mindset you defend your position and being wrong feels like defeat. In scout mindset you want your map of yourself and the world to be as accurate as possible, and a change of mind is an update to the map.
She also notes that militarized metaphors for argument, such as 'defending beliefs' or 'shooting down claims', reinforce the soldier mindset.
why: Soldier mindset has real benefits: comfort, self-esteem and a sense of belonging. That is why scout mindset is hard to sustain and needs concrete practices.

stories.text: In the Dreyfus affair, French army officers explained away the evidence that the handwriting on the spy's memo did not match Dreyfus. Colonel Picquart, who had believed in Dreyfus's guilt, studied the letters of another officer, Esterhazy, and saw that the handwriting matched the memo. He changed his view and identified Esterhazy as the real spy.

steps: Selective skeptic test: imagine the evidence supported the other side and ask how credible you would find it then.
Outsider test: imagine someone else stepped into your shoes and ask what you expect they would do.
Treat a change of mind as updating the map.

quotes.text: Being in scout mindset means wanting your "map"—your perception of yourself and the world—to be as accurate as possible.
quotes.source: Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Apply the selective skeptic test to the agent's output and to your own: if a test result or a review comment supported the opposite conclusion, would you accept it as readily? Ask the agent what you would advise a colleague to do in the same situation and compare that to your plan.

concepts.concept: At least three successes plus a good explanation
concepts.name: Believability

card.title: Believability
idea: Dalio weights a person's opinion by believability: a track record in that specific thing and good explanations when the person is probed.
why: It gives a rule for whose opinion to follow that does not depend on rank or confidence.

steps: Judge believability: at least three successes in the domain, and a clear explanation of the approach.
Decide your role: student (less believable), teacher (more believable) or peer.
With someone more believable, switch from arguing to asking.
Build believability-weighted decisions into tools and run them alongside human judgment.

limits: Believability is domain-specific.

quotes.text: I define believable people as those who have repeatedly and successfully accomplished the thing in question
quotes.source: Ray Dalio, Principles

quotes.text: great explanations of their approach when probed
quotes.source: Ray Dalio, Principles

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: I think at the end end of the day, it really just comes back to how much do you trust, you know, me and Matt, right?

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Keep a record of what each agent setup has done well, by task type. Trust an agent on a kind of task after it has succeeded at that kind at least three times and can explain how it worked, and review its work closely on kinds it has not yet done.

concepts.concept: Finish without handing leftovers up; responsibility grows
concepts.name: Earned autonomy

card.title: Earned autonomy
idea: Managers extend responsibility to people who take ownership, anticipate obstacles and finish without handing leftover work back up. Wiseman describes this as how people move from the edge of a team to its center.
Beane describes a related path in which trust grows by exposure: from shadowing to practice to independent work as trust is verified.
why: Responsibility given to someone who hands the leftovers back costs the manager more than doing the job. Responsibility given to someone who finishes reduces the manager's load, so more is given.

stories.text: Monica Padman went from babysitting for Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard to assistant, then to co-host and creative partner on Armchair Expert.
Jojo is a surgical technician at Santa Clara Valley Medical Center. She lays out instruments in the order needed and hands residents the right one before they ask.

Beane's examples include the chef Andre trusting his line cook and steward with closing the kitchen, sales executive Emily building trust with sales development reps such as Nadine, and the tinsmith and his apprentice.

steps: Do the job that is needed, beyond the job description.
Step up when leadership is unclear and step back when you are done.
Finish stronger: see it through and do not pass leftover work up.
Ask for help in a targeted, solution-oriented way.

quotes.text: The working relationship between experts and novices is a bundle of three Cs that humans need to develop mastery: challenge, complexity, and connection.
quotes.source: Matt Beane, The Skill Code

conversation.speaker: Lauren Tan
conversation.text: building skills and tools, you can get stuck in this mode where you're very low on that trust ladder, right? you don't

apply.label: Our adaptation
apply.text: Give an agent small tasks and require it to finish them, with tests run and loose ends listed, before it gets a larger one. Widen its permissions after it has done a kind of task without handing leftovers back to you. Beane's progression suggests letting it watch the work, then do supervised work, then work alone.

concepts.concept: Work on the business, not in it; a business that works without you
concepts.name: Work on it, not in it

card.title: Work on it, not in it
idea: Gerber says an owner should treat the business as a product that is designed, and not as a place where the owner does the work. The book's example is Ray Kroc, who built a systems-dependent business and not a people-dependent one.
The business runs on documented procedures. Technicians follow the procedures, managers run the system, and the owner works on the system.
why: A business that depends on one person's hands stops when that person stops. A prototype that is documented can be copied.

Build the prototype through innovation, quantification and orchestration.
Write manuals for each position.
Let technicians follow the procedures and managers run the system.

concepts.concept: Standards that follow past results erode; keep them absolute
concepts.name: Drift to low performance

card.title: Drift to low performance
idea: When standards follow past performance, they erode. Meadows calls this archetype drift to low performance: a reinforcing loop of eroding goals lets a system drift down. A sudden drop gets a reaction, but a slow drift gets accepted.
Her examples include falling market share in a business and eroding quality of service at a hospital.
why: Perception of past performance often has a negative bias, so each cycle sets the next standard lower than the last.

stories.text: After the Windsor Castle fire, The Independent on Sunday wrote of "the ominous feeling that the Windsor fire is symptomatic of the country at large, that it stems from the new national characteristic of ineptitude." Meadows uses the passage as an example of how a decline narrative gets accepted. Separately, she notes that physical capital drains through depreciation and needs constant reinvestment.

method.intro: The way out:
steps: Keep performance standards absolute.
Let standards be enhanced by the best actual performances instead of the worst.
Reinvest faster than depreciation.

quotes.text: Allowing performance standards to be influenced by past performance, especially if there is a negative bias in perceiving past performance, sets up a reinforcing feedback loop of eroding goals that sets a system drifting toward low performance.
quotes.source: Donella H. Meadows, Thinking in Systems

concepts.concept: Shortcuts as loans: technical, management, design debt
concepts.name: Technical and management debt

card.title: Technical and management debt
idea: Shortcuts taken now accumulate debt that has to be paid back later through rewrites. Weinberg and McCann extend the idea from code to management debt, design debt and diversity debt.
why: The cost of a shortcut is deferred, so it is easy to take too many. Slow decline also goes unnoticed, as in the boiling frog.

steps: Treat shortcuts as deliberate, temporary loans.
Schedule time to pay the debt down.
Set standards that prevent new debt.
Watch for slow decline so you do not become the boiling frog.

limits: Some debt is fine when speed matters, as long as it is paid down.

quotes.text: if you prioritize short-term code fixes, or "hacks," over long-term, well-designed code and processes, then you accumulate debt that will eventually have to be paid down by future code rewrites and refactors.
